The PR's stated goal is that "dash/folder creator can access the dashboard/folder that they've just created". The `Check` path now falls through to the DB when the cached permission map does not contain the requested resource. `List`, however, was only changed to use `getCachedIdentityPermissions` first; it still returns whatever the cache holds when there is a hit, with no equivalent "cache hit but resource not present -> requery" step. For a user whose cached permission scope map predates the new dashboard/folder, `List` will silently omit the newly created item until the cache expires (`shortCacheTTL`, 30 s). The same `cachedPerms` -> DB fallback used in `Check` needs to apply when the List is asked about a name/folder that is not present in the cached scope map.

No test verifies the denial cache is populated when Check returns false

The new branch `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` is the only place where `permDenialCache` is ever written to (other than the test's manual `Set` in `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`). The existing `TestService_Check` "should deny user without permission" case asserts `resp.Allowed == false` but does not check `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)` afterwards. As a result, if a future change accidentally removes or breaks the `Set` call, the denial cache would silently stop being populated and no CI signal would fire. The test should explicitly read `s.permDenialCache` (e.g. via `userPermDenialCacheKey`) and assert the entry was written.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem causes React warnings and list update issues

Inside the rules.map(...) switch, the previously-rendered GrafanaRuleLoader had `key={key}` (using `key` destructured from `ruleWithOrigin` at line 152), but the new GrafanaRuleListItem element at line 157 is rendered without any key prop, and the destructured `key` is now unused. React will emit "Each child in a list should have a unique 'key' prop" warnings for every grafana rule rendered here. More importantly, without a key React cannot correctly match components across reorders or insertions, leading to incorrect component identity, lost local state in children, and unpredictable DOM/state reuse in the large rule lists this view exists for. Restore the `key={key}` prop on the GrafanaRuleListItem element.

false_negatives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Comment about ruler preload is stale after removal of ruler prefetch

Lines 81-82 read 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded'. The matching code, `dispatch(alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...))`, was deleted in this PR, and the enclosing local variable `cacheAndRulerPreload` no longer does any ruler preload - it only upserts Prometheus groups cache entries. Both the comment and the variable name still claim to be about ruler preloading and will mislead future readers. Update the comment and rename the variable (e.g. `cachePriming`) to reflect that only Prometheus groups cache priming is happening now.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range variable queries will now be incorrectly split

The new code interpolates queries via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)` before the `querySupportsSplitting` check is evaluated. The existing check at line 287 (`!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)`) is supposed to prevent queries containing `$__range` from being split, with a comment explaining that otherwise the interpolated `$__range` value is wrong because it gets interpolated against the split (sub-request) time range. After this change the interpolation runs first on the original full range, so `$__range` is already replaced with a literal value (e.g. `2d`) by the time `isQueryWithRangeVariable` is consulted, and the function returns `false`. As a result, queries that were previously excluded from splitting will now be split, and each sub-request will receive the same `$__range` value computed from the full time range instead of the per-chunk range. The corresponding code path is hit by `runSplitQuery` and by `runShardSplitQuery` (which calls `runSplitQuery` for each shard group), so this affects both splitting modes. The PR adds no test for a `$__range` expression to guard this behavior.

New interpolation test reuses the outer `datasource` variable but bypasses beforeEach mocks

The 'Interpolates queries before execution' test reassigns `datasource` after the `beforeEach` has already installed `applyTemplateVariables` and `languageProvider.fetchLabelValues` mocks. The new datasource is created with a custom `replace` function and is intended to exercise the real `applyTemplateVariables`, but the previous test file conventions (see 'Interpolates queries before running' at line 110) explicitly mock `applyTemplateVariables` to control interpolation. Mixing the two approaches in the same `describe` block means the behavior under test is not really 'does querySplitting interpolate before execution?' but 'does it call applyTemplateVariables that happens to interpolate via this replace function?'. The test is also fragile to any future change in the real `applyTemplateVariables` (e.g. handling of `$__range`) because it does not stub it explicitly. Consider mocking `applyTemplateVariables` here too, or moving this case to a dedicated test that documents the use of the real implementation.

No test covers the $__range case after the interpolation change

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' test only exercises `$__auto` and `$step` and uses a `replace` mock that does not touch `$__range`. There is also no existing test in either `querySplitting.test.ts` or `shardQuerySplitting.test.ts` that asserts what happens to a query containing `$__range` when it goes through `runSplitQuery` or `runShardSplitQuery`. Given that the change moves interpolation ahead of the `querySupportsSplitting` check, a regression test using `$__range` (or `__range`, `${__range}`) is needed to ensure the existing 'do not split range-variable queries' invariant still holds.

Queries are interpolated twice in the sharded path

`runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` for every target on line 52, and then `splitQueriesByStreamShard` forwards those (already-interpolated) targets into `runSplitQuery`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again for each target of every sub-request (line 299 of `querySplitting.ts`). The shard test was updated to assert this redundancy: `expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5)` for a single-target request that issues 4 sub-requests. Beyond the wasted work, the second interpolation runs over expressions that have already been mutated to add `__stream_shard__` selectors; if any of those new literal substrings happen to collide with template-variable syntax used by the templateSrv, the result is non-obvious. Either `runShardSplitQuery` should pass already-interpolated targets through and skip the re-interpolation in `runSplitQuery`, or the interpolation should be done only inside `runSplitQuery` as before.

Stale comment about $__range interpolation

The comment in `querySupportsSplitting` states that `$__range` 'is interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange'. After this PR, interpolation is performed on the frontend inside `runSplitQuery` (and inside `runShardSplitQuery`) before the split happens, using the full time range from `request.range`. The comment is now misleading and contradicts the new behavior; it should be updated to describe the new interpolation point and the implication for `$__range` queries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

false_positives.candidate:
FromContext doc comment does not match implementations

The new `FromContext` doc comment says it returns a new contextual Logger that has 'this logger's context plus the given context', but the two implementations in the diff (`grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` in `pkg/plugins/log/logger.go` and `TestLogger.FromContext` in `pkg/plugins/log/fake.go`) only use the passed-in context and ignore the receiver's state. Either the comment should be corrected to describe the actual behavior (e.g. 'returns a Logger derived from the given context') or the implementations should be updated to also include the receiver's existing context.

No test for new ContextualLoggerMiddleware

The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` was extracted from the old `InstrumentationMiddleware` but no corresponding test file was added. The `instrumentContext` helper, which sets the `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname` attributes on the request context, should be covered by tests to ensure these attributes are correctly set for QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics, and that they are absent for the streaming methods (SubscribeStream, PublishStream, RunStream) which intentionally pass through.

Test function name not updated after rename

The test function is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` after the file and middleware were renamed to `metrics_middleware.go`/`MetricsMiddleware`. The function name should be renamed to `TestMetricsMiddleware` to match the new naming and avoid confusion for future maintainers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows exceeding the configured device limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` does `CountDevices(...)` and then, if below the limit, performs an unconditional INSERT. Two concurrent requests on different server instances can both observe `count < deviceLimit`, both pass the gate, and both INSERT, causing the actual device count to exceed `deviceLimit`. The PR makes no attempt to take a row-level lock, use an atomic INSERT-with-cap, or wrap the count+insert in a transaction. In multi-instance / HA deployments the limit becomes approximate and can grow without bound under load. This needs to be either documented as best-effort or enforced atomically.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device tagging moved to synchronous, authentication now fails on device-limit error

Previously the call to `anonDeviceService.TagDevice` ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and any error was logged; authentication always succeeded. After this change, `TagDevice` runs synchronously on the request context, and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned from `Authenticate`, causing the authn flow to deny anonymous authentication entirely. This is a significant behavior change that is not described in the PR description, has no docs/release-notes update, and offers no way for the caller to distinguish "limit reached" from any other auth failure. This should be an explicit, documented breaking change; consider a feature toggle or a dedicated error type that the authn layer can map to a friendly response (e.g., 429) rather than a generic auth failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the DB call, defeating the device limit on retry

In `tagDeviceUI`, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called, and the entry is not removed on failure. The cache TTL is 29 minutes. With the new synchronous behavior, a device rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` on the first request is silently allowed on any subsequent request within 29 minutes, because `tagDeviceUI` returns `nil` on a cache hit before ever consulting the DB. An attacker (or a normal user) who is denied once can simply retry and pass; after ~29 minutes the denial returns. The cache should be set only after a successful DB write, or explicitly invalidated on failure, otherwise the new `device_limit` setting is bypassable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now performs extra synchronous DB work per request

When the limit is enabled, every `TagDevice` call (which is now on the auth path) runs an extra `CountDevices` SELECT against `anon_device` before the INSERT/UPDATE. The local cache (`localcache.New(29*time.Minute, 15*time.Minute)`) only mitigates repeated tags of already-known devices; new devices always incur the extra query. This adds latency to the anonymous auth hot path. Consider gating the count behind the cache as well (e.g., only check the limit when the cache misses, or only enforce the limit on first-seen devices), or otherwise documenting the performance trade-off.

New auth.anonymous.device_limit setting is undocumented

A new configurable option `device_limit` is added to the `[auth.anonymous]` section and exposed to the frontend via `AnonymousDeviceLimit`. No change is made to Grafana's configuration documentation (`docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/index.md` or equivalent), no sample/commented entry is added to `conf/defaults.ini`, and the PR description is empty (no "Why do we need this feature?", no linked issue, no release notes). Operators have no way to discover that the setting exists, what value to pick, what 0 means, or that it changes the semantics of anonymous authentication from "always allowed" to "denied when limit reached".

No test for the authn flow when the device limit is reached

`client.go` now propagates `ErrDeviceLimitReached` out of `Authenticate`, but no test in `impl_test.go` (or a `client_test.go`) verifies that behavior. The new feature is supposed to deny authentication when the limit is hit, yet the existing `TestIntegrationDeviceService_tag` uses `deviceLimit = 0` (via `setting.NewCfg()` defaults), so it never exercises the limit code path through the auth client. At minimum, a test that sets a small `AnonymousDeviceLimit`, attempts `Authenticate` for a new device, and asserts the returned error, is required.

No test that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only verifies that a NEW device ID is rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` once the limit is hit. It never exercises the intended happy path of `updateDevice`: tagging an already-known, still-active device when the limit is reached should succeed (the device's `updated_at` should be refreshed in place). Without that test, regressions in the `WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ?` clause (e.g., the Postgres `$N` placeholder bug) would not be caught.

device_limit has no validation; negative values silently disable the limit

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` accepts any int64 from the ini file. The store treats anything `<= 0` as "no limit" (`if s.deviceLimit > 0`). A misconfiguration such as `device_limit = -1` (or a stray negative value) silently disables the feature without any error, log line, or warning. Negative values should be rejected at startup with a clear error, or at least clamped to 0 with a warning.

updateDevice SQL breaks on Postgres

The `updateDevice` function hardcodes `?` placeholders, but Grafana supports Postgres (which uses `$1, $2, ...`). `CreateOrUpdateDevice` in the same file branches on `s.sqlStore.GetDBType()` and emits `$N` placeholders for Postgres; `updateDevice` does not. When the device limit is reached and the deployment is Postgres, this UPDATE will fail to parse and the error returned to `TagDevice`/`Authenticate` is a raw SQL syntax error rather than `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The new device-limit feature will be effectively broken on Postgres.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level with nil errors

The new cleanup code logs every routine operation at Error level: r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) and r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y). Cleanup runs as a background job that should never be considered an error; previously this code did not log at all. The "err" field is always nil at these sites (errors are returned early), so the messages convey no actionable signal but will spam the error log on every cycle, making real errors harder to find and tripping error-rate alerts in monitoring. The level should be Info or Debug, and the meaningless "err" field should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker frequency silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The diff changes the cleanup ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, a 10x increase in how often the entire cleanup job (including annotation cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs and query history) runs. This change is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the deadlock fix. It will significantly increase database query load and log volume (especially given the new Error-level logging above) on every Grafana instance. Either it should be reverted, made configurable, or at minimum called out in the PR description / release notes.

false_positives.candidate:
Annotation cleanup tests now skipped under -short

The tests `TestAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` have been renamed to `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` and now call `t.Skip` when `testing.Short()` is true. Previously these tests always ran. Any developer or CI step that runs `go test -short ./pkg/services/annotations/...` will lose coverage of the new split-statement cleanup logic (including the SQLite 32767-batch path that was added). If the intent is to keep this as a required test, the skip should be removed or the package should ensure integration tests are always run in CI.

Full annotation IDs and full WHERE condition dumped into logs on every batch

Each batch emits "ids", ids (the entire int64 slice) and the raw SQL condition into the log. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize set in the tens of thousands (the new test case uses 32767), this produces extremely verbose log entries on every cycle. Logging thousands of integers is not useful and increases log volume/cost; an only the count and a truncated identifier (or none) should be logged.

O(n^2) string concatenation when inlining IDs into SQLite DELETE

In `deleteByIDs`, when SQLite is used with a batch size greater than 999 the IDs are concatenated into a single SQL string via repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`. This is O(n^2) in the number of IDs and, with the new default-style batch size of 32767 (and tests using batch sizes in that range), produces hundreds of thousands of intermediate string allocations per batch. Using `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join` after pre-formatting) would be linear and cheaper.

Stale/incorrect "condition must be supplied" error message

`fetchIDs` checks `if condition == ""` and returns `fmt.Errorf("condition must be supplied; cannot fetch IDs from entire table")`, but `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` passes a non-empty condition that begins with `NOT EXISTS (...)` followed directly by the LIMIT clause with no `WHERE` keyword. The error message implies a missing WHERE clause would result in a full-table SELECT, but the guard will still fire whenever any caller forgets to prepend a WHERE. This is a minor wording/logic mismatch and could mask a real bug in future callers; the message should describe the actual invariant (e.g., "condition cannot be empty") or be removed in favor of a real precondition.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete uses d.Log instead of log with structured fields

In `Delete`, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used, while Create/Update/DeleteCollection/DeleteCollection all use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` where `log` includes `name`, `kind`, and `method` fields. As a result, any klog calls inside `Storage.Delete` (or inside the async legacy `Delete`) won't carry the structured `kind=`, `method=delete`, `name=` context, making it harder to filter logs by operation. Also, the async legacy `Delete` goroutine inherits this weaker logger (it references the outer `ctx`) so legacy delete errors logged downstream will be missing context too.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Wrong metric function in DeleteCollection async legacy block

The async goroutine for the legacy `DeleteCollection` records the result via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. This is the legacy call, so it should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` (matching the corresponding calls in Create/Update/Delete). The current code will mislabel legacy failures as storage failures, breaking SLO dashboards.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kind label uses object name instead of options.Kind in Delete

The Delete success branch records `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` where the third argument is the resource `name` parameter, while every other call site uses `options.Kind`. The metric label is supposed to be the Kind, so this passes a different value into the same label, producing inconsistent time series in the dual_writer_* metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy failures are not logged

Inside the goroutines that perform the asynchronous legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the only signal on failure is the metrics counter (`recordLegacyDuration(... true ...)`); there is no `log.Error(...)` call. If unified storage diverges from legacy (the very thing mode 3 is supposed to mitigate), operators will see no log line and no test will detect the failure because errors are swallowed. Add `log.Error(err, "async legacy ... failed")` (or equivalent) inside each goroutine after the legacy call.

Async legacy writes inherit cancelled request context

Each async legacy call derives its context from the incoming `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. When the API caller cancels or times out, the parent `ctx` is already cancelled, so the child context is cancelled immediately and the legacy write never happens. The PR description frames legacy writes as a "safe measure" to keep legacy store in sync, but under request cancellation (which is common for slow upstream) the legacy side will drift from unified storage silently. The async legacy write should be derived from a non-cancelled context (e.g. `context.Background()` with timeout) so it survives caller disconnection.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes

`Destroy` calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()` immediately, but there is no synchronization with the goroutines launched by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. If a shutdown happens while async legacy writes are still pending (within their 10 s timeout), they will run against destroyed backends, producing confusing errors or panics. Consider tracking the goroutines with a `sync.WaitGroup` (or similar) and waiting for them in `Destroy` (with a bounded timeout).

Mode3 read tests do not verify legacy is bypassed

The PR's stated semantics for mode 3 are: "reads (get, list): only use unified storage". `TestMode3_Get` and `TestMode3_List` never call `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "Get", ...)` / `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "List", ...)`. The Mode1 Get test does check this for storage (`us.AssertNotCalled(...)`); the analogous assertion for mode 3 (legacy must not be called) is missing. A bug that silently falls back to legacy on reads would not be caught.

Mode3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3's defining behaviour is that writes go to storage synchronously and then to legacy asynchronously. None of `TestMode3_Create`, `TestMode3_Update`, `TestMode3_Delete`, or `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` actually asserts the legacy mock was called. `setupLegacyFn` sets up `m.On(...)` expectations but there is no `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (and the async goroutine may run after the test function returns). The Create and Update tests register legacy expectations that may simply never be exercised, and the Delete/DeleteCollection tests don't even register them. Without synchronization (e.g. wait group, channel, or retry on the mock) plus `AssertExpectations`, a regression that removes the async legacy call entirely would still pass the test suite.

TestMode3_Get creates a local prometheus registry

`TestMode3_Get` calls `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally even though a package-level `p` already exists (used by every other test in the file, and now exclusively by `TestMode1_Get` after this PR). The local registry is unused by the assertions in the test and just creates inconsistency. Use the package-level `p` like the rest of the suite.

Wrong metric function in Create error path

When `d.Storage.Create` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure is on the unified storage side. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures in the metrics, polluting dashboards/alerts built on `dual_writer_*` metrics. The call should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match the symmetric success branch on line 48.

Wrong metric function in Update error path

When `d.Storage.Update` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though this is a storage failure, not a legacy one. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses `recordStorageDuration`. The error branch should do the same: `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Otherwise storage Update failures are silently misattributed to legacy.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent callers may redundantly re-read the manifest

After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache`. If multiple goroutines call GetWebAssets concurrently before the cache is populated (e.g., during startup in non-dev mode), each will serialize on the write lock and redundantly read assets-manifest.json from disk and re-decode it. The proper double-checked locking pattern requires a second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write lock (gated on `cfg.Env != setting.Dev`, since dev mode intentionally bypasses the cache), so that only the first caller does the I/O and subsequent callers return the cached value. As written, every concurrent caller that arrives between the RUnlock at line 43 and the Lock at line 48 pays the full disk-read cost.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No test exercises the concurrent path; the race fix is not regression-protected

The PR adds synchronization to fix a data race on the global `entryPointAssetsCache`, but no test file is added or modified (the changed-files list contains only `pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go`). Without a concurrent test run under `go test -race` that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines, future refactors could easily reintroduce the race — for example by reverting to a bare read of the global, by moving the `defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()` above the assignment on line 70, or by replacing the RWMutex with a non-sync primitive. A test that spawns N goroutines all calling GetWebAssets and waits on a sync.WaitGroup would have caught the original race and will catch any regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Confusing logic in enableSqlExpressions that always returns false

The new `enableSqlExpressions` function uses unnecessarily complex logic to always return false. The variable `enabled` is assigned `!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, meaning `enabled` is true when the flag is OFF — the opposite of what the name suggests. Both branches then return `false`, so the feature flag value is completely ignored. This is confusing and error-prone: a future maintainer may attempt to 'fix' what looks like an inverted boolean bug and inadvertently re-enable SQL Expressions, reintroducing CVE-2024-9264. A safer implementation would simply be `return false` with a comment explaining that SQL Expressions are permanently disabled due to CVE-2024-9264, making the intent unambiguous and removing any appearance that the feature flag is consulted.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests verifying SQL Expressions are disabled

This is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that hard-disables SQL Expressions, but no tests are added to `pkg/expr/reader_test.go` (or any new test file) to verify that a `QueryTypeSQL` query now returns the expected 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' error. Without a regression test, a future change could re-enable the SQL code path silently. At minimum, a test that constructs an `ExpressionQueryReader`, calls `ReadQuery` with a `QueryTypeSQL` JSON payload, and asserts the returned error would lock in the security fix.

SQL command construction path still reachable if reader check is removed

`NewSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` still calls `sql.TablesList` which constructs a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)`. Currently this is unreachable because `reader.go` rejects `QueryTypeSQL` upfront, but the code path remains live and `TablesList` is still an exported function in `pkg/expr/sql`. If the `enableSqlExpressions` gate in `reader.go` is later weakened or removed (e.g., because someone misreads the confusing boolean logic in `enableSqlExpressions`), the original DuckDB-based command construction — including the string interpolation that contributed to CVE-2024-9264 — would be reachable again. Consider making `TablesList` and `NewSQLCommand` return an 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' error directly rather than relying solely on the reader-level gate, so the vulnerable code path cannot be reached even if the reader check is bypassed.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition introduced by removing BuildIndex global lock

The diff removes `b.cacheMu.Lock()` at the start of `BuildIndex` and only acquires it around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` assignment. As a result, two concurrent calls for the same key can both pass through `GetIndex` (which takes only an RLock and returns nil for a missing entry) and concurrently execute `BuildIndex` for the same key. Both will then race on `b.cache[key] = idx` with last-writer-wins. At startup this is reachable whenever a gRPC request lands while `searchSupport.init` is still building a namespace, and at runtime it is reachable whenever a search request races with `getOrCreateIndex`. Previously the lock held for the whole build prevented this entirely; now the cache can contain stale indexes, and the second build allocates a whole new bleve index (potentially on disk under `b.opts.Root`) that is then orphaned. The fix in `getOrCreateIndex` only acquires the index after the build returns, so callers that retrieved the earlier index write to an index that is no longer the cached one. A per-key mutex, singleflight.Group, or sync.Map with double-checked loading is needed to make this safe.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex still discards the traced context

This PR's stated goal is to "fix trace propagation by passing span contexts down". `searchSupport.init`, `searchSupport.build`, and `backend.GetResourceStats` were all updated from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...` so the new context flows into downstream calls. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` is the only other function touched in this PR that still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")`. The span exists but the returned context is dropped, which is the same bug the PR claims to fix. Apply the same `ctx, span :=` change here for consistency, even though the builder closure currently captures its own context from the caller.

Data race on outer `err` variable inside errgroup goroutine

Inside `searchSupport.init`, the errgroup goroutine does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, where `err` is the outer named variable declared just above the `for` loop. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) > 1`, multiple goroutines write to the same outer `err` concurrently. The race is benign here because the goroutines also `return err` and `group.Wait()` is reassigned to `err` immediately after, but it is still a data race per the Go memory model and a race detector run will flag it. Use `_, _, buildErr := s.build(...)` and return `buildErr`.

NewResourceServer leaks backend resources when Init fails

When `s.lifecycle.Init(ctx)` succeeds (which is what opens the SQL database connection in the SQL backend's `initLocked`) but a later step in `s.once.Do` (search init or `initWatcher`) fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `(nil, err)` without calling `s.Stop`. There is no `defer` to call `s.cancel()` or to call `s.lifecycle.Stop`. The SQL backend's database handle (`b.db`), open bleve file indices on disk under `b.opts.Root`, and any goroutines started during partial init are left running. A successful subsequent `NewResourceServer` call for the same backend then races against the leaked resources. Add a cleanup path on the failure branch.

NewResourceServer now fails if init fails, breaking callers that relied on lazy init

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously and returns `(nil, err)` on any init failure (lifecycle hook, search init, or watcher startup). Previously, init was deferred to the first RPC and a server object was always returned. Callers (e.g., the storage server module wiring) that construct the server, register it, and then serve traffic will now fail at construction time on any transient init failure. The PR description explicitly flags this as a question for the reviewer ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") but the chosen behavior change is significant: a slow/unhealthy database at startup, a corrupt bleve index directory, or any failure in `s.lifecycle.Init` / `s.search.init` will now prevent the storage server module from starting at all. Either keep the lazy path (with a context that isn't the per-RPC deadline) or ensure every caller of `NewResourceServer` is updated and tested for the eager-failure case.

Postgres support in the storage-server integration test is skipped rather than fixed

The diff adds a `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` with a TODO to fix the test. This PR changes the most fundamental part of the storage server lifecycle (where initialization runs) but provides no new test coverage for that change, and the only integration test that exercises `InitializeModuleServer` with `modules.StorageServer` is now skipped on the very backend the storage server is required to support. Combined with the eager-init behavior change in `NewResourceServer`, this leaves a regression in postgres untested. Either unblock the test or add a dedicated test that exercises `NewResourceServer` -> eager init -> a Search gRPC call end-to-end on a real backend.

Reordering search.init before initWatcher loses events written in the gap

The diff reorders `Init` to call `s.search.init(ctx)` first and then `s.initWatcher()`. Previously the broadcaster/stream was attached before the search index was built. `searchSupport.init` builds the index from a snapshot taken via `GetResourceStats`/`ListIterator` that returns when its last `ListIterator` completes. Any writes that hit the SQL backend between that point and when `s.initWatcher` starts (and calls `WatchWriteEvents` -> `listLatestRVs` to compute its `since`) are NOT in the search index snapshot AND are NOT yet visible to the watcher, so they are silently dropped from the search index. With the old order, the watcher (poller) was already running, so its `since` was at or after the build's last read RV. The fix is either to keep the original order or to pass an explicit `since` (the last RV read by `searchSupport.init`) into `initWatcher` so its polling starts at that RV.

Trace propagation fix is incomplete in backend.go

The PR description says "Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down" and updates `GetResourceStats` from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...`. Other methods in the same file (`WriteEvent` at line 158, `ReadResource` at line 353, `ListIterator` at line 388, `poll` at line 664, `resourceVersionAtomicInc` at line 718) still use `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, discarding the returned context. Downstream DB calls made with the outer `ctx` (not the traced context) therefore do not appear as children of these spans. Either the fix is intentionally scoped (in which case the PR description is misleading) or these should all be updated to `ctx, span :=`.

successful index build still logs duration but index size is constant

The new `s.log.Info("search index initialized", "duration_secs", end-start, "total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs())` reports `total_docs` from `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()`, which iterates `b.cache` at the moment init's search goroutines return. Because `searchSupport.init` uses `errgroup.Group` with `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)`, multiple `BuildIndex` calls may still be in flight when init's group.Wait() returns only the FIRST error; if no error occurred, `group.Wait` returns nil and the cache may not yet contain every index that was being built (the cache assignment happens inside `bleveBackend.BuildIndex`, after `builder(idx)` and `idx.Flush()`, and is only protected by `cacheMu`). Worse, if any one of those last in-flight builds fails after some succeed, the log line is never reached but partial state is reported earlier. This is a minor observability concern, but combined with the bleve lock-removal race it understates how many indexes were actually built.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of an IDP with alias 'alias' (literal) instead of the alias variable

In the loop creating IDPs the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)`. The argument is the literal string "alias", not the loop variable (e.g. `alias`). This will attempt to remove an IDP with alias "alias" at cleanup time, which does not exist. The pattern is pre-existing in testCacheIDPByOrg, but the PR copies it into the new test instead of fixing it. The fix is to use `alias` (the variable) rather than the literal string.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache is over-invalidated because wrapped isEnabled() on idpById returns false whenever the linked org is currently disabled

In registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated), the `original` argument is `idpById` from getById(model.getInternalId()), which is wrapped via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...) and overrides isEnabled() to additionally check the linked organization's runtime status (provider.isEnabled() && org.isEnabled() && super.isEnabled()). The `updated` argument is the raw model passed to update(...), whose isEnabled() only reflects the model's ENABLED field. When the IDP is linked to an org that is currently disabled or removed, getLoginPredicate().test(original) returns false (wrapped isEnabled returns false because of the org status), while getLoginPredicate().test(updated) returns true (raw isEnabled is true). Neither early-return branch matches, so the login cache is invalidated even though the update did not change the IDP's static login configuration. The cache state would still be functionally correct (the wrapped isEnabled at read time filters out the IDP), so the impact is wasted work rather than incorrect results, but the optimization described in the Javadoc ('IDP is currently a login IDP' vs 'currently NOT a login IDP') is undermined for org-linked IDPs. Consider obtaining the underlying model for the comparison (e.g., look up cached via realmCache.getCache().get(internalId, CachedIdentityProvider.class) or idpDelegate.getById) rather than the org-aware wrapped instance.

Misleading comment in remove(): comment refers to a cache lookup that actually goes to the JPA delegate

The comment '//lookup idp by alias in cache to be able to invalidate its internalId' sits next to the use of `storedIdp`, which is populated from idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) — i.e. a JPA delegate lookup, not a cache lookup. The refactor hoisted idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) out of the `if (isInvalid(cacheKey))` branch into a local variable used by both branches of the if/else, but the wording still implies a cache read. The lookup never consults the cache.

testCacheIDPForLogin does not cover organization-level changes that affect login availability

The new test exercises IDP create/remove/update and the cache invalidations they cause. It does not exercise organization-level changes that affect IDP login availability: disabling an organization, removing an organization, or unlinking an IDP from its organization. None of these trigger registerIDPLoginInvalidation/OnUpdate, so the login cache may stay stale until some unrelated IDP change triggers an invalidation. The wrapped isEnabled() at read time filters out IDPs whose org is disabled, so correctness is preserved, but the cache freshness behavior in those scenarios is untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider does not return a BouncyCastle provider

`AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the provider backing the default JCA keystore (typically SunJCE on a standard JDK, or the BC provider only if it has been registered globally). The method is named `getBouncyCastleProvider` and the interface contract in `CryptoProvider` documents it as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, so any caller that relies on this method to obtain BouncyCastle (e.g. to invoke BC-specific APIs) will silently get the wrong provider. Since the authz-client is intended to avoid the BouncyCastle dependency, the method should return `null` or the implementation should be renamed/document so the contract is not violated.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER discards encoder results

The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write to them, and immediately discard the results. The actual encoding used for the return value is produced by the subsequent `writeDerSeq(...)` call. The dead code is confusing and wasteful, and should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding returned as -1 but not handled by callers

`readLength()` returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (length byte 0x80). Callers like `readSequence()` then evaluate `while (length > 0)`, which immediately exits and returns an empty list, while `readInteger()` would pass `-1` to `read(int)`, which throws an `IOException` with a misleading 'EOF found reading -1 bytes' message. Indefinite-length encoding is not legal in DER and should be rejected explicitly (e.g. throw an `IOException` for `0x80`) instead of being silently passed through.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding order() to CryptoProvider is a binary-incompatible API change

A new abstract method `int order()` has been added to the `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` interface. This is part of the public `keycloak-common` artifact: any out-of-tree implementation of `CryptoProvider` (extensions, integrators, third-party crypto providers) will fail to compile/link against the new interface. This should be called out in the release notes / migration guide so downstream users know they must add an `order()` method to their implementation. Additionally, consider providing a `default` implementation (e.g. `return 0;`) to make the change source-compatible for the common case.

false_positives.candidate:
Test does not cover the case where R/S is shorter than the curve length

The test only exercises the round-trip with default JDK-generated EC keys and a fixed message. For typical ES256 signatures the BigInteger byte arrays of R and S are 32 or 33 bytes long, so the `qLength > bytes.length` branch of `integerToBytes` is never entered and the `return bytes` bug on line 160 of `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` is not detected. A test that explicitly constructs DER signatures where R or S is shorter than `algorithm.getSignatureLength() / 2` (e.g. by zero-padding the high byte) would trigger the `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` described above. Without such a test the bug will not be caught by CI.

integerToBytes returns wrong array in left-padding branch

In the `qLength > bytes.length` branch of `integerToBytes`, the method allocates a left-padded `tmp` array of `qLength` bytes and copies `bytes` into it, but then returns `bytes` (the original shorter array) instead of `tmp`. The left-padding is therefore never applied. This causes `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` to call `System.arraycopy(r, 0, concatenatedSignatureValue, 0, len)` with `r.length < len`, which throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` whenever the BigInteger R or S value happens to be shorter than `qLength` (e.g. when the high byte of the value is 0, which is statistically possible for ECDSA signatures). The fix is to return `tmp` on line 160.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Listener no longer cleans up authz data for V2-only realms

The event listener for RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent is now wrapped in a check for Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (the V1 feature). For realms that enable only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2, the listener never runs at all, so on client/role/group removal no cleanup of the corresponding resources in the admin-permissions client occurs. Resources representing deleted clients (and any scope-based policies referencing them) become orphans in the authorization store. The change is needed to avoid UnsupportedOperationException from ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled, but the V2 side does not implement equivalent cleanup, so data integrity is now degraded. Either a V2 path that deletes the orphaned resources in the admin permissions client should be added, or the wrapper should also include the V2 feature and dispatch to a V2 cleanup.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission can return the resource type name as a client id

ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission iterates all resources whose type is 'Clients' and adds resource.getName() to the returned set for each resource the admin has the scope on. This includes the 'all-clients' resource whose name is the literal string 'Clients' (set in AdminPermissionsSchema.init). So when an admin has the scope for all clients, the returned set contains the entry 'Clients', which is not a client internal id. Callers expecting a Set<String> of client ids will then attempt to look up a client with id 'Clients' and fail. The method should skip the type-level resource (or filter its name) so only actual client ids end up in the set.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE risk when all-clients resource is missing

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when there is no resource for the specific client, the code falls back to loading the type-level resource via AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource(...). That method can return null (e.g., when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false, the type is unknown, or no resource has been created for the type yet). The subsequent authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource).isEmpty() call then dereferences a null resource and throws NullPointerException. The code should guard against a null 'resource' before passing it to findByResource, returning false instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unused imports, unused logger, and dead private method

ClientPermissionsV2 imports org.keycloak.authorization.model.Scope (line 27) and the static AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE (line 46) but neither symbol is referenced anywhere in the file. It also declares 'private static final Logger logger = Logger.getLogger(ClientPermissionsV2.class);' (line 51) and a private getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) method (lines 262-272) which is never called. These should be removed to keep the new file clean; if getEvaluationContext is intended for later use it should be marked as such or actually wired into the permission evaluation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Mixed JUnit 4 / JUnit 5 imports in same test

PermissionClientTest imports 'static org.junit.Assert.fail' (JUnit 4) while every other fgap test in this PR (e.g. UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest) imports 'static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.fail' (JUnit 5), and the rest of PermissionClientTest already uses JUnit 5 annotations (@Test, @AfterEach from org.junit.jupiter.api). The mixed import is inconsistent and can lead to confusing failure signatures if the wrong Assert is ever picked up; switch to org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.fail to match the surrounding test suite.

canMapRoles / canMapCompositeRoles / canMapClientScopeRoles skip the admin-role check

Other V2 overrides such as canManage(ClientModel) and canManageClientScopes() first short-circuit on root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS), then fall back to the schema permission. canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission(client, ...) and never consult the admin roles. As a result, a caller that holds the MANAGE_CLIENTS realm role can manage/configure/view a client (and the V2 canView chains through canConfigure which calls canManage) but cannot map roles on it. This is inconsistent with the rest of the V2 evaluators and may surprise administrators; verify whether the V1 canMapRoles also gated on the admin role and, if so, restore the hasOneAdminRole short-circuit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Breaking change of exit code for recreate upgrade (4 -> 3)

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` was changed from 4 to 3, and a new `FEATURE_DISABLED` constant took the value 4. Any external automation (CI/CD scripts, GitOps pipelines) that key off exit code 4 to detect 'recreate upgrade needed' will now interpret it as 'feature disabled' instead, taking the wrong branch. The previous public exit-code contract (4 == recreate, per the prior docs and code) is broken without a migration note. Either keep 4 as recreate and pick a new value for FEATURE_DISABLED, or call out the breaking change explicitly so downstream users can update their scripts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Caution claim that the Operator will fail is inaccurate

The CAUTION block states: 'While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' But the very next NOTE in the same section documents a default behavior that works without the feature: 'the update strategy defaults to mimicking Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior'. The Operator does not 'fail' when the feature is disabled; it only fails if the user supplies the new `spec.update.strategy` field without enabling the feature. The wording should be tightened to make that conditional explicit (e.g., '...must be enabled if you set `spec.update.strategy`').

Exit code 4 description is misleading

The documentation for exit code 4 says 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible. The feature `rolling-updates` is disabled.', but the actual behavior (see `printFeatureDisabled()` in `AbstractUpdatesCommand.java` and the new `testFeatureNotEnabled` in `UpdateCommandDistTest.java`) is that the command never runs at all and prints 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled.' Scripts that rely on exit code 4 to decide between rolling and recreate will be misled: the deployment may be perfectly eligible for a rolling upgrade; the code only signals that the user must enable the feature first. The row should describe 'Command unavailable: preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled' (or similar), not 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible'.

No test for `check` subcommand with feature disabled

The new `testFeatureNotEnabled` only exercises the `metadata` subcommand (line 48: `@Launch({UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.NAME})`). The same feature gate was added to `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` (UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java lines 46-50), but there is no equivalent test for the `check` subcommand to confirm it also prints 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled.' and exits with code 4. A symmetric test (e.g., `testFeatureNotEnabledForCheck`) should be added.

YAML example uses non-YAML placeholder `Recreate|<not set>`

The CR example shows `strategy: Recreate|<not set>`, which is not a valid YAML scalar and will be rejected (or stored as the literal string 'Recreate|<not set>') if a user copies the snippet verbatim. The pre-existing doc had the same issue and the PR was a natural place to fix it. The placeholder should be replaced with a valid value (e.g., a separate example with `strategy: Recreate` and a NOTE explaining that omitting the field means default behavior).

picocli.exit() does not halt execution; rely on `return` only

In `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` (and the identical block in `UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()` at lines 46-50), the disabled-feature branch uses `picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED);` followed by `return;`. picocli's `CommandLine.exit(int)` only stores the requested exit code; it does not terminate the JVM or the run() method. The `return` is what actually prevents `validateConfig()` and the rest of the body from running. The code is correct, but the chosen API is misleading and a future refactor that drops the `return` (or calls `picocli.exit()` from a helper) would silently execute the rest of the command. Consider using `throw new ParameterException(...)` or letting the framework short-circuit, so the early-return contract is enforced rather than incidental.

printFeatureDisabled hard-codes the feature name in the error message

`printFeatureDisabled()` hard-codes the literal string 'rolling-updates' in the message: `printError("Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled.");`. The method is now a reusable helper in `AbstractUpdatesCommand` and other preview-gated commands may follow the same pattern; if any of them is gated on a different feature, the message will be wrong. Either parameterize the method with the feature name, or rename it to something feature-specific (e.g., `printRollingUpdatesDisabled()`) so misuse is obvious.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert exit code 4

The new `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr error message; it does not verify that the process actually exits with `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` (4). If a future change accidentally leaves the default 0 exit code, this test would still pass. The other tests in this file (e.g., `testCompatible` at line 75) do call `assertEquals(0, result.exitCode())`, so adding a similar exit-code assertion here would be consistent and catch regressions in the exit-code wiring in `UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() in V2 treats VIEW permission as sufficient for MANAGE actions

canManage() returns true when the caller has either VIEW or MANAGE permission on the all-groups schema resource: return hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE). This means an admin with only VIEW permission on Groups can call requireManage() (no-arg) at GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup and successfully create new top-level groups, even though they explicitly lack MANAGE. This is also inconsistent with canManage(GroupModel group) in the same file (lines 73-80), which only permits MANAGE, not VIEW. In V1, canManage() required only the MANAGE_USERS admin role, so VIEW_USERS-like capabilities were correctly excluded. The docstring was updated to mention VIEW, but the behavior contradicts least-privilege and makes 'has VIEW on all groups' grant more capability than 'has MANAGE on a specific group'. The new testManageAllGroups test grants MANAGE explicitly and therefore does not cover or detect this case.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes resource UUID where group ID is needed

Inside the lambda passed to resourceStore.findByType(), the code calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the granted set. However, hasPermission(String groupId, ...) does findByName(server, groupId), which looks up the resource by NAME (the group's ID), not by the resource's database UUID. In V2 per-group resources are named with the group ID, but getId() returns the resource's own UUID - these are different. findByName will always return null for these lookups, and hasPermission will fall back to the schema (all-groups) resource for every iteration. Consequences: (1) An admin with VIEW_MEMBERS permission only on a specific group will get an empty granted set, so the user search will not filter by groups and no users will be visible (in V2 mode, testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers and testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers in the new test class would fail). (2) When the admin has the VIEW_MEMBERS scope on the all-groups schema resource, the granted set is populated with the resource UUIDs instead of group IDs, making the value unusable downstream. The V1 analogue in GroupPermissions correctly passes the Resource object directly and strips the name prefix; the V2 version should use groupResource.getName() both in the hasPermission call and when adding to the granted set.

GroupResource.getManagementPermissions/setManagementPermissionsEnabled will crash if invoked under V2

false_positives.candidate:
Comment about `<!-- -->` placement is unclear and possibly wrong

The block comment on lines 96-97 reads `// Sanitizer will add them when there are double curly braces`, where 'them' is ambiguous (HTML comments? entities?). The actual rationale is that the OWASP policy inserts an HTML comment to separate ambiguous sequences, not specifically 'when there are double curly braces'. Anyone reading this code in the future will not understand the dependency on OWASP's exact placeholder format. A short, accurate comment (and ideally an OWASP API that exposes skipped content) would prevent future breakage.

HTML_TAGS regex misses closing tags and uppercase tags The regex `Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` only matches opening tags whose name consists of lowercase ASCII letters. Closing tags like `

` and uppercase tags like `
` will not be detected. The `containsHtml` decision gates whether POLICY_SOME_HTML or POLICY_NO_HTML is applied to translations, so any English source that contains only closing tags or uppercase tags will be treated as having no HTML. The translation will then be sanitized with POLICY_NO_HTML, which will escape those tags (e.g., `

` becomes `</p>`), making them appear as literal text in the rendered UI.

Locale-suffix regex doesn't accept digits, blocking non-Latin locale files

The path translation `replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` only matches locale suffixes that consist entirely of ASCII letters, hyphen and underscore. BCP-47 derived locales that include digits (e.g. `es_419`, `en_US_POSIX`, or numeric region sub-tags) will not match the regex, so `replaceAll` is a no-op and `englishFile` equals `file`. The code then tries to load the same file as its own English source and either crashes (because the regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*` excludes digits) or silently validates a translation against itself. The character class also includes the underscore, which is fragile when suffixes themselves contain underscores (e.g. `zh_CN`).

Magic string `<!-- -->` removed unconditionally from sanitized output

After `policy.sanitize(value)` and `unescapeHtml4`, the code does `sanitized = sanitized.replace("<!-- -->", "")`. This hardcoded string is presumed to be what the OWASP sanitizer inserts to disambiguate content, but the OWASP library is not part of the project's source, so this is an undocumented and version-dependent contract. If a future OWASP release inserts a different placeholder (e.g. `<!---->` without space, `<!---->`, or HTML-escaped form), the replacement will silently stop working and the sanitizer output will be reported as illegal HTML for any translation containing double curly braces. Worse, the replacement is applied unconditionally even when the original `value` legitimately contains the substring `<!-- -->`, in which case legitimate comments are silently stripped and the comparison will erroneously consider the value 'clean'.

Missing English file throws RuntimeException, crashing the verifier

When the English counterpart file cannot be found (e.g., for a brand new translation that has no `_en.properties` source yet, or for a locale like `es_419` whose suffix contains digits and so does not match the locale-detection regex on line 75), the FileInputStream constructor throws FileNotFoundException, which is caught and rewrapped as `new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + englishFile, e)`. Because `verifySafeHtml` does not declare any checked exceptions and `verify()` only catches `IOException`, this RuntimeException propagates out of the Mojo, bypassing the normal MojoExecutionException error path. The result is that any file whose English source is missing will abort the entire verification, instead of producing a clean message.

No test coverage for closing/uppercase HTML tags or English missing file The new tests cover duplicate keys, illegal HTML tags in an English file (`illegalHtmlTag_en.properties`), a non-English file with `` (noHtml_de.properties) and a changed anchor (`changedAnchor_de.properties`). They do not cover the scenarios where the English source contains only a closing tag (e.g. `

`), only uppercase tags, a translation that is missing keys present in the English source, an English source file that is missing entirely, or translations where the order of identical anchors differs. Given that the verifier's correctness depends on these edge cases, at least one negative test for 'English has only closing tags -> POLICY_NO_HTML is wrongly applied' should be added.

POLICY_SOME_HTML and POLICY_NO_HTML should be static final

`PolicyFactory POLICY_SOME_HTML = new org.owasp.html.HtmlPolicyBuilder()...toFactory();` and the corresponding `POLICY_NO_HTML` are declared as instance fields on a class that has only instance state (`file`, `messages`). They should be `private static final` so they are constructed once per JVM rather than per VerifyMessageProperties instance and so that the class clearly expresses they are constants.

replaceFirst in santizeAnchors operates on a value mutated by previous iterations

In `santizeAnchors`, the Matcher is constructed from the original `value`, so `matcher.find()` continues to identify anchors at their original positions even after the body of the loop has replaced earlier occurrences in `value`. When the value contains the same anchor twice (e.g. two `<a href="X">`), the first iteration replaces the first occurrence in the (still identical) value, but the second iteration tries `value.replaceFirst(englishMatcher.group(), "")` on the already-shortened string, which no longer contains that anchor at that position. The replacement becomes a no-op, the loop advances to the next match in the original string, and the second anchor ends up compared against the next English anchor (or causes a spurious 'did not find anchor tag' message). The logic should either rebuild the Matcher after each replacement or use indices rather than `replaceFirst` to align modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding abstract method to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory breaks existing implementations

`getShortcut()` is added to `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` without a default implementation. Although the interface lives in `server-spi-private`, external grant-type extensions routinely implement it (every Keycloak extension that adds a custom grant does so). Adding a non-default method is a compile-time breaking change for any such extension and a runtime ClassCastException/NoSuchMethodError for those loaded by reflection before recompilation. Consider providing a default (e.g. returning the first two characters of `getId()`, or `UNKNOWN`) so that existing custom factories keep working.

No integration coverage for the encoded access-token format

The PR introduces a new on-the-wire format for `jti` (e.g. `onrtrt:<uuid>`) and changes every test helper that asserts on `Details.TOKEN_ID`. There is no integration test that round-trips through `createClientAccessToken` -> JWT signing -> token manager decode to confirm that `TokenManager` and the introspection / UMA / account endpoints all still recognise tokens minted under the new format. Because the matching helper in `AssertEvents` is also broken, the existing tests cannot act as a safety net for this either. At least one integration test exercising a token-end-to-end (login + introspection + refresh) is needed.

Refresh path double-lookups the map

`getShortcutByGrantType` first does `grantsToShortcuts.get(grantType)`, and if null, then potentially recomputes the entry and then does a second `grantsToShortcuts.get(grantType)`. For an unknown grant type this is two map lookups; for a known one it's also two if you count the assignment on line 116. Minor, but more importantly the asynchronous refresh logic in `getGrantTypeByShortcut` walks the entire `OAuth2GrantType` factory stream every time the cached map misses - on a server with many grant types this is wasteful, especially as `findFirst` after `filter` could short-circuit earlier. Consider caching the per-shortcut lookup result the first time it is computed.

Removed Context copy constructor

The `Context(Context context)` copy constructor that was previously on `OAuth2GrantType.Context` is deleted. The diff message is misleading - the constructor was not just unused inside these files, but is part of a private SPI that custom grant extensions may rely on (e.g. to clone context to a sub-task or to wrap it for retries). The deleted constructor also closes the door on the previously available pattern of reusing one `Context`. Either keep it, deprecate it, or document clearly that this SPI is consumed by external extensions.

Shortcut-collision validation does not catch duplicate shortcuts

The startup validation only compares the sizes of `grantsByShortcuts` and `grantsToShortcuts`:

    if (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()) { throw ... }

If two different grant factories ever happen to use the same shortcut string (or, more subtly, two factories with both the same ID and the same shortcut), both `HashMap.put` calls collapse into a single entry per map and the sizes remain equal, so the check passes silently. The resulting collision means `encodeTokenId` may pick the wrong grant shortcut for a given grant, or vice versa `getTokenContextFromTokenId` may mis-decode the grant type - both of which have downstream behaviour implications (e.g. session-lookup optimisation in #37662). A more thorough check should iterate the entries and assert that each shortcut and each grant id is unique (e.g. by counting distinct keys vs. insert count).

Stale comment about clientSession note remains

The diff `sessionContext.setAttribute(Constants.GRANT_TYPE, ...)` is added next to the unchanged `clientSession.setNote(VC_ISSUANCE_FLOW, ...)`. There is no comment explaining why both are needed (the note stores the VC flow marker, the attribute stores the grant type for the encoder). The PR would benefit from a single-line comment indicating the dual-purpose nature of these two assignments so the next reader does not delete the attribute thinking it duplicates the note.

Unchecked cast to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory in postInit

`postInit` performs `(OAuth2GrantTypeFactory) factory1` for every factory returned by `getProviderFactoriesStream(OAuth2GrantType.class)`. The stream type only guarantees `ProviderFactory<OAuth2GrantType>`, not `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory`. Any third-party extension that registers an `OAuth2GrantType` without implementing `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` will cause a `ClassCastException` at server startup. Either filter on `instanceof OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` or guarantee the relationship contractually.

getShouldUseLightweightToken widened from package-private to public

`getShouldUseLightweightToken` is changed from package-private to `public static`. This is required for the new encoder to reach it, but it is also expanding the public surface of an unrelated class in ways not strictly required by the PR (a small package-private helper on a wrapper class would have been enough). Either keep it package-private and move the lightweight-token resolution into `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper` itself, or accept the API widening and document it.

After a successful recovery code match, the authenticator looks up the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) which prefers getFederatedCredentialsStream().
