processAction reads generatedAtTimeString and generatedCodesString via formParamsMap.getFirst(...) and immediately compares them with .equals(...). If either parameter is missing, .getFirst returns null and the .equals call throws NullPointerException. The subsequent line uses Long.valueOf(generatedAtTimeString), which throws NumberFormatException if the value is present but not a valid long. Test reader thread is not joined before assertion

The new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background reader thread with `new Thread(...).start()` but never joins it. After the main thread deletes all groups it sets `deletedAll.set(true)`, but the reader may still be inside a `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` call when the assertion runs. Reader thread is a non-daemon Thread without a name

Dead code: _create_process_for_shard method is never called

The _create_process_for_shard method (lines 127-132) is defined but never called. The _ensure_processes_alive method calls _create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards) directly, not _create_process_for_shard. This is dead code that should be removed or the call site should be updated to use it.

Inconsistent default for flusher_processes between CLI and factory

The CLI option --flusher-processes defaults to 1, but the factory parameter flusher_processes defaults to None, which becomes len(buffer.assigned_shards) in the flusher (via `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`). This means direct callers of the factory (e.g., tests) get a different default (one process per shard) than CLI users (1 process). This is a behavior change from the old code, which always created exactly 1 process regardless of shard count. Direct callers that don't pass flusher_processes and have multiple partitions will get N processes instead of 1.

test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify actual flushing with multiple processes

The test_flusher_processes_limit test only verifies the process count (len(flusher.processes) == 2) and shard distribution (total_shards == 4), but does not verify that the flusher actually works correctly with multiple processes. Since the main purpose of this PR is to introduce multiprocessed flushing, the test should submit messages to all shards, trigger flushing, and verify that all messages are correctly flushed across the multiple processes. Without this, a bug in the multi-process flushing logic could go undetected.

CLI help text is misleading about the default behavior

The help text says 'Maximum number of processes for the span flusher. Defaults to 1.' but this is only true for CLI usage. The factory parameter flusher_processes defaults to None, which results in one process per shard when called directly. The help text should clarify that the default is 1 for the CLI, and that the factory default is None (meaning one process per shard).

Naming inconsistency: flusher_processes vs max_processes

The parameter is called flusher_processes in the CLI option and factory, but max_processes in the SpanFlusher constructor. This naming inconsistency could be confusing for maintainers. Consider using the same name across all layers (e.g., flusher_processes everywhere).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

The feature `rolling-updates` is disabled.', but the actual behavior (see `printFeatureDisabled()` in `AbstractUpdatesCommand.java` and the new `testFeatureNotEnabled` in `UpdateCommandDistTest.java`) is that the command never runs at all and prints 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled.' Scripts that rely on exit code 4 to decide between rolling and recreate will be misled: the deployment may be perfectly eligible for a rolling upgrade; the code only signals that the user must enable the feature first. The row should describe 'Command unavailable: preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled' (or similar), not 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible'.

Caution claim that the Operator will fail is inaccurate

The CAUTION block states: 'While on preview stage, the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail.' But the very next NOTE in the same section documents a default behavior that works without the feature: 'the update strategy defaults to mimicking Keycloak 26.1 or older behavior'. The Operator does not 'fail' when the feature is disabled; it only fails if the user supplies the new `spec.update.strategy` field without enabling the feature. The wording should be tightened to make that conditional explicit (e.g., '...must be enabled if you set `spec.update.strategy`').

No test for `check` subcommand with feature disabled

The new `testFeatureNotEnabled` only exercises the `metadata` subcommand (line 48: `@Launch({UpdateCompatibility.NAME, UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.NAME})`). The same feature gate was added to `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` (UpdateCompatibilityCheck.java lines 46-50), but there is no equivalent test for the `check` subcommand to confirm it also prints 'Unable to use this command. The preview feature `rolling-updates` is not enabled.' and exits with code 4. A symmetric test (e.g., `testFeatureNotEnabledForCheck`) should be added.

testFeatureNotEnabled does not assert exit code 4

The new `testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr error message; it does not verify that the process actually exits with `CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED` (4). If a future change accidentally leaves the default 0 exit code, this test would still pass. The other tests in this file (e.g., `testCompatible` at line 75) do call `assertEquals(0, result.exitCode())`, so adding a similar exit-code assertion here would be consistent and catch regressions in the exit-code wiring in `UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()`.

YAML example uses non-YAML placeholder `Recreate|<not set>`

The CR example shows `strategy: Recreate|<not set>`, which is not a valid YAML scalar and will be rejected (or stored as the literal string 'Recreate|<not set>') if a user copies the snippet verbatim. The pre-existing doc had the same issue and the PR was a natural place to fix it. The placeholder should be replaced with a valid value (e.g., a separate example with `strategy: Recreate` and a NOTE explaining that omitting the field means default behavior).

printFeatureDisabled hard-codes the feature name in the error message

`printFeatureDisabled()` hard-codes the literal string 'rolling-updates' in the message: `printError("Unable to use this command. The preview feature 'rolling-updates' is not enabled.");`. The method is now a reusable helper in `AbstractUpdatesCommand` and other preview-gated commands may follow the same pattern; if any of them is gated on a different feature, the message will be wrong. Either parameterize the method with the feature name, or rename it to something feature-specific (e.g., `printRollingUpdatesDisabled()`) so misuse is obvious.

picocli.exit() does not halt execution; rely on `return` only

In `UpdateCompatibilityCheck.run()` (and the identical block in `UpdateCompatibilityMetadata.run()` at lines 46-50), the disabled-feature branch uses `picocli.exit(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED);` followed by `return;`. picocli's `CommandLine.exit(int)` only stores the requested exit code; it does not terminate the JVM or the run() method. The `return` is what actually prevents `validateConfig()` and the rest of the body from running. The code is correct, but the chosen API is misleading and a future refactor that drops the `return` (or calls `picocli.exit()` from a helper) would silently execute the rest of the command. Consider using `throw new ParameterException(...)` or letting the framework short-circuit, so the early-return contract is enforced rather than incidental.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition introduced by removing BuildIndex global lock

The diff removes `b.cacheMu.Lock()` at the start of `BuildIndex` and only acquires it around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` assignment. As a result, two concurrent calls for the same key can both pass through `GetIndex` (which takes only an RLock and returns nil for a missing entry) and concurrently execute `BuildIndex` for the same key. Both will then race on `b.cache[key] = idx` with last-writer-wins. At startup this is reachable whenever a gRPC request lands while `searchSupport.init` is still building a namespace, and at runtime it is reachable whenever a search request races with `getOrCreateIndex`. Previously the lock held for the whole build prevented this entirely; now the cache can contain stale indexes, and the second build allocates a whole new bleve index (potentially on disk under `b.opts.Root`) that is then orphaned. The fix in `getOrCreateIndex` only acquires the index after the build returns, so callers that retrieved the earlier index write to an index that is no longer the cached one. A per-key mutex, singleflight.Group, or sync.Map with double-checked loading is needed to make this safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition in `BuildIndex` caused by moving `b.cacheMu.Lock()` to only cover the final map assignment `b.cache[key] = idx`, leading to concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
Reordering search.init before initWatcher loses events written in the gap

The diff reorders `Init` to call `s.search.init(ctx)` first and then `s.initWatcher()`. Previously the broadcaster/stream was attached before the search index was built. `searchSupport.init` builds the index from a snapshot taken via `GetResourceStats`/`ListIterator` that returns when its last `ListIterator` completes. Any writes that hit the SQL backend between that point and when `s.initWatcher` starts (and calls `WatchWriteEvents` -> `listLatestRVs` to compute its `since`) are NOT in the search index snapshot AND are NOT yet visible to the watcher, so they are silently dropped from the search index. With the old order, the watcher (poller) was already running, so its `since` was at or after the build's last read RV. The fix is either to keep the original order or to pass an explicit `since` (the last RV read by `searchSupport.init`) into `initWatcher` so its polling starts at that RV.

NewResourceServer now fails if init fails, breaking callers that relied on lazy init

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously and returns `(nil, err)` on any init failure (lifecycle hook, search init, or watcher startup). Previously, init was deferred to the first RPC and a server object was always returned. Callers (e.g., the storage server module wiring) that construct the server, register it, and then serve traffic will now fail at construction time on any transient init failure. The PR description explicitly flags this as a question for the reviewer ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") but the chosen behavior change is significant: a slow/unhealthy database at startup, a corrupt bleve index directory, or any failure in `s.lifecycle.Init` / `s.search.init` will now prevent the storage server module from starting at all. Either keep the lazy path (with a context that isn't the per-RPC deadline) or ensure every caller of `NewResourceServer` is updated and tested for the eager-failure case.

NewResourceServer leaks backend resources when Init fails

When `s.lifecycle.Init(ctx)` succeeds (which is what opens the SQL database connection in the SQL backend's `initLocked`) but a later step in `s.once.Do` (search init or `initWatcher`) fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `(nil, err)` without calling `s.Stop`. There is no `defer` to call `s.cancel()` or to call `s.lifecycle.Stop`. The SQL backend's database handle (`b.db`), open bleve file indices on disk under `b.opts.Root`, and any goroutines started during partial init are left running. A successful subsequent `NewResourceServer` call for the same backend then races against the leaked resources. Add a cleanup path on the failure branch.

Data race on outer `err` variable inside errgroup goroutine

Inside `searchSupport.init`, the errgroup goroutine does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, where `err` is the outer named variable declared just above the `for` loop. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) > 1`, multiple goroutines write to the same outer `err` concurrently. The race is benign here because the goroutines also `return err` and `group.Wait()` is reassigned to `err` immediately after, but it is still a data race per the Go memory model and a race detector run will flag it. Use `_, _, buildErr := s.build(...)` and return `buildErr`.

BuildIndex still discards the traced context

This PR's stated goal is to "fix trace propagation by passing span contexts down". `searchSupport.init`, `searchSupport.build`, and `backend.GetResourceStats` were all updated from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...` so the new context flows into downstream calls. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` is the only other function touched in this PR that still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")`. The span exists but the returned context is dropped, which is the same bug the PR claims to fix. Apply the same `ctx, span :=` change here for consistency, even though the builder closure currently captures its own context from the caller.

Trace propagation fix is incomplete in backend.go

The PR description says "Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down" and updates `GetResourceStats` from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...`. Other methods in the same file (`WriteEvent` at line 158, `ReadResource` at line 353, `ListIterator` at line 388, `poll` at line 664, `resourceVersionAtomicInc` at line 718) still use `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, discarding the returned context. Downstream DB calls made with the outer `ctx` (not the traced context) therefore do not appear as children of these spans. Either the fix is intentionally scoped (in which case the PR description is misleading) or these should all be updated to `ctx, span :=`.

Postgres support in the storage-server integration test is skipped rather than fixed

The diff adds a `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` with a TODO to fix the test. This PR changes the most fundamental part of the storage server lifecycle (where initialization runs) but provides no new test coverage for that change, and the only integration test that exercises `InitializeModuleServer` with `modules.StorageServer` is now skipped on the very backend the storage server is required to support. Combined with the eager-init behavior change in `NewResourceServer`, this leaves a regression in postgres untested. Either unblock the test or add a dedicated test that exercises `NewResourceServer` -> eager init -> a Search gRPC call end-to-end on a real backend.

successful index build still logs duration but index size is constant

The new `s.log.Info("search index initialized", "duration_secs", end-start, "total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs())` reports `total_docs` from `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()`, which iterates `b.cache` at the moment init's search goroutines return. Because `searchSupport.init` uses `errgroup.Group` with `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)`, multiple `BuildIndex` calls may still be in flight when init's group.Wait() returns only the FIRST error; if no error occurred, `group.Wait` returns nil and the cache may not yet contain every index that was being built (the cache assignment happens inside `bleveBackend.BuildIndex`, after `builder(idx)` and `idx.Flush()`, and is only protected by `cacheMu`). Worse, if any one of those last in-flight builds fails after some succeed, the log line is never reached but partial state is reported earlier. This is a minor observability concern, but combined with the bleve lock-removal race it understates how many indexes were actually built.

Sentry transaction name in OrderedQueueWorker is hardcoded to monitors.*

The transaction name in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` is `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`. This module lives under `sentry.remote_subscriptions.consumers.queue_consumer` and is now used by the uptime consumer (`identifier="uptime"`) and potentially other consumers. Hardcoding the `monitors.` prefix will produce misleading transaction names like `monitors.uptime.worker_3` in Sentry's performance UI, making it harder to filter and group transactions correctly. The prefix should be derived from the identifier or removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Django ORM raises AssertionError on negative slice indices

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset set to a negative value. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that slice indices are non-negative and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` when they are not. The in-line comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. Any superuser or global admin who sends a cursor URL parameter like `cursor=0:-1:0` to the audit logs endpoint (which unconditionally sets enable_advanced_features=True for those users) will cause an unhandled AssertionError, producing a 500 response.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue precisely matches the golden comment. Both identify the exact same bug in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result()` where a negative `cursor.offset` is passed as `start_offset` to queryset slicing when `enable_advanced_features` is True.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative offset still crashes BasePaginator for is_prev=True

The BasePaginator.get_result change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for the non-prev branch. When cursor.is_prev is True and cursor.offset is negative, start_offset stays negative and the subsequent `queryset[start_offset:stop]` triggers Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' AssertionError. The accompanying comment ('This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') is incorrect; Django explicitly disallows negative slice indices on querysets.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: in BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, start_offset is set to offset without clamping to 0, which allows negative values to be passed into queryset slicing.

false_positives.candidate:
Endpoint unconditionally enables broken advanced pagination path

When the user is a superuser or has global access, the endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to OptimizedCursorPaginator. Combined with the fact that `Cursor.__str__`/`from_string` round-trip a user-supplied integer offset verbatim, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative value (e.g. `?cursor=0:-1:0`) to crash the endpoint with AssertionError. There is no validation, no length/offset bound check, and no fallback; the new paginator code path is a denial-of-service for the most privileged users. The gating mechanism is also confused: `optimized_pagination=true` from the request is checked but plays no role, while the actual crash vector (cursor.offset) is unvalidated.

Silent per-span data loss replaces whole-segment drop

When the post-union ZSET cardinality exceeds 1000, the script executes `zpopmin` to drop the oldest (lowest end_timestamp_precise) members. This is a fundamental semantic change from the previous consumer-side check in buffer.py (which dropped the entire segment via `del payloads[key]`) to silently dropping individual members during insertion. For traces where the root span arrives late, child spans already buffered can be evicted before the root arrives, producing incomplete segments that are still flushed downstream with no error. There is no metric for evicted spans, no test coverage, and the eviction strategy (lowest end_timestamp_precise) is not justified.

Redirect chain depth limit silently lowered 10x

The redirect-resolution loop cap was reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the previous safety comment about depth 10k. The PR description provides no rationale for this change. Any trace whose segment tree has a redirect chain between 1001 and 10000 deep will now exit the loop before resolving to the final set_span_id, leaving the new span attached to a stale set and producing a split/broken segment instead of one correctly-merged segment. This change affects production correctness for deeply nested traces and is not covered by tests.

KeyError if end_timestamp_precise is missing from event

The factory reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct subscript access. Unlike `parent_span_id`, which is read via `val.get(...)`, this field is treated as required. The SpanEvent schema may evolve or upstream producers (older relays, batched ingest) may omit it; any such event will raise KeyError inside the consumer, killing the batch and potentially stalling the partition. The newly added test only covers the happy path where the field is present.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation distorts end_timestamp_precise scores

Both unions use the default `AGGREGATE SUM` semantics: when the same member is present in both the destination set_key and the incoming source (parent_key on the second union, span_key on the first if a previous batch had landed it there), the resulting score becomes `original_score + new_score` instead of staying at `end_timestamp_precise`. This makes scores meaningless sums of microsecond-precision timestamps, which silently changes the ordering produced by `zscan` and biases `zpopmin` eviction (summed members get higher scores, making them less likely to be evicted). It is also undocumented and not tested.

max_segment_spans parameter no longer enforced

SpansBuffer still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` in __init__ but the consumer-side enforcement that used this limit in _load_segment_data was deleted without removing the parameter. The limit is now controlled entirely by the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Any caller that tuned max_segment_spans is silently overridden by a magic number in the Lua script; the parameter is dead config.

zscan on legacy SET keys will raise WRONGTYPE during deploys

The consumer now issues `p.zscan(key, ...)` against every segment key, but the on-disk format previously used Redis SETs. On rolling deploys where new consumer instances coexist with old data, or after a partial rollback, zscan against a SET key returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`. There is no version/key-type check, no migration step, and no metric for this condition, so segments will silently fail to load and the consumer will lose data for the affected trace until the keys TTL out.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates Paginator almost verbatim

The new OptimizedCursorPaginator re-implements get_item_key and value_from_cursor exactly as Paginator does (Paginator already inherits these from BasePaginator), and re-implements get_result as a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result. The only meaningful difference is the `enable_advanced_features` branch that itself crashes. This is dead code masquerading as a feature; it is brittle (any future change to BasePaginator.get_result will need to be mirrored) and the misleading docstring advertises capabilities (negative offsets) that don't actually work.

Cursor accepts arbitrary int offset with no validation

Cursor.__init__ now advertises 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' but accepts any integer without bound or sign validation. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling downstream, this lets any caller of Cursor.from_string feed extreme or malicious values (e.g. -2**31) into the paginator. Even with negative-offset slicing eventually corrected upstream, an attacker can still trigger expensive queries via large positive offsets (which are also unbounded).

No tests cover the new >1000-span eviction behavior

The Lua script's `zpopmin`-based eviction when span_count > 1000 is a new behavioral guarantee with data-integrity implications, but no test inserts more than a handful of spans per segment. There is no test for: (a) which spans get evicted (oldest by end_timestamp_precise?); (b) that the eviction actually caps cardinality at 1000; (c) that segments exceeding 1000 spans still flush correctly and don't get dropped; (d) that the metric/observability for evictions exists. The PR therefore lacks coverage of its headline feature.

Test payloads omit end_timestamp_precise validation

Existing tests were retrofitted to add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`, but the only new test value is a constant used uniformly. There is no test asserting that missing end_timestamp_precise produces a clear error (vs. the KeyError that the current code raises), no test for non-finite or negative values, and no test verifying that two spans with the same end_timestamp_precise are still both retained (zadd behavior on score collision is not asserted).

Comments describe a feature that does not exist

The added inline comments describe 'Performance optimization for high-volume audit log access patterns', 'optimized paginator for high-performance audit log navigation', and 'enhanced cursor support' — but the OptimizedCursorPaginator it routes to is a copy of Paginator with a feature (negative offsets) that crashes Django. The `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter is checked but does not influence which features are actually exposed. The comments mislead future maintainers about what the code does and why.

Comments falsely claim queryset handles negative slicing

Both the BasePaginator change at line ~179 and the OptimizedCursorPaginator comment at line ~876 assert 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' / 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. This is incorrect: Django raises AssertionError on negative slice indices. Comments that document safety properties that are not true make future debugging harder and may cause contributors to rely on a guarantee that does not exist.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` instead of the dataset actually being queried

Inside `_get_event_stats`, the helper is invoked with the closure-captured `dataset` (the dataset requested by the client) rather than the function's `scoped_dataset` argument, which is the dataset actually executed against. In `get_event_stats_factory`, widget-splitting can pass a different `split_dataset` (e.g. `discover` when the original requested dataset is `transactions`), and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` then evaluates `dataset == errors/transactions/discover` against the wrong dataset. The result is that upsampling is silently skipped (or wrongly applied) for any query where the requested dataset and the executed dataset differ, including the widget split path. Pass `scoped_dataset` (or both) to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` so the decision is based on the dataset that will actually run.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer/closure `dataset` instead of the `scoped_dataset` argument, causing upsampling to be improperly skipped during dataset/widget splitting (e.g., when switching to `discover`).

false_positives.candidate:
Only the literal token `count()` is rewritten; other common count-style aggregations are silently left as raw counts

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites columns whose stripped/lowercased form is exactly the string `"count()"`. Any column with arguments (`count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_distinct(...)`), aliased forms (`count() AS total`), whitespace inside the parens (`count(  )`), or counts appearing inside an `equation` expression is left untouched and will be executed against `sample_weight` semantics on some datasets and raw event semantics on others. The docstring says it "transforms aggregation functions to use sum(sample_weight) instead of count()" implying plural coverage; in reality it is a single literal-string match. Either expand the matcher to cover the realistic variants or document the limitation clearly and reject unhandled inputs so callers cannot get silently-mixed semantics.

_is_error_focused_query misses queries that target errors by exclusion

The check only looks for the substring `event.type:error` in the raw `query` parameter. Common Sentry search syntax that targets errors by negating the transaction type (e.g. `!event.type:transaction`, or `event.type:error OR ...`) is missed — `!event.type:transaction` will return False even though it is an errors-only query, so upsampling is skipped for those queries. Worse, the substring match is naive: a query like `event.type:errorcount` (an unknown tag name in user queries) would also pass. Use the parsed token list from `event_search.parse_search_query` (the same parser the rest of this endpoint uses) and inspect the `event.type` clause's value rather than substring-matching on the raw query string.

Upsampling integration tests assert an upsampled value that requires `sample_weight` to be populated by ingest

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10`, deriving that 10 from the stored `client_sample_rate=0.1` and the Snuba `upsampled_count() = sum(sample_weight)` definition in `discover.py`. In `SnubaTestCase` no Relay pipeline runs and `sample_weight` is not populated from the `sample_rate` set by `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling`; `sum(NULL)` over the column will be NULL/0 and the assertion will fail, or — even worse — pass only by accident and silently never validate the upsampling transformation. Either populate `sample_weight` in the test fixture (or wrap the assertion in a mock that returns the expected sample_weight), or split the test so that it verifies (a) the SQL emitted by `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` and (b) the upsampled result via a controlled sample_weight fixture.

Integration tests do not invalidate the upsampling eligibility cache, so order-dependent failures are likely

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` writes `is_eligible` to the shared cache under a key derived only from `organization.id` and the sorted project IDs. The new test class exercises four different allowlist configurations against the same `(organization, [project, project2])` tuple. Without invalidating the cache (e.g. by calling the exposed `invalidate_upsampling_cache` helper or clearing the cache backend in `setUp`/`tearDown`), the first test that runs caches its result and subsequent tests will read that stale value and silently skip the upsampling path they are trying to exercise. Add cache cleanup in `setUp`/`tearDown`, or assert on the emitted SnQL instead of the response value to make the tests order-independent.

The main public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` have no direct tests

The unit test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. It does not test the actual public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (including its caching behavior, short-circuit when the allowlist is missing, or that it combines the allowlist check with the dataset/query check correctly), nor does it test `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given that the function is the one wired into the request hot-path and contains the non-trivial cache logic flagged in other findings, it deserves direct unit tests.

Cache value caches only the allowlist result; the transform check still runs on every cache hit

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches only the boolean returned by `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`. On a cache hit the function still executes `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)`, which performs module-identity comparisons, parses the query string, and runs lazy imports of `sentry.snuba.discover/errors/transactions` on every call. To make the 60 s TTL actually pay off, include the relevant decision inputs (or the combined boolean) in the cache value so cache hits short-circuit the full check. At minimum, hoist the `from sentry.snuba import …` statements to module scope so a cache hit is genuinely cheap.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling accepts arbitrary floats including invalid sample rates

The helper writes `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever `client_sample_rate` is truthy and converts cleanly. It does not validate the resulting value: 0 (everything dropped → sample_weight = ∞), negative values, or values > 1 are all accepted. A client (or a misbehaving test fixture) can supply `client_sample_rate=0.0` and silently produce divide-by-zero / infinity in the server-side upsampling, or supply `client_sample_rate=-1.0` and corrupt aggregated metrics. Validate the value is in the open interval (0.0, 1.0] before assigning.

Overly broad `except Exception: pass` in _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling hides real bugs

Two nested `try/except Exception: pass` blocks silently swallow everything, including programming errors like the `normalized_data` object not being a `MutableMapping` at all (e.g. someone refactors `store_event` and passes the wrong value). The first block only needs to handle the case where `contexts` is not a mapping (AttributeError / TypeError), and the second only needs to handle `ValueError` from `float()`. Narrow the exception types so genuine bugs surface instead of being papered over.

Repeated in-function imports of sentry.snuba modules on every call

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` does `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` and `from sentry.snuba import transactions` inside the function body, executing those imports on every invocation (including every cache-hit path from `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`). There is no circular-import reason to defer them — `sentry.snuba` does not import this helper. Move the three imports to module top-level so each call is a constant-time identity comparison.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache precedence test setup does not actually prove precedence

In `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`, the perm cache is set with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. Because `checkPermission` only inspects the boolean via `if scopeMap[t.scope(req.Name)]`, a value of `false` is indistinguishable from a missing key — the check would return `false` even without the denial cache entry. To actually demonstrate that `permDenialCache` is consulted first and short-circuits a would-be allow, the perm cache should be set to `true` for `dashboards:uid:dash1` (matching folder inheritance), so that removing the denial entry would change the response from `false` to `true`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same test bug: the permission cache map sets `dashboards:uid:dash1` to `false` instead of `true`, meaning `checkPermission` treats it as not allowed instead of allowed as intended by the test.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key uses raw subject UID while permission cache key uses resolved UID

In Check, the denial cache key is built with `userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, ...)`, where `checkReq.UserUID` is the raw value parsed from `req.GetSubject()` (e.g., "123" for subject `user:123`). However, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (called shortly after) resolves the same user through `GetUserIdentifiers`, which can translate a numeric ID into the actual UID (e.g., "abc123") and then uses that for `userPermCacheKey`. The two caches therefore live under different namespaces for the same user: denial entries are stored under the raw input string, permission entries under the resolved UID. Consequences: (1) the denial cache will store duplicate entries for the same user depending on how the caller formats the subject, wasting memory; (2) more importantly, denial behavior becomes inconsistent — a denial cached for `user:123` will not be hit when the same user is checked via `user:<actualUID>`, so a user could be allowed on one path and denied on another for the same resource. The denial key should be derived from `userIdentifiers.UID` (after the lookup) the same way the permission cache key is.

Denial cache TTL will keep returning false for up to 30 s after a permission grant

`permDenialCache` is set with `shortCacheTTL = 30 * time.Second` and is consulted before any other source of truth. Once a denial is recorded for a (user, action, name, parent) tuple, the service will continue returning `Allowed: false` for that tuple for up to 30 seconds with no way to invalidate it on permission grant. The PR explicitly targets scenarios where a user gains a new permission (e.g. they just created a dashboard/folder) and immediately needs access; in the unhappy path where the same (name, parent) was previously checked and denied, the new grant will be invisible until the denial entry expires. There is no invalidation hook tied to permission changes and no `Delete` call on `permDenialCache` anywhere in the file. At minimum the key should be tied to a shorter TTL than the permission grant path, or the service should be invalidated whenever roles/permissions are mutated.

No test verifies the denial cache is populated when Check returns false

The new branch `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` is the only place where `permDenialCache` is ever written to (other than the test's manual `Set` in `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`). The existing `TestService_Check` "should deny user without permission" case asserts `resp.Allowed == false` but does not check `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)` afterwards. As a result, if a future change accidentally removes or breaks the `Set` call, the denial cache would silently stop being populated and no CI signal would fire. The test should explicitly read `s.permDenialCache` (e.g. via `userPermDenialCacheKey`) and assert the entry was written.

List still serves stale permission cache, so newly created dashboards/folders can be invisible

The PR's stated goal is that "dash/folder creator can access the dashboard/folder that they've just created". The `Check` path now falls through to the DB when the cached permission map does not contain the requested resource. `List`, however, was only changed to use `getCachedIdentityPermissions` first; it still returns whatever the cache holds when there is a hit, with no equivalent "cache hit but resource not present -> requery" step. For a user whose cached permission scope map predates the new dashboard/folder, `List` will silently omit the newly created item until the cache expires (`shortCacheTTL`, 30 s). The same `cachedPerms` -> DB fallback used in `Check` needs to apply when the List is asked about a name/folder that is not present in the cached scope map.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration.metadata lacks 'sender' field

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the user-mismatch check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. The `sender` key is populated only by the GitHub installation webhook handler — not by build_integration (which only sets sender from state if present) — so any path where the webhook has not yet been processed, has failed, or otherwise did not set `metadata["sender"]` will raise KeyError and 500. This is reachable in normal operation: the first user that installs via OAuth creates the Integration before the webhook lands, and any subsequent install on that installation_id will crash. Should be `integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")` and treat None as a mismatch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` directly without checking if the `'sender'` key exists, which raises a `KeyError` when `sender` metadata was not set.

false_positives.candidate:
get_user_info() exception not handled, can cause 500

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` makes an authenticated call to GitHub's /user endpoint. If this call raises (network failure, DNS error, GitHub 5xx, rate-limit response, ApiError, etc.) the view returns 500 to the user instead of the graceful `error()` page shown for all other failure modes. The surrounding OAuth token-exchange path already wraps everything in `try/except Exception`, so for consistency (and to avoid leaking a stack trace on a transient GitHub failure) this should be wrapped the same way and a missing/invalid `login` should also fall back to `error()`.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path

After the change the test does two GETs: first `setup_path?installation_id=...`, then `setup_path?code=...&state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. Because the second GET uses a state value that does not match `pipeline.signature`, the view short-circuits with the state-mismatch branch and returns the generic `Invalid installation request.` error before `build_integration` (which is what actually calls the 404-stubbed `/app/installations/<id>` endpoint) ever runs. The 404 stub is therefore dead code in this test. The assertion was also weakened from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic error string, so a regression that silently swallows the 404 would not be caught. Either use the correct state so the test reaches build_integration and assert the specific 404 message, or rename the test to reflect what it now covers (state mismatch).

Hardcoded webhook signature does not match the modified payload

`test_github_user_mismatch` mutates the JSON loaded from `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` (changes `installation.id` and `sender.login`) before POSTing to `/extensions/github/webhook/`, but reuses the signature `sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486` that was computed for the original (unmodified) fixture body. With signature verification enabled the webhook handler will refuse the event and no Integration with `sender.login == "attacker"` will be created, so the subsequent assertion that `GitHubInstallation` correctly rejects the second install does not actually exercise the mismatch branch — it would behave identically with or without the new check. The signature should be recomputed for the modified body (or the test should bypass signature verification explicitly).

installation_id bound to pipeline before CSRF state is validated

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch the very first action is `pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", installation_id)`, which executes before the `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` CSRF/state check on the OAuth callback path. So a request that supplies a forged `state` (e.g. forged-state scenario) will still mutate pipeline state in Redis before being rejected. This is low impact because the next legitimate request will re-bind or the error returns immediately, but defensively the state validation should run before any side effects on the pipeline.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of an IDP with alias 'alias' (literal) instead of the alias variable

In the loop creating IDPs the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)`. The argument is the literal string "alias", not the loop variable (e.g. `alias`). This will attempt to remove an IDP with alias "alias" at cleanup time, which does not exist. The pattern is pre-existing in testCacheIDPByOrg, but the PR copies it into the new test instead of fixing it. The fix is to use `alias` (the variable) rather than the literal string.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: the cleanup registration uses the hardcoded literal string "alias" instead of the actual alias generated for the IDP inside the loop.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache is over-invalidated because wrapped isEnabled() on idpById returns false whenever the linked org is currently disabled

In registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated), the `original` argument is `idpById` from getById(model.getInternalId()), which is wrapped via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...) and overrides isEnabled() to additionally check the linked organization's runtime status (provider.isEnabled() && org.isEnabled() && super.isEnabled()). The `updated` argument is the raw model passed to update(...), whose isEnabled() only reflects the model's ENABLED field. When the IDP is linked to an org that is currently disabled or removed, getLoginPredicate().test(original) returns false (wrapped isEnabled returns false because of the org status), while getLoginPredicate().test(updated) returns true (raw isEnabled is true). Neither early-return branch matches, so the login cache is invalidated even though the update did not change the IDP's static login configuration. The cache state would still be functionally correct (the wrapped isEnabled at read time filters out the IDP), so the impact is wasted work rather than incorrect results, but the optimization described in the Javadoc ('IDP is currently a login IDP' vs 'currently NOT a login IDP') is undermined for org-linked IDPs. Consider obtaining the underlying model for the comparison (e.g., look up cached via realmCache.getCache().get(internalId, CachedIdentityProvider.class) or idpDelegate.getById) rather than the org-aware wrapped instance.

Misleading comment in remove(): comment refers to a cache lookup that actually goes to the JPA delegate

The comment '//lookup idp by alias in cache to be able to invalidate its internalId' sits next to the use of `storedIdp`, which is populated from idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) — i.e. a JPA delegate lookup, not a cache lookup. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache`. If multiple goroutines call GetWebAssets concurrently before the cache is populated (e.g., during startup in non-dev mode), each will serialize on the write lock and redundantly read assets-manifest.json from disk and re-decode it. The proper double-checked locking pattern requires a second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write lock (gated on `cfg.Env != setting.Dev`, since dev mode intentionally bypasses the cache), so that only the first caller does the I/O and subsequent callers return the cached value. As written, every concurrent caller that arrives between the RUnlock at line 43 and the Lock at line 48 pays the full disk-read cost.

Without a concurrent test run under `go test -race` that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines, future refactors could easily reintroduce the race — for example by reverting to a bare read of the global, by moving the `defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()` above the assignment on line 70, or by replacing the RWMutex with a non-sync primitive. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Wrong metric function in Create error path

When `d.Storage.Create` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure is on the unified storage side. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures in the metrics, polluting dashboards/alerts built on `dual_writer_*` metrics. The call should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match the symmetric success branch on line 48.

Wrong metric function in Update error path

When `d.Storage.Update` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though this is a storage failure, not a legacy one. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses `recordStorageDuration`. The error branch should do the same: `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Otherwise storage Update failures are silently misattributed to legacy.

Async legacy writes inherit cancelled request context

Each async legacy call derives its context from the incoming `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. When the API caller cancels or times out, the parent `ctx` is already cancelled, so the child context is cancelled immediately and the legacy write never happens. The PR description frames legacy writes as a "safe measure" to keep legacy store in sync, but under request cancellation (which is common for slow upstream) the legacy side will drift from unified storage silently. The async legacy write should be derived from a non-cancelled context (e.g. `context.Background()` with timeout) so it survives caller disconnection.

Async legacy failures are not logged

Inside the goroutines that perform the asynchronous legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the only signal on failure is the metrics counter (`recordLegacyDuration(... true ...)`); there is no `log.Error(...)` call. If unified storage diverges from legacy (the very thing mode 3 is supposed to mitigate), operators will see no log line and no test will detect the failure because errors are swallowed. Add `log.Error(err, "async legacy ... failed")` (or equivalent) inside each goroutine after the legacy call.

Mode3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3's defining behaviour is that writes go to storage synchronously and then to legacy asynchronously. None of `TestMode3_Create`, `TestMode3_Update`, `TestMode3_Delete`, or `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` actually asserts the legacy mock was called. `setupLegacyFn` sets up `m.On(...)` expectations but there is no `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (and the async goroutine may run after the test function returns). The Create and Update tests register legacy expectations that may simply never be exercised, and the Delete/DeleteCollection tests don't even register them. Without synchronization (e.g. wait group, channel, or retry on the mock) plus `AssertExpectations`, a regression that removes the async legacy call entirely would still pass the test suite.

Mode3 read tests do not verify legacy is bypassed

The PR's stated semantics for mode 3 are: "reads (get, list): only use unified storage". `TestMode3_Get` and `TestMode3_List` never call `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "Get", ...)` / `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "List", ...)`. The Mode1 Get test does check this for storage (`us.AssertNotCalled(...)`); the analogous assertion for mode 3 (legacy must not be called) is missing. A bug that silently falls back to legacy on reads would not be caught.

TestMode3_Get creates a local prometheus registry

`TestMode3_Get` calls `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally even though a package-level `p` already exists (used by every other test in the file, and now exclusively by `TestMode1_Get` after this PR). The local registry is unused by the assertions in the test and just creates inconsistency. Use the package-level `p` like the rest of the suite.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight async legacy writes

`Destroy` calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()` immediately, but there is no synchronization with the goroutines launched by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. If a shutdown happens while async legacy writes are still pending (within their 10 s timeout), they will run against destroyed backends, producing confusing errors or panics. Consider tracking the goroutines with a `sync.WaitGroup` (or similar) and waiting for them in `Destroy` (with a bounded timeout).

$__range variable queries will now be incorrectly split

The new code interpolates queries via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...)` before the `querySupportsSplitting` check is evaluated. The comment in `querySupportsSplitting` states that `$__range` 'is interpolated on the backend with the split timeRange'. `runShardSplitQuery` now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables` for every target on line 52, and then `splitQueriesByStreamShard` forwards those (already-interpolated) targets into `runSplitQuery`, which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again for each target of every sub-request (line 299 of `querySplitting.ts`). true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Previously the call to `anonDeviceService.TagDevice` ran in a goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and any error was logged; authentication always succeeded. After this change, `TagDevice` runs synchronously on the request context, and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned from `Authenticate`, causing the authn flow to deny anonymous authentication entirely. true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

In `tagDeviceUI`, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` is executed before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called, and the entry is not removed on failure. The cache TTL is 29 minutes. With the new synchronous behavior, a device rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` on the first request is silently allowed on any subsequent request within 29 minutes, because `tagDeviceUI` returns `nil` on a cache hit before ever consulting the DB. An attacker (or a normal user) who is denied once can simply retry and pass; after ~29 minutes the denial returns. The cache should be set only after a successful DB write, or explicitly invalidated on failure, otherwise the new `device_limit` setting is bypassable.

updateDevice SQL breaks on Postgres

The `updateDevice` function hardcodes `?` placeholders, but Grafana supports Postgres (which uses `$1, $2, ...`). `CreateOrUpdateDevice` in the same file branches on `s.sqlStore.GetDBType()` and emits `$N` placeholders for Postgres; `updateDevice` does not. When the device limit is reached and the deployment is Postgres, this UPDATE will fail to parse and the error returned to `TagDevice`/`Authenticate` is a raw SQL syntax error rather than `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The new device-limit feature will be effectively broken on Postgres.

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` accepts any int64 from the ini file. The store treats anything `<= 0` as "no limit" (`if s.deviceLimit > 0`). A misconfiguration such as `device_limit = -1` (or a stray negative value) silently disables the feature without any error, log line, or warning. Negative values should be rejected at startup with a clear error, or at least clamped to 0 with a warning.

Anonymous authentication now performs extra synchronous DB work per request

When the limit is enabled, every `TagDevice` call (which is now on the auth path) runs an extra `CountDevices` SELECT against `anon_device` before the INSERT/UPDATE. The local cache (`localcache.New(29*time.Minute, 15*time.Minute)`) only mitigates repeated tags of already-known devices; new devices always incur the extra query. This adds latency to the anonymous auth hot path. Consider gating the count behind the cache as well (e.g., only check the limit when the cache misses, or only enforce the limit on first-seen devices), or otherwise documenting the performance trade-off.

No test that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only verifies that a NEW device ID is rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached` once the limit is hit. It never exercises the intended happy path of `updateDevice`: tagging an already-known, still-active device when the limit is reached should succeed (the device's `updated_at` should be refreshed in place). Without that test, regressions in the `WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ?` clause (e.g., the Postgres `$N` placeholder bug) would not be caught.

No test for the authn flow when the device limit is reached

`client.go` now propagates `ErrDeviceLimitReached` out of `Authenticate`, but no test in `impl_test.go` (or a `client_test.go`) verifies that behavior. true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a DB write during read-only validation

should_block? is named like a predicate but has the side effect of incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at whenever a record exists. The EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) calls it on every email validation, including runs that ultimately fail to save the user. Consequences: (1) match_count gets incremented even when the signup ultimately fails for unrelated reasons, distorting statistics; (2) every blocked-email signup now performs an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table inside what should be a validation pass, increasing contention; (3) if record.save fails it is silently swallowed, leaving an inconsistent mix of "returned true because record existed" but with no recorded hit. EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) with the raw, mixed-case value supplied by the user. Existing flows normalize emails to lowercase in some places (e.g., users_controller#change_email uses Email.downcase), but neither the BlockedEmail model nor the validator does any normalization. An admin who adds 'Spammer@Evil.com' to the blocklist will not stop a signup from 'spammer@evil.com', 'SPAMMER@evil.com', etc. Worse, because the unique index is case-sensitive, you cannot even add both casings as separate rows. Normalize via before_validation (self.email = Email.downcase(self.email.to_s).strip) and either store lowercase + add a functional unique index, or use a citext column.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows users to bypass the blocklist by varying the casing of their email address.

record.save failure is silently swallowed

should_block? calls record.save with no error handling. If the save raises or returns false (e.g., a validation error on the BlockedEmail record, a DB error, or an ActionView::Template::Error from a future before_save), the exception bubbles up out of the EmailValidator and aborts user signup. The user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean validation message. At minimum, wrap in a rescue and log; ideally restructure so hit recording is not coupled to the block decision (see the related side-effect finding).

rejectedEmails list never cleared and is case-sensitive

rejectedEmails is initialized once as Em.A([]) and only ever pushObject'd to. It is never cleared, and the contains(email) check is case-sensitive. Consequences: (1) once a controller instance flags an email as rejected, the user cannot clear that rejection (e.g., if they fix a typo and try the corrected address it's fine, but if they re-type the same address with different casing, e.g. 'Bad@Spam.com' vs 'bad@spam.com', the rejection check silently misses it because the case-sensitive contains returns false even though the server already rejected it); (2) the array grows without bound for the lifetime of the controller. The pushObject site should normalize the email (e.g., toLowerCase()) on both insert and check, and there should be a way to clear it on success/reset.

The only tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercise the whitelist/blacklist code paths (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist). These paths were carried over verbatim from user.rb and were never tested before either, but now that the logic has been moved into a shared validator it's the right time to add coverage: an email rejected by the whitelist, an email rejected by the blacklist, and an email that passes both. Without tests, regressions in the gsub('.', '\.') / regexp interpolation (which is also unsafe if the setting contains regex metacharacters like '|' or '*') will slip in.

The model spec only exercises should_block? with an exact-case email and a single call. It does not cover (1) case-insensitive lookup, which is the main correctness gap of this PR (see EmailValidator finding), and (2) the lost-update race condition in match_count. At least one spec should demonstrate that 'Foo@Spam.com' blocks 'FOO@spam.com' (after the model is fixed), and a spec using threads or raw SQL should illustrate the concurrent-update behavior so the regression is caught if someone removes the atomic update later.

The new file ends without a final newline (the diff explicitly notes "\ No newline at end of file"). Most Ruby tools, editors, and POSIX conventions expect source files to end with a newline. Add a trailing newline.

The line `sed -i '' -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` uses BSD/macOS sed syntax. Concrete consequence: for working hours 09:00-17:00 and a 60-minute slot starting at 16:30, the slot occupies 16:30-17:30 and crosses the end of the working day, yet the predicate evaluates `16:30 > 17:00` (false) and `16:30 < 09:00` (false), so `find` never returns truthy, the slot is not rejected, and it is returned as available even though part of it lies outside working hours. Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string equality

The secret check is `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. For a shared webhook secret the practical risk is low, but a remote attacker who can repeatedly send crafted requests and measure response times can in principle narrow down the secret byte-by-byte. Compare with a constant-time function such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

Redundant prisma.app lookup; appStoreMetadata is the source of truth

The PR description states the parent's app store is the source of truth for apps, but this handler queries `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and 404s if the local `app` row is missing. The `app` table is only populated by the app metadata sync (`CRON_ENABLE_APP_SYNC`, etc.), so a self-hoster whose env is fine but whose app sync has not run yet will see 404 for every valid slug. The very next line uses `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`, which is the in-memory registry that the database is synced from, so the DB hit is unnecessary. Replace with `appStoreMetadata[reqBody.appSlug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata]` and a single 404 if undefined.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` uses `&&` rather than `!!(...)`. The value is therefore the encryption-key string (a non-empty string is truthy, so the constant is the second operand's value), or `undefined` when either is missing. Every use site does a truthy check, so behaviour accidentally works today, but the type is wrong, the name is misleading, and a stricter consumer that does `=== true` or `Boolean(APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` would break. Should be `!!(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`.

Outbound refresh request to self-hoster endpoint is unauthenticated

When credential sharing is enabled, the Cal.com server POSTs to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the form body. There is no shared-secret header, no mTLS, no signature, and no per-user token; the only way the self-hoster can know the request is legitimate is by IP allowlist. The self-hoster's endpoint must return a valid access token to that Cal.com, so anyone able to reach the URL can mint tokens for arbitrary (calcomUserId, appSlug) pairs that the parent will then trust. Add an HMAC over the body using a shared secret (the same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` already configured would be the natural fit), or otherwise authenticate the caller.

Outbound refresh fetch has no timeout and no error handling

The `fetch` to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no `AbortController` / timeout, no try/catch, and no response-status check. If the self-hoster's endpoint is slow, the entire Cal.com request handler that triggered the refresh hangs (booking flow, calendar lookup, etc.); if it returns 5xx or fails DNS, the unhandled rejection bubbles up. Wrap in a timeout (e.g. 5–10s) and treat any non-2xx or network error as a refresh failure (which should invalidate the credential, the way direct-OAuth refreshes already do).

Salesforce access token is refreshed on every API call

`getClient` is called from the constructor, before any expiry check, and unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint. There is no `isExpired` / `isTokenValid` short-circuit like the other integrations (Google, HubSpot, Lark, O365, Zoho) use. Every single Salesforce interaction (contact search, create event, update event, delete event) now incurs a synchronous network round trip to Salesforce, plus a credential-row write. Add the usual expiry check on `credentialKey.expires_in`/`expiry_date` and only call the refresh path when actually needed.

Header name is documented as lowercase but the code does not normalize

The .env.example comment says "This is the header name that will be used to verify the webhook secret. Should be in lowercase." The handler reads `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. In Next.js / Node, incoming HTTP header names are lower-cased, but the configured `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is used as-is to index into `req.headers`. If a self-hoster sets it to anything but lower-case, the lookup silently fails and the request is rejected as 403 with no actionable message. Either enforce/document lowercase validation at startup, or normalize the configured name with `.toLowerCase()` before use.

New webhook endpoint and OAuth helpers have no tests

The PR description explicitly says "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works". The two new endpoints (`/api/webhook/app-credential`), the two new helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`), and the new `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` constant together introduce a security-sensitive credential-syncing path. At a minimum: (1) webhook secret check accepts correct header and rejects wrong/absent; (2) Zod schema rejects malformed bodies and gives a 400; (3) symmetricDecrypt with wrong key is caught and is a 4xx, not a 500; (4) race against a concurrent identical webhook does not 500 (or returns idempotently); (5) `parseRefreshTokenResponse` does not silently fabricate a refresh_token; (6) `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is a boolean, not a string. None of these are covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

Backup code entropy is only 40 bits per code

Each backup code is generated as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, producing a 10-character hex string with only 40 bits of entropy. Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B) recommends at least 64 bits of entropy for OTP secrets, and 128 bits is common. Because the code is the only thing standing between an attacker and account access (it bypasses the TOTP factor), 40 bits is brute-forceable in a realistic timeframe, especially since failed attempts do not consume the code and the API has no per-user rate limiting on the credentials provider beyond the existing email-based limiter.

Backup code is not consumed on failed attempt; timing-unsafe comparison

Two problems compound here: (1) `Array.prototype.indexOf` is not a constant-time comparison, so the time taken to find (or not find) a user-supplied backup code leaks information about how many leading bytes matched, enabling a timing side-channel that lets an attacker enumerate codes character by character. Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. compare each code with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` after length-checking). (2) The supplied code is only removed from the array after a successful match (`backupCodes[index] = null`), so failed attempts leave all 10 codes intact. Combined with the 40-bit entropy per code, this makes online brute force feasible: an attacker can submit unlimited guesses until one matches.

Same `backupCodes.indexOf(...)` timing leak as in the credentials provider: a constant-time comparison should be used. More importantly, the password check at line 40 is gated on `user.password && user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL`, so for SAML/Google users the only thing required to disable 2FA is a single valid backup code. A leaked backup code therefore gives an attacker the ability to log in via the credentials provider and then turn off 2FA entirely, reducing the account to a single factor. The credentials provider should still demand something only the legitimate user possesses (e.g. re-prompt for password, or require the SAML/Google re-authentication) before 2FA can be disabled.

The new backup-codes test only exercises the display/copy/download UI on the setup flow.
