Inside the lambda passed to resourceStore.findByType(), the code calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the granted set. However, hasPermission(String groupId, ...) does findByName(server, groupId), which looks up the resource by NAME (the group's ID), not by the resource's database UUID. In V2 per-group resources are named with the group ID, but getId() returns the resource's own UUID - these are different. findByName will always return null for these lookups, and hasPermission will fall back to the schema (all-groups) resource for every iteration. Consequences: (1) An admin with VIEW_MEMBERS permission only on a specific group will get an empty granted set, so the user search will not filter by groups and no users will be visible (in V2 mode, testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers and testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers in the new test class would fail). (2) When the admin has the VIEW_MEMBERS scope on the all-groups schema resource, the granted set is populated with the resource UUIDs instead of group IDs, making the value unusable downstream. The V1 analogue in GroupPermissions correctly passes the Resource object directly and strips the name prefix; the V2 version should use groupResource.getName() both in the hasPermission call and when adding to the granted set.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same resource-ID versus group-ID mismatch in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission: getId() is passed to a name-based permission lookup and added to the granted set, whereas the underlying group ID stored in the resource name is required for downstream filtering and counts. Both also identify unintended fallback to the all-groups resource.

false_positives.candidate:
resolveGroup only resolves by ID, not by name/path

resolveGroup just calls session.groups().getGroupById(realm, id) and returns null when the group is not found. In contrast, resolveUser additionally falls back to getUserByUsername and resolveClient falls back to getClientByClientId. If the id passed to getOrCreateResource is a group name or path (which can happen if a caller misinterprets the field, or if group representation identifiers evolve), getOrCreateResource will fail with 'Could not map resource object with type [Groups] and id [name]'. While the current code paths pass group.getId() (a UUID), the asymmetry with users and clients is worth a comment or alignment so a future caller is not surprised by the silent null.

GroupResource.getManagementPermissions/setManagementPermissionsEnabled will crash if invoked under V2

GroupPermissionsV2 throws UnsupportedOperationException for isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, viewPermission, managePermission, viewMembersPermission, manageMembersPermission, manageMembershipPermission, and getPermissions. The REST endpoints GroupResource.getManagementPermissions and setManagementPermissionsEnabled (lines 321-365 of GroupResource.java) call these methods after only gating on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ. If a deployment enables ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 together with (or instead of) V1 such that the endpoint is reachable but mgmt() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, the endpoint will throw UnsupportedOperationException on the first request. The endpoints should at least be gated on Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 being absent (i.e., only callable when V1 is the active mode), or V2 should provide a meaningful non-throwing implementation that returns the resource representation for the V2 resource-type resource.

New V2 group permissions behavior is not exercised in V2 mode

The five new tests in GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest rely on the V1 path: they create permissions via createPermission/createAllPermission scoped under the FGAP-managed client. If the same test is run with ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, the implementations in GroupPermissionsV2 (canView, canManage, canViewMembers, canManageMembers, canManageMembership, getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, etc.) will be invoked, and - given the bug in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission - several tests (notably testCanViewUserByViewGroupMembers and testCanViewUserByManageGroupMembers, where the search filter depends on UserModel.GROUPS being set from getGroupIdsWithViewPermission) will fail. Add a parallel V2 test class (or a parameterized config that also enables ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) to cover the new V2 code paths before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider does not return a BouncyCastle provider

`AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the provider backing the default JCA keystore (typically SunJCE on a standard JDK, or the BC provider only if it has been registered globally). The method is named `getBouncyCastleProvider` and the interface contract in `CryptoProvider` documents it as returning the BouncyCastle security provider, so any caller that relies on this method to obtain BouncyCastle (e.g. to invoke BC-specific APIs) will silently get the wrong provider. Since the authz-client is intended to avoid the BouncyCastle dependency, the method should return `null` or the implementation should be renamed/document so the contract is not violated.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore's provider instead of the BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER discards encoder results

The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write to them, and immediately discard the results. The actual encoding used for the return value is produced by the subsequent `writeDerSeq(...)` call. The dead code is confusing and wasteful, and should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify redundant ASN1Encoder creation and write operations whose results are discarded, while the subsequent return expression performs the actual encoding.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding returned as -1 but not handled by callers

`readLength()` returns `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (length byte 0x80). Callers like `readSequence()` then evaluate `while (length > 0)`, which immediately exits and returns an empty list, while `readInteger()` would pass `-1` to `read(int)`, which throws an `IOException` with a misleading 'EOF found reading -1 bytes' message. Indefinite-length encoding is not legal in DER and should be rejected explicitly (e.g. throw an `IOException` for `0x80`) instead of being silently passed through.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: indefinite-length encoding produces a length of -1 that callers use without proper handling, causing incorrect processing. The candidate describes different consequences of that invalid length rather than the specific subtraction highlighted by the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding order() to CryptoProvider is a binary-incompatible API change

A new abstract method `int order()` has been added to the `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` interface. This is part of the public `keycloak-common` artifact: any out-of-tree implementation of `CryptoProvider` (extensions, integrators, third-party crypto providers) will fail to compile/link against the new interface. This should be called out in the release notes / migration guide so downstream users know they must add an `order()` method to their implementation. Additionally, consider providing a `default` implementation (e.g. `return 0;`) to make the change source-compatible for the common case.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility concern: adding an abstract order() method to CryptoProvider can break existing implementations that do not implement it.

false_positives.candidate:
integerToBytes returns wrong array in left-padding branch

In the `qLength > bytes.length` branch of `integerToBytes`, the method allocates a left-padded `tmp` array of `qLength` bytes and copies `bytes` into it, but then returns `bytes` (the original shorter array) instead of `tmp`. The left-padding is therefore never applied. This causes `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` to call `System.arraycopy(r, 0, concatenatedSignatureValue, 0, len)` with `r.length < len`, which throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` whenever the BigInteger R or S value happens to be shorter than `qLength` (e.g. when the high byte of the value is 0, which is statistically possible for ECDSA signatures). The fix is to return `tmp` on line 160.

Test does not cover the case where R/S is shorter than the curve length

The test only exercises the round-trip with default JDK-generated EC keys and a fixed message. For typical ES256 signatures the BigInteger byte arrays of R and S are 32 or 33 bytes long, so the `qLength > bytes.length` branch of `integerToBytes` is never entered and the `return bytes` bug on line 160 of `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` is not detected. A test that explicitly constructs DER signatures where R or S is shorter than `algorithm.getSignatureLength() / 2` (e.g. by zero-padding the high byte) would trigger the `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` described above. Without such a test the bug will not be caught by CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount silently returns null instead of invalidating cache

Before the change, `getSubGroupsCount()` would NPE on a missing underlying group. After the change it returns `null` without invalidating the cached entry, without going through `getDelegateForUpdate()`, and without calling `registerGroupInvalidation`. The other 'updated' paths in this class (`getDelegateForUpdate`, `isUpdated`) consistently treat 'group missing in DB' as `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`, so this method now diverges from the rest of the contract: callers (e.g. `GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount`, which calls `representation.setSubGroupCount(group.getSubGroupsCount())`) silently receive a `null` Long that may surface as a `null` field in the serialized representation. Either the cache should be invalidated and an empty/0 count returned, or an `IllegalStateException` should be raised like the sibling methods do.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same problematic null return from getSubGroupsCount() and its impact on callers expecting a valid count. Although it emphasizes cache invalidation and serialization rather than the Javadoc guarantee and potential NPEs, the underlying non-null contract violation is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test reader thread is not joined before assertion

The new test `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti` starts a background reader thread with `new Thread(...).start()` but never joins it. After the main thread deletes all groups it sets `deletedAll.set(true)`, but the reader may still be inside a `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(...)` call when the assertion runs. Any exception raised by that in-flight call (or by a subsequent loop iteration before the thread observes `deletedAll`) will be appended to `caughtExceptions` AFTER `assertThat(caughtExceptions, Matchers.empty())` has already executed, so the test will silently pass even when the bug it is meant to catch is still present. The reader thread should be stored in a local, joined (with a timeout) before the assertion, and `deletedAll` should not be set until after the reader is observed to have exited the read loop.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the reader thread is not awaited before the assertion, so exceptions recorded after deletedAll is set may be missed. The candidate's questionable additional fix suggestion does not change the underlying issue it identifies.

false_positives.candidate:
Same NPE pattern remains on getSubGroupsStream overloads

The PR only adds a null guard to `getSubGroupsCount()`, but the three `getSubGroupsStream(...)` overloads immediately below (lines 256, 262, 268 in the head file) still use the exact pattern that was reported as NPE: `return modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)`. When the underlying delegate group has been deleted concurrently, `modelSupplier.get()` returns null and these methods will dereference null just like the original `getSubGroupsCount()` did. If the regression test is meant to prove the NPE is gone, it should cover these methods too, or the fix should be applied to all four methods (e.g. extracting the cached-load into a helper that returns null safely).

Regression test does not exercise the fixed code path

The test only calls `managedRealm.admin().groups().groups(null, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, true)`, which lists top-level groups. The fix targets `GroupAdapter.getSubGroupsCount()`, which is reached through subgroup-count population (`GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount`, only invoked when `subGroupsCount=true` is passed down). The listing call used here may not traverse the subgroup-count code path, so even if the fix were reverted the test could still pass by exercising only the un-fixed `getSubGroupsStream` paths. The test should either pass `false` for brief representation and use a parent group with subgroups, or directly invoke the admin endpoint that returns `subGroupCount` (e.g. fetching a single group with `?subGroupsCount=true`) to actually exercise the patched line.

Reader thread is a non-daemon Thread without a name

The reader thread is created with `new Thread(() -> {...})` and is not marked as a daemon. If the test fails or the thread is not joined (see previous finding), it can outlive the test method and keep issuing admin REST calls against the server after the test reports its result, polluting subsequent tests' state. The thread should be created as a daemon thread (or joined) and given a descriptive name so failures show up in stack traces.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

However, the only method that exists in UsernamePasswordForm (which UsernameForm extends) is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)`. The intended call is almost certainly `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` — without the argument the method body would have referenced an undefined symbol, and even if it compiled it would still need the UserModel to check `user != null` correctly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() without the required UserModel argument.

Callers must always pass `context.getUser()` rather than the more natural `null` when querying the realm-level toggle. Stale inline comment after refactor

The comment on the USER_SET_BEFORE_USERNAME_PASSWORD_AUTH field still reads "In this case we skip clearing of the user after unsuccessful password authentication", which is fine, but the inlined `AuthenticatorUtils.setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError(context)` call in `badPasswordHandler` no longer carries its own explanatory comment. Given that the helper now also affects the re-authentication form layout (USERNAME_HIDDEN/REGISTRATION_DISABLED), callers may not realize the side-effect. A short Javadoc on `setupReauthenticationInUsernamePasswordFormError` documenting what form attributes it sets and why would help — currently the Javadoc is just an implementation comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing crashes Django QuerySet

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the advanced-features branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (which can be negative) and then does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly disallows negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or the equivalent TypeError on newer Django). The "negative offset support" advertised by the new class therefore crashes the request whenever a client sends a cursor with a negative offset. There is no defensive clamp (`max(0, ...)`) and no fallback, so the feature is non-functional in practice.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator slices a Django QuerySet using a negative offset, which Django does not support and causes an exception.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime fields

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key does `int(math.floor(value) if self._is_asc(for_prev) else math.ceil(value))` after `value = getattr(item, self.key)`. The endpoint wires this paginator in with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is `"datetime"` and `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a `datetime.datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: a float is required`, so every call through the new path (including the very first request, because `build_cursor` calls `key(...)` to seed the next/prev cursor) will raise 500. The optimized paginator should subclass `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion (multiplier + strftime) or be otherwise datetime-aware.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key applies numeric math.floor/ceil conversion to a datetime value because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator.get_result now passes negative offsets to QuerySet slicing

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` deliberately lets a negative `offset` flow into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` when the cursor is a prev cursor. Cursor offsets are parsed straight from the URL via `int(bits[1])` in `Cursor.from_string`, so any client (or buggy prior response) that produces a negative offset will now hit Django's negative-indexing AssertionError. The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is factually wrong: Django does NOT handle negative slicing and the previous code did not claim to. This change advertises a behavior that does not work.

Comment falsely claims QuerySet handles negative offsets

The comment block above the new offset calculation says "This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions." Django's QuerySet raises on negative slicing (see the related finding at line 182/882). The comment is misleading and should either be removed or replaced with a real explanation of the intent plus a real guard, e.g. clamping to `>= 0` like the not-is_prev branch.

No tests cover the new optimized pagination path

The PR introduces a new request gate (`optimized_pagination=true`) and a new paginator class but does not add any tests for the new code path in `organization_auditlogs.py` or `paginator.py`. Given that the new path currently 500s on any non-trivial cursor (see other findings), tests would have caught the regression. At minimum, a test should cover (a) that `optimized_pagination=true` for an admin uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and succeeds end-to-end on `order_by="-datetime"`, and (b) that bad/negative cursors do not crash the endpoint.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result without a real perf win

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a near-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result; the only behavioral difference is the negative-offset branch (which is itself broken — see other findings). The endpoint always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` when it opts in, so the flag is effectively dead. There is no documented or measurable performance improvement over DateTimePaginator/BasePaginator: the same queryset is built, sliced, and `build_cursor` is invoked identically. Either delete the class and the gating code, or implement the actual optimization (e.g. a keyset pagination scheme or a bounded lookup) and benchmark it.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition introduced by removing BuildIndex global lock

The diff removes `b.cacheMu.Lock()` at the start of `BuildIndex` and only acquires it around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` assignment. As a result, two concurrent calls for the same key can both pass through `GetIndex` (which takes only an RLock and returns nil for a missing entry) and concurrently execute `BuildIndex` for the same key. Both will then race on `b.cache[key] = idx` with last-writer-wins. At startup this is reachable whenever a gRPC request lands while `searchSupport.init` is still building a namespace, and at runtime it is reachable whenever a search request races with `getOrCreateIndex`. Previously the lock held for the whole build prevented this entirely; now the cache can contain stale indexes, and the second build allocates a whole new bleve index (potentially on disk under `b.opts.Root`) that is then orphaned. The fix in `getOrCreateIndex` only acquires the index after the build returns, so callers that retrieved the earlier index write to an index that is no longer the cached one. A per-key mutex, singleflight.Group, or sync.Map with double-checked loading is needed to make this safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same lock-scope change in BuildIndex and the resulting duplicate concurrent construction of an expensive index for the same key. Its additional claims do not change the underlying match, though the final cache assignments are protected by the mutex rather than being an unsynchronized data race.

false_positives.candidate:
Reordering search.init before initWatcher loses events written in the gap

The diff reorders `Init` to call `s.search.init(ctx)` first and then `s.initWatcher()`. Previously the broadcaster/stream was attached before the search index was built. `searchSupport.init` builds the index from a snapshot taken via `GetResourceStats`/`ListIterator` that returns when its last `ListIterator` completes. Any writes that hit the SQL backend between that point and when `s.initWatcher` starts (and calls `WatchWriteEvents` -> `listLatestRVs` to compute its `since`) are NOT in the search index snapshot AND are NOT yet visible to the watcher, so they are silently dropped from the search index. With the old order, the watcher (poller) was already running, so its `since` was at or after the build's last read RV. The fix is either to keep the original order or to pass an explicit `since` (the last RV read by `searchSupport.init`) into `initWatcher` so its polling starts at that RV.

NewResourceServer now fails if init fails, breaking callers that relied on lazy init

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously and returns `(nil, err)` on any init failure (lifecycle hook, search init, or watcher startup). Previously, init was deferred to the first RPC and a server object was always returned. Callers (e.g., the storage server module wiring) that construct the server, register it, and then serve traffic will now fail at construction time on any transient init failure. The PR description explicitly flags this as a question for the reviewer ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") but the chosen behavior change is significant: a slow/unhealthy database at startup, a corrupt bleve index directory, or any failure in `s.lifecycle.Init` / `s.search.init` will now prevent the storage server module from starting at all. Either keep the lazy path (with a context that isn't the per-RPC deadline) or ensure every caller of `NewResourceServer` is updated and tested for the eager-failure case.

NewResourceServer leaks backend resources when Init fails

When `s.lifecycle.Init(ctx)` succeeds (which is what opens the SQL database connection in the SQL backend's `initLocked`) but a later step in `s.once.Do` (search init or `initWatcher`) fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `(nil, err)` without calling `s.Stop`. There is no `defer` to call `s.cancel()` or to call `s.lifecycle.Stop`. The SQL backend's database handle (`b.db`), open bleve file indices on disk under `b.opts.Root`, and any goroutines started during partial init are left running. A successful subsequent `NewResourceServer` call for the same backend then races against the leaked resources. Add a cleanup path on the failure branch.

Data race on outer `err` variable inside errgroup goroutine

Inside `searchSupport.init`, the errgroup goroutine does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, where `err` is the outer named variable declared just above the `for` loop. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) > 1`, multiple goroutines write to the same outer `err` concurrently. The race is benign here because the goroutines also `return err` and `group.Wait()` is reassigned to `err` immediately after, but it is still a data race per the Go memory model and a race detector run will flag it. Use `_, _, buildErr := s.build(...)` and return `buildErr`.

BuildIndex still discards the traced context

This PR's stated goal is to "fix trace propagation by passing span contexts down". `searchSupport.init`, `searchSupport.build`, and `backend.GetResourceStats` were all updated from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...` so the new context flows into downstream calls. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` is the only other function touched in this PR that still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")`. The span exists but the returned context is dropped, which is the same bug the PR claims to fix. Apply the same `ctx, span :=` change here for consistency, even though the builder closure currently captures its own context from the caller.

Trace propagation fix is incomplete in backend.go

The PR description says "Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down" and updates `GetResourceStats` from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...`. Other methods in the same file (`WriteEvent` at line 158, `ReadResource` at line 353, `ListIterator` at line 388, `poll` at line 664, `resourceVersionAtomicInc` at line 718) still use `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, discarding the returned context. Downstream DB calls made with the outer `ctx` (not the traced context) therefore do not appear as children of these spans. Either the fix is intentionally scoped (in which case the PR description is misleading) or these should all be updated to `ctx, span :=`.

Postgres support in the storage-server integration test is skipped rather than fixed

The diff adds a `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` with a TODO to fix the test. This PR changes the most fundamental part of the storage server lifecycle (where initialization runs) but provides no new test coverage for that change, and the only integration test that exercises `InitializeModuleServer` with `modules.StorageServer` is now skipped on the very backend the storage server is required to support. Combined with the eager-init behavior change in `NewResourceServer`, this leaves a regression in postgres untested. Either unblock the test or add a dedicated test that exercises `NewResourceServer` -> eager init -> a Search gRPC call end-to-end on a real backend.

successful index build still logs duration but index size is constant

The new `s.log.Info("search index initialized", "duration_secs", end-start, "total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs())` reports `total_docs` from `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()`, which iterates `b.cache` at the moment init's search goroutines return. Because `searchSupport.init` uses `errgroup.Group` with `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)`, multiple `BuildIndex` calls may still be in flight when init's group.Wait() returns only the FIRST error; if no error occurred, `group.Wait` returns nil and the cache may not yet contain every index that was being built (the cache assignment happens inside `bleveBackend.BuildIndex`, after `builder(idx)` and `idx.Flush()`, and is only protected by `cacheMu`). Worse, if any one of those last in-flight builds fails after some succeed, the log line is never reached but partial state is reported earlier. This is a minor observability concern, but combined with the bleve lock-removal race it understates how many indexes were actually built.

When the user is a superuser or has global access, the endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to OptimizedCursorPaginator. Combined with the fact that `Cursor.__str__`/`from_string` round-trip a user-supplied integer offset verbatim, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative value (e.g. `?cursor=0:-1:0`) to crash the endpoint with AssertionError. There is no validation, no length/offset bound check, and no fallback; the new paginator code path is a denial-of-service for the most privileged users. The gating mechanism is also confused: `optimized_pagination=true` from the request is checked but plays no role, while the actual crash vector (cursor.offset) is unvalidated.

Silent per-span data loss replaces whole-segment drop

When the post-union ZSET cardinality exceeds 1000, the script executes `zpopmin` to drop the oldest (lowest end_timestamp_precise) members. This is a fundamental semantic change from the previous consumer-side check in buffer.py (which dropped the entire segment via `del payloads[key]`) to silently dropping individual members during insertion. For traces where the root span arrives late, child spans already buffered can be evicted before the root arrives, producing incomplete segments that are still flushed downstream with no error. There is no metric for evicted spans, no test coverage, and the eviction strategy (lowest end_timestamp_precise) is not justified.

Redirect chain depth limit silently lowered 10x

The redirect-resolution loop cap was reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the previous safety comment about depth 10k. The PR description provides no rationale for this change. Any trace whose segment tree has a redirect chain between 1001 and 10000 deep will now exit the loop before resolving to the final set_span_id, leaving the new span attached to a stale set and producing a split/broken segment instead of one correctly-merged segment. This change affects production correctness for deeply nested traces and is not covered by tests.

KeyError if end_timestamp_precise is missing from event

The factory reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct subscript access. Unlike `parent_span_id`, which is read via `val.get(...)`, this field is treated as required. The SpanEvent schema may evolve or upstream producers (older relays, batched ingest) may omit it; any such event will raise KeyError inside the consumer, killing the batch and potentially stalling the partition. The newly added test only covers the happy path where the field is present.

ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation distorts end_timestamp_precise scores

Both unions use the default `AGGREGATE SUM` semantics: when the same member is present in both the destination set_key and the incoming source (parent_key on the second union, span_key on the first if a previous batch had landed it there), the resulting score becomes `original_score + new_score` instead of staying at `end_timestamp_precise`. This makes scores meaningless sums of microsecond-precision timestamps, which silently changes the ordering produced by `zscan` and biases `zpopmin` eviction (summed members get higher scores, making them less likely to be evicted). It is also undocumented and not tested.

max_segment_spans parameter no longer enforced

SpansBuffer still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` in __init__ but the consumer-side enforcement that used this limit in _load_segment_data was deleted without removing the parameter. The limit is now controlled entirely by the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Any caller that tuned max_segment_spans is silently overridden by a magic number in the Lua script; the parameter is dead config.

The consumer now issues `p.zscan(key, ...)` against every segment key, but the on-disk format previously used Redis SETs. On rolling deploys where new consumer instances coexist with old data, or after a partial rollback, zscan against a SET key returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`. There is no version/key-type check, no migration step, and no metric for this condition, so segments will silently fail to load and the consumer will lose data for the affected trace until the keys TTL out.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates Paginator almost verbatim

The new OptimizedCursorPaginator re-implements get_item_key and value_from_cursor exactly as Paginator does (Paginator already inherits these from BasePaginator), and re-implements get_result as a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result. The only meaningful difference is the `enable_advanced_features` branch that itself crashes. This is dead code masquerading as a feature; it is brittle (any future change to BasePaginator.get_result will need to be mirrored) and the misleading docstring advertises capabilities (negative offsets) that don't actually work.

Cursor accepts arbitrary int offset with no validation

Cursor.__init__ now advertises 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' but accepts any integer without bound or sign validation. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling downstream, this lets any caller of Cursor.from_string feed extreme or malicious values (e.g. -2**31) into the paginator. Even with negative-offset slicing eventually corrected upstream, an attacker can still trigger expensive queries via large positive offsets (which are also unbounded).

No tests cover the new >1000-span eviction behavior

The Lua script's `zpopmin`-based eviction when span_count > 1000 is a new behavioral guarantee with data-integrity implications, but no test inserts more than a handful of spans per segment. There is no test for: (a) which spans get evicted (oldest by end_timestamp_precise?); (b) that the eviction actually caps cardinality at 1000; (c) that segments exceeding 1000 spans still flush correctly and don't get dropped; (d) that the metric/observability for evictions exists. The PR therefore lacks coverage of its headline feature.

Test payloads omit end_timestamp_precise validation

Existing tests were retrofitted to add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`, but the only new test value is a constant used uniformly. There is no test asserting that missing end_timestamp_precise produces a clear error (vs. the KeyError that the current code raises), no test for non-finite or negative values, and no test verifying that two spans with the same end_timestamp_precise are still both retained (zadd behavior on score collision is not asserted).

The added inline comments describe 'Performance optimization for high-volume audit log access patterns', 'optimized paginator for high-performance audit log navigation', and 'enhanced cursor support' — but the OptimizedCursorPaginator it routes to is a copy of Paginator with a feature (negative offsets) that crashes Django. The `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter is checked but does not influence which features are actually exposed. The comments mislead future maintainers about what the code does and why.

Comments falsely claim queryset handles negative slicing

Both the BasePaginator change at line ~179 and the OptimizedCursorPaginator comment at line ~876 assert 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' / 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. This is incorrect: Django raises AssertionError on negative slice indices. Comments that document safety properties that are not true make future debugging harder and may cause contributors to rely on a guarantee that does not exist.

Any column with arguments (`count_if(...)`, `count_unique(...)`, `count_distinct(...)`), aliased forms (`count() AS total`), whitespace inside the parens (`count(  )`), or counts appearing inside an `equation` expression is left untouched and will be executed against `sample_weight` semantics on some datasets and raw event semantics on others. Either expand the matcher to cover the realistic variants or document the limitation clearly and reject unhandled inputs so callers cannot get silently-mixed semantics.

Worse, the substring match is naive: a query like `event.type:errorcount` (an unknown tag name in user queries) would also pass. Use the parsed token list from `event_search.parse_search_query` (the same parser the rest of this endpoint uses) and inspect the `event.type` clause's value rather than substring-matching on the raw query string.

`OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `data[0][1][0]["count"] == 10`, deriving that 10 from the stored `client_sample_rate=0.1` and the Snuba `upsampled_count() = sum(sample_weight)` definition in `discover.py`. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` writes `is_eligible` to the shared cache under a key derived only from `organization.id` and the sorted project IDs. The new test class exercises four different allowlist configurations against the same `(organization, [project, project2])` tuple. Add cache cleanup in `setUp`/`tearDown`, or assert on the emitted SnQL instead of the response value to make the tests order-independent.

The main public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` have no direct tests

The unit test file only exercises the private helpers `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, and `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`. It does not test the actual public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` (including its caching behavior, short-circuit when the allowlist is missing, or that it combines the allowlist check with the dataset/query check correctly), nor does it test `invalidate_upsampling_cache`. Given that the function is the one wired into the request hot-path and contains the non-trivial cache logic flagged in other findings, it deserves direct unit tests.

Cache value caches only the allowlist result; the transform check still runs on every cache hit

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches only the boolean returned by `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`. On a cache hit the function still executes `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform(dataset, request)`, which performs module-identity comparisons, parses the query string, and runs lazy imports of `sentry.snuba.discover/errors/transactions` on every call. To make the 60 s TTL actually pay off, include the relevant decision inputs (or the combined boolean) in the cache value so cache hits short-circuit the full check. At minimum, hoist the `from sentry.snuba import …` statements to module scope so a cache hit is genuinely cheap.

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling accepts arbitrary floats including invalid sample rates

The helper writes `normalized_data["sample_rate"] = float(client_sample_rate)` whenever `client_sample_rate` is truthy and converts cleanly. It does not validate the resulting value: 0 (everything dropped → sample_weight = ∞), negative values, or values > 1 are all accepted. A client (or a misbehaving test fixture) can supply `client_sample_rate=0.0` and silently produce divide-by-zero / infinity in the server-side upsampling, or supply `client_sample_rate=-1.0` and corrupt aggregated metrics. Validate the value is in the open interval (0.0, 1.0] before assigning.

Overly broad `except Exception: pass` in _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling hides real bugs

Two nested `try/except Exception: pass` blocks silently swallow everything, including programming errors like the `normalized_data` object not being a `MutableMapping` at all (e.g. someone refactors `store_event` and passes the wrong value). The first block only needs to handle the case where `contexts` is not a mapping (AttributeError / TypeError), and the second only needs to handle `ValueError` from `float()`. Narrow the exception types so genuine bugs surface instead of being papered over.

Repeated in-function imports of sentry.snuba modules on every call

`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` does `from sentry.snuba import discover, errors` and `from sentry.snuba import transactions` inside the function body, executing those imports on every invocation (including every cache-hit path from `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`). There is no circular-import reason to defer them — `sentry.snuba` does not import this helper. Move the three imports to module top-level so each call is a constant-time identity comparison.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache precedence test setup does not actually prove precedence

In `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`, the perm cache is set with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. Because `checkPermission` only inspects the boolean via `if scopeMap[t.scope(req.Name)]`, a value of `false` is indistinguishable from a missing key — the check would return `false` even without the denial cache entry. To actually demonstrate that `permDenialCache` is consulted first and short-circuits a would-be allow, the perm cache should be set to `true` for `dashboards:uid:dash1` (matching folder inheritance), so that removing the denial entry would change the response from `false` to `true`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the permission cache stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so it does not allow access as intended. The candidate explains the resulting failure to test denial-cache precedence and proposes setting the value to true.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key uses raw subject UID while permission cache key uses resolved UID

In Check, the denial cache key is built with `userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, ...)`, where `checkReq.UserUID` is the raw value parsed from `req.GetSubject()` (e.g., "123" for subject `user:123`). However, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` (called shortly after) resolves the same user through `GetUserIdentifiers`, which can translate a numeric ID into the actual UID (e.g., "abc123") and then uses that for `userPermCacheKey`. The two caches therefore live under different namespaces for the same user: denial entries are stored under the raw input string, permission entries under the resolved UID. Consequences: (1) the denial cache will store duplicate entries for the same user depending on how the caller formats the subject, wasting memory; (2) more importantly, denial behavior becomes inconsistent — a denial cached for `user:123` will not be hit when the same user is checked via `user:<actualUID>`, so a user could be allowed on one path and denied on another for the same resource. The denial key should be derived from `userIdentifiers.UID` (after the lookup) the same way the permission cache key is.

Denial cache TTL will keep returning false for up to 30 s after a permission grant

`permDenialCache` is set with `shortCacheTTL = 30 * time.Second` and is consulted before any other source of truth. Once a denial is recorded for a (user, action, name, parent) tuple, the service will continue returning `Allowed: false` for that tuple for up to 30 seconds with no way to invalidate it on permission grant. The PR explicitly targets scenarios where a user gains a new permission (e.g. they just created a dashboard/folder) and immediately needs access; in the unhappy path where the same (name, parent) was previously checked and denied, the new grant will be invisible until the denial entry expires. There is no invalidation hook tied to permission changes and no `Delete` call on `permDenialCache` anywhere in the file. At minimum the key should be tied to a shorter TTL than the permission grant path, or the service should be invalidated whenever roles/permissions are mutated.

No test verifies the denial cache is populated when Check returns false

The new branch `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true) }` is the only place where `permDenialCache` is ever written to (other than the test's manual `Set` in `Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`). The existing `TestService_Check` "should deny user without permission" case asserts `resp.Allowed == false` but does not check `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)` afterwards. As a result, if a future change accidentally removes or breaks the `Set` call, the denial cache would silently stop being populated and no CI signal would fire. The test should explicitly read `s.permDenialCache` (e.g. via `userPermDenialCacheKey`) and assert the entry was written.

List still serves stale permission cache, so newly created dashboards/folders can be invisible

The PR's stated goal is that "dash/folder creator can access the dashboard/folder that they've just created". The `Check` path now falls through to the DB when the cached permission map does not contain the requested resource. `List`, however, was only changed to use `getCachedIdentityPermissions` first; it still returns whatever the cache holds when there is a hit, with no equivalent "cache hit but resource not present -> requery" step. For a user whose cached permission scope map predates the new dashboard/folder, `List` will silently omit the newly created item until the cache expires (`shortCacheTTL`, 30 s). The same `cachedPerms` -> DB fallback used in `Check` needs to apply when the List is asked about a name/folder that is not present in the cached scope map.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when integration.metadata lacks 'sender' field

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the user-mismatch check reads `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. The `sender` key is populated only by the GitHub installation webhook handler — not by build_integration (which only sets sender from state if present) — so any path where the webhook has not yet been processed, has failed, or otherwise did not set `metadata["sender"]` will raise KeyError and 500. This is reachable in normal operation: the first user that installs via OAuth creates the Integration before the webhook lands, and any subsequent install on that installation_id will crash. Should be `integration.metadata.get("sender") or {}).get("login")` and treat None as a mismatch.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unchecked access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"], which raises a KeyError when sender metadata was not populated during integration creation.

false_positives.candidate:
get_user_info() exception not handled, can cause 500

`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` makes an authenticated call to GitHub's /user endpoint. If this call raises (network failure, DNS error, GitHub 5xx, rate-limit response, ApiError, etc.) the view returns 500 to the user instead of the graceful `error()` page shown for all other failure modes. The surrounding OAuth token-exchange path already wraps everything in `try/except Exception`, so for consistency (and to avoid leaking a stack trace on a transient GitHub failure) this should be wrapped the same way and a missing/invalid `login` should also fall back to `error()`.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 path

After the change the test does two GETs: first `setup_path?installation_id=...`, then `setup_path?code=...&state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`. Because the second GET uses a state value that does not match `pipeline.signature`, the view short-circuits with the state-mismatch branch and returns the generic `Invalid installation request.` error before `build_integration` (which is what actually calls the 404-stubbed `/app/installations/<id>` endpoint) ever runs. The 404 stub is therefore dead code in this test. The assertion was also weakened from `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."` to the generic error string, so a regression that silently swallows the 404 would not be caught. Either use the correct state so the test reaches build_integration and assert the specific 404 message, or rename the test to reflect what it now covers (state mismatch).

Hardcoded webhook signature does not match the modified payload

`test_github_user_mismatch` mutates the JSON loaded from `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE` (changes `installation.id` and `sender.login`) before POSTing to `/extensions/github/webhook/`, but reuses the signature `sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486` that was computed for the original (unmodified) fixture body. With signature verification enabled the webhook handler will refuse the event and no Integration with `sender.login == "attacker"` will be created, so the subsequent assertion that `GitHubInstallation` correctly rejects the second install does not actually exercise the mismatch branch — it would behave identically with or without the new check. The signature should be recomputed for the modified body (or the test should bypass signature verification explicitly).

installation_id bound to pipeline before CSRF state is validated

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch the very first action is `pipeline.bind_state("installation_id", installation_id)`, which executes before the `if request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature` CSRF/state check on the OAuth callback path. So a request that supplies a forged `state` (e.g. forged-state scenario) will still mutate pipeline state in Redis before being rejected. This is low impact because the next legitimate request will re-bind or the error returns immediately, but defensively the state validation should run before any side effects on the pipeline.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of an IDP with alias 'alias' (literal) instead of the alias variable

In the loop creating IDPs the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)`. The argument is the literal string "alias", not the loop variable (e.g. `alias`). This will attempt to remove an IDP with alias "alias" at cleanup time, which does not exist. The pattern is pre-existing in testCacheIDPByOrg, but the PR copies it into the new test instead of fixing it. The fix is to use `alias` (the variable) rather than the literal string.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup using the literal "alias" instead of the actual per-iteration IDP alias ('idp-alias-' + i). Using the alias variable addresses the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache is over-invalidated because wrapped isEnabled() on idpById returns false whenever the linked org is currently disabled

In registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate(original, updated), the `original` argument is `idpById` from getById(model.getInternalId()), which is wrapped via createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(...) and overrides isEnabled() to additionally check the linked organization's runtime status (provider.isEnabled() && org.isEnabled() && super.isEnabled()). The `updated` argument is the raw model passed to update(...), whose isEnabled() only reflects the model's ENABLED field. When the IDP is linked to an org that is currently disabled or removed, getLoginPredicate().test(original) returns false (wrapped isEnabled returns false because of the org status), while getLoginPredicate().test(updated) returns true (raw isEnabled is true). Neither early-return branch matches, so the login cache is invalidated even though the update did not change the IDP's static login configuration. The cache state would still be functionally correct (the wrapped isEnabled at read time filters out the IDP), so the impact is wasted work rather than incorrect results, but the optimization described in the Javadoc ('IDP is currently a login IDP' vs 'currently NOT a login IDP') is undermined for org-linked IDPs. Consider obtaining the underlying model for the comparison (e.g., look up cached via realmCache.getCache().get(internalId, CachedIdentityProvider.class) or idpDelegate.getById) rather than the org-aware wrapped instance.

Misleading comment in remove(): comment refers to a cache lookup that actually goes to the JPA delegate

The comment '//lookup idp by alias in cache to be able to invalidate its internalId' sits next to the use of `storedIdp`, which is populated from idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) — i.e. a JPA delegate lookup, not a cache lookup. The refactor hoisted idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias) out of the `if (isInvalid(cacheKey))` branch into a local variable used by both branches of the if/else, but the wording still implies a cache read. The lookup never consults the cache.

testCacheIDPForLogin does not cover organization-level changes that affect login availability

The new test exercises IDP create/remove/update and the cache invalidations they cause. It does not exercise organization-level changes that affect IDP login availability: disabling an organization, removing an organization, or unlinking an IDP from its organization. None of these trigger registerIDPLoginInvalidation/OnUpdate, so the login cache may stay stale until some unrelated IDP change triggers an invalidation. The wrapped isEnabled() at read time filters out IDPs whose org is disabled, so correctness is preserved, but the cache freshness behavior in those scenarios is untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Confusing logic in enableSqlExpressions that always returns false

The new `enableSqlExpressions` function uses unnecessarily complex logic to always return false. The variable `enabled` is assigned `!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)`, meaning `enabled` is true when the flag is OFF — the opposite of what the name suggests. Both branches then return `false`, so the feature flag value is completely ignored. This is confusing and error-prone: a future maintainer may attempt to 'fix' what looks like an inverted boolean bug and inadvertently re-enable SQL Expressions, reintroducing CVE-2024-9264. A safer implementation would simply be `return false` with a comment explaining that SQL Expressions are permanently disabled due to CVE-2024-9264, making the intent unambiguous and removing any appearance that the feature flag is consulted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that enableSqlExpressions always returns false regardless of the feature flag, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions. The candidate's additional security context and suggested simplification do not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests verifying SQL Expressions are disabled

This is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) that hard-disables SQL Expressions, but no tests are added to `pkg/expr/reader_test.go` (or any new test file) to verify that a `QueryTypeSQL` query now returns the expected 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' error. Without a regression test, a future change could re-enable the SQL code path silently. At minimum, a test that constructs an `ExpressionQueryReader`, calls `ReadQuery` with a `QueryTypeSQL` JSON payload, and asserts the returned error would lock in the security fix.

SQL command construction path still reachable if reader check is removed

`NewSQLCommand` in `pkg/expr/sql_command.go` still calls `sql.TablesList` which constructs a DuckDB command via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)`. Currently this is unreachable because `reader.go` rejects `QueryTypeSQL` upfront, but the code path remains live and `TablesList` is still an exported function in `pkg/expr/sql`. If the `enableSqlExpressions` gate in `reader.go` is later weakened or removed (e.g., because someone misreads the confusing boolean logic in `enableSqlExpressions`), the original DuckDB-based command construction — including the string interpolation that contributed to CVE-2024-9264 — would be reachable again. Consider making `TablesList` and `NewSQLCommand` return an 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' error directly rather than relying solely on the reader-level gate, so the vulnerable code path cannot be reached even if the reader check is bypassed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is incomplete; concurrent callers may redundantly re-read the manifest

After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check `entryPointAssetsCache`. If multiple goroutines call GetWebAssets concurrently before the cache is populated (e.g., during startup in non-dev mode), each will serialize on the write lock and redundantly read assets-manifest.json from disk and re-decode it. The proper double-checked locking pattern requires a second check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the write lock (gated on `cfg.Env != setting.Dev`, since dev mode intentionally bypasses the cache), so that only the first caller does the I/O and subsequent callers return the cached value. As written, every concurrent caller that arrives between the RUnlock at line 43 and the Lock at line 48 pays the full disk-read cost.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets, allowing concurrent callers to redundantly populate the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
No test exercises the concurrent path; the race fix is not regression-protected

The PR adds synchronization to fix a data race on the global `entryPointAssetsCache`, but no test file is added or modified (the changed-files list contains only `pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go`). Without a concurrent test run under `go test -race` that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines, future refactors could easily reintroduce the race — for example by reverting to a bare read of the global, by moving the `defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()` above the assignment on line 70, or by replacing the RWMutex with a non-sync primitive. A test that spawns N goroutines all calling GetWebAssets and waits on a sync.WaitGroup would have caught the original race and will catch any regression.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup operations logged at Error level with nil errors

The new cleanup code logs every routine operation at Error level: r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err) and r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", "count", len(ids), "affected", x, "err", y). Cleanup runs as a background job that should never be considered an error; previously this code did not log at all. The "err" field is always nil at these sites (errors are returned early), so the messages convey no actionable signal but will spam the error log on every cycle, making real errors harder to find and tripping error-rate alerts in monitoring. The level should be Info or Debug, and the meaningless "err" field should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify routine or debugging information logged at Error level, polluting production error logs, and recommend using Debug or Info instead. The candidate's additional concern about nil error fields does not change the underlying match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker frequency silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The diff changes the cleanup ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`, a 10x increase in how often the entire cleanup job (including annotation cleanup, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs and query history) runs. This change is not mentioned in the PR description and is unrelated to the deadlock fix. It will significantly increase database query load and log volume (especially given the new Error-level logging above) on every Grafana instance. Either it should be reverted, made configurable, or at minimum called out in the PR description / release notes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the cleanup ticker change from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting risk of increased database load from more frequent cleanup execution.

false_positives.candidate:
Full annotation IDs and full WHERE condition dumped into logs on every batch

Each batch emits "ids", ids (the entire int64 slice) and the raw SQL condition into the log. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize set in the tens of thousands (the new test case uses 32767), this produces extremely verbose log entries on every cycle. Logging thousands of integers is not useful and increases log volume/cost; an only the count and a truncated identifier (or none) should be logged.

Annotation cleanup tests now skipped under -short

The tests `TestAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` have been renamed to `TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp` and `TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst` and now call `t.Skip` when `testing.Short()` is true. Previously these tests always ran. Any developer or CI step that runs `go test -short ./pkg/services/annotations/...` will lose coverage of the new split-statement cleanup logic (including the SQLite 32767-batch path that was added). If the intent is to keep this as a required test, the skip should be removed or the package should ensure integration tests are always run in CI.

O(n^2) string concatenation when inlining IDs into SQLite DELETE

In `deleteByIDs`, when SQLite is used with a batch size greater than 999 the IDs are concatenated into a single SQL string via repeated `fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`. This is O(n^2) in the number of IDs and, with the new default-style batch size of 32767 (and tests using batch sizes in that range), produces hundreds of thousands of intermediate string allocations per batch. Using `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join` after pre-formatting) would be linear and cheaper.

Stale/incorrect "condition must be supplied" error message

`fetchIDs` checks `if condition == ""` and returns `fmt.Errorf("condition must be supplied; cannot fetch IDs from entire table")`, but `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` passes a non-empty condition that begins with `NOT EXISTS (...)` followed directly by the LIMIT clause with no `WHERE` keyword. The error message implies a missing WHERE clause would result in a full-table SELECT, but the guard will still fire whenever any caller forgets to prepend a WHERE. This is a minor wording/logic mismatch and could mask a real bug in future callers; the message should describe the actual invariant (e.g., "condition cannot be empty") or be removed in favor of a real precondition.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete uses d.Log instead of log with structured fields

In `Delete`, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` is used, while Create/Update/DeleteCollection/DeleteCollection all use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` where `log` includes `name`, `kind`, and `method` fields. As a result, any klog calls inside `Storage.Delete` (or inside the async legacy `Delete`) won't carry the structured `kind=`, `method=delete`, `name=` context, making it harder to filter logs by operation. Also, the async legacy `Delete` goroutine inherits this weaker logger (it references the outer `ctx`) so legacy delete errors logged downstream will be missing context too.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: passing d.Log rather than the enriched log variable to klog.NewContext prevents the name, kind, and method fields from propagating to downstream logging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kind label uses object name instead of options.Kind in Delete

The Delete success branch records `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` where the third argument is the resource `name` parameter, while every other call site uses `options.Kind`. The metric label is supposed to be the Kind, so this passes a different value into the same label, producing inconsistent time series in the dual_writer_* metrics.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: metrics recording uses the resource name instead of options.Kind, unlike other methods or call sites.

false_positives.candidate:
Wrong metric function in Create error path

When `d.Storage.Create` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though the failure is on the unified storage side. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures in the metrics, polluting dashboards/alerts built on `dual_writer_*` metrics. The call should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match the symmetric success branch on line 48.

Wrong metric function in Update error path

When `d.Storage.Update` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` even though this is a storage failure, not a legacy one. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses `recordStorageDuration`. The error branch should do the same: `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Otherwise storage Update failures are silently misattributed to legacy.

Wrong metric function in DeleteCollection async legacy block

The async goroutine for the legacy `DeleteCollection` records the result via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. This is the legacy call, so it should be `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` (matching the corresponding calls in Create/Update/Delete). The current code will mislabel legacy failures as storage failures, breaking SLO dashboards.

Async legacy writes inherit cancelled request context

Each async legacy call derives its context from the incoming `ctx` via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. When the API caller cancels or times out, the parent `ctx` is already cancelled, so the child context is cancelled immediately and the legacy write never happens. The PR description frames legacy writes as a "safe measure" to keep legacy store in sync, but under request cancellation (which is common for slow upstream) the legacy side will drift from unified storage silently. The async legacy write should be derived from a non-cancelled context (e.g. `context.Background()` with timeout) so it survives caller disconnection.

Async legacy failures are not logged

Inside the goroutines that perform the asynchronous legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection, the only signal on failure is the metrics counter (`recordLegacyDuration(... true ...)`); there is no `log.Error(...)` call. If unified storage diverges from legacy (the very thing mode 3 is supposed to mitigate), operators will see no log line and no test will detect the failure because errors are swallowed. Add `log.Error(err, "async legacy ... failed")` (or equivalent) inside each goroutine after the legacy call.

Mode3 tests do not verify the asynchronous legacy writes

Mode 3's defining behaviour is that writes go to storage synchronously and then to legacy asynchronously. None of `TestMode3_Create`, `TestMode3_Update`, `TestMode3_Delete`, or `TestMode3_DeleteCollection` actually asserts the legacy mock was called. `setupLegacyFn` sets up `m.On(...)` expectations but there is no `m.AssertExpectations(t)` (and the async goroutine may run after the test function returns). The Create and Update tests register legacy expectations that may simply never be exercised, and the Delete/DeleteCollection tests don't even register them. Without synchronization (e.g. wait group, channel, or retry on the mock) plus `AssertExpectations`, a regression that removes the async legacy call entirely would still pass the test suite.

The PR's stated semantics for mode 3 are: "reads (get, list): only use unified storage". `TestMode3_Get` and `TestMode3_List` never call `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "Get", ...)` / `ls.AssertNotCalled(t, "List", ...)`. The Mode1 Get test does check this for storage (`us.AssertNotCalled(...)`); the analogous assertion for mode 3 (legacy must not be called) is missing. A bug that silently falls back to legacy on reads would not be caught.

`TestMode3_Get` calls `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally even though a package-level `p` already exists (used by every other test in the file, and now exclusively by `TestMode1_Get` after this PR). The local registry is unused by the assertions in the test and just creates inconsistency. Use the package-level `p` like the rest of the suite.

`Destroy` calls `d.Storage.Destroy()` and `d.Legacy.Destroy()` immediately, but there is no synchronization with the goroutines launched by Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection. If a shutdown happens while async legacy writes are still pending (within their 10 s timeout), they will run against destroyed backends, producing confusing errors or panics. Consider tracking the goroutines with a `sync.WaitGroup` (or similar) and waiting for them in `Destroy` (with a bounded timeout).
